Surah 34 opens with ﴿Praise belongs to God, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to whom belongs praise in the Hereafter. And He is the All-Wise, the All-Aware.﴾ The surah begins with *al-Hamdu lillah* (all praise is God's) to draw attention to the fact that the surah contains, among the proofs of His unique divinity and His attributes of greatness, what calls for the making of praise to Him and for the declaration that praise is exclusively His. The phrase *al-Hamdu lillah* here may be a statement that the category of praise is due to God Most High, in which case the *lam* in *lillah* is the *lam* of ownership (*lam al-milk*). It may also be an act of praising God, in order to teach people that they should dedicate praise exclusively to Him, in which case the *lam* is the *lam* of specification (*lam al-tabyin*), because the meaning of the statement is: "I praise God."

The discussion of *al-Hamdu lillah* has already occurred in Surah al-Fatiha, and the discussion of its being followed by a relative pronoun has already occurred at the beginning of Surah al-An'am and at the beginning of Surah al-Kahf.

This is one of five surahs that open with *al-Hamdu lillah*, all of them Meccan. They have been placed in the arrangement of the Qur'an at its beginning, its middle, and the final quarter, so that the quarters of the Qur'an begin with *al-Hamdu lillah*. Whether that was by divine guidance (*tawfiq*) or by divine instruction (*tawqif*), it was from God.

The relative clause implies that what is in the heavens and the earth belongs to God Most High, which makes this clause suitable to serve as the cause (*'illa*) for the making of praise to Him, because His ownership of what is in the heavens and the earth is true ownership. Its basis is His bringing those owned things into existence, and that bringing into existence is a beautiful act which entitles its doer to praise. Furthermore, it includes abundant blessings. It also calls for praising the Benefactor, since praise is due for excellences and bounties. From what is in the heavens come the descent-places of lights, both real and figurative, in which there is guidance, both sensory and spiritual; and toward Him are the ascent-paths of souls through the levels of perfections by which the course is made upright, changes are removed, and rains of abundance descend. And from what is on the earth come the pastures of the sights of those who reflect, the sources of the sustenance of those who seek provision, and the arenas of the souls of travelers.

In this relative clause there is also an allusion to the ingratitude of the polytheists, who praised things that have no least influence in these worlds and no least awareness of what they contain, and who forgot to praise their Owner and all that is in the heavens and the earth.

The clause ﴿and to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter﴾ is coordinated with the relative clause, meaning: "and He to whom belongs praise in the Hereafter." This is an announcement that He is the owner of the whole matter in the Hereafter.

In this praise lies the excellence of opening with the purpose of the surah. The fronting of the prepositional phrase (*al-majrur*, "to Him") serves to convey restriction (*hasr*), meaning: there is no praise in the Hereafter except to Him. Thus souls do not turn toward praising anyone other than Him, because people on that day are in the world of truth, so images are not confused for them.

Know that although the statement *al-Hamdu lillah* implies restricting praise to God Most High, this restriction is figurative (*qasr majazi*), for the sake of emphasis, as has been mentioned in Surah al-Fatiha. This is based on the fact that praising other than God is done in recognition that God's blessing came through their hands. When this became common in the phrase *al-Hamdu lillah*, and it was intended to convey that praise belongs exclusively to God Most High in the Hereafter in actuality, the usual form of praise was changed to the form *lahu al-hamd* ("to Him belongs praise") for this reason. This is similar in meaning to His saying: ﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is God's, the One, the Subduer.﴾ [Ghafir: 16]. So the meaning is: restricting praise to Him in the Hereafter is more fitting, because the disposal of affairs on that day is restricted to Him, with no other's disposal mingled with His.

Since His praise in this world and the Hereafter has been tied to what requires that the return of all dispositions is to Him in both abodes, He followed that with the two attributes ﴿the All-Wise, the All-Aware﴾, because the One who brought into being the conditions of the two states of existence is the One of great wisdom, the All-Aware of the subtleties of things and their secrets. *Al-Hikma* (wisdom) is perfecting the disposal of affairs in bringing into existence and its opposite; *al-khibra* (awareness) requires knowledge of the beginnings of matters and their outcomes.

The joining of the two attributes here is because each of them indicates a primary meaning and a necessary consequential meaning, and these two are different. The primary meaning of *al-Hakim* is that He is perfect in disposal and workmanship, since *al-Hakim* is derived from *al-ihkam*, which is perfection, and this entails knowledge of the realities of things as they are. *Al-Khabir* is the One who knows the subtleties and the outward aspects of things, with priority, such that nothing of them escapes Him, and this entails the capacity to direct them. So in concluding with these two attributes there is an indication that the purpose of the sentence before it is to show the foolishness of those who, in their affairs, turned toward false gods.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 2:**

﴿He knows what enters into the earth and what comes out of it, and what descends from the sky and what ascends into it. And He is the Most Merciful, the Oft-Forgiving.﴾ This is an elaboration of the phrase ﴿And He is the All-Wise, the All-Aware﴾ [Saba': 1], because knowledge of what is mentioned here is knowledge of their essences, their properties, their causes and their reasons. That is the very essence of wisdom and expertise, for knowledge calls for action, and perfecting action comes through knowledge.

He specified, regarding the objects of knowledge, what enters the earth and what comes out of it, rather than what crawls on its surface, and what descends and what ascends to the sky, rather than what roams its expanses. This is because what is mentioned cannot be free of being something that crawls in or roams within them. He who knows what enters the earth and what comes out of it knows what crawls upon it and what creeps above it. He who knows what descends from the sky and what ascends to it knows what is in the atmosphere and the open space of creatures, visible and otherwise, and He knows the movement of the stars and their order.

Al-wulūj (entering) means to enter and to penetrate, such as the entry of rain into the depths of the earth and the entry of a seed. What comes out of the earth includes plants, minerals, and creatures that dwell in their burrows and caves. This also includes those who are buried in the earth and their conditions. What descends from the sky is rain, snow and winds. What ascends into it is what rises through the layers of the atmosphere, such as sea vapours, dust storms, and the elements that evaporate in the atmospheric layers above the earth, along with what swims in space, what flies in the air, and the ascent of souls at the moment they leave the bodies. God the Exalted said: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4].

Know that the two words (yalij, "enters") and (yakhruj, "comes out") are the clearest expressions for the states of all earthly existents with respect to their connection to the earth, and that the two words (yanzil, "descends") and (ya'ruj, "ascends") are the clearest expressions for the states of celestial existents with respect to their connection to the sky, among the words of the language that indicate the meanings laid down for them, by direct denotation (dalāla muṭābaqiyya), in their literal sense, not by figurative usage (majāz) or by metonymy (kināya). For this reason, the verse did not conjoin the sky with the earth, so it does not say: "He knows what enters into the earth and the sky, and what comes out of them both," nor did it suffice with one of the two sentences over the other. It has occurred to me that this verse should be counted among non-declarative speech (inshā'), like what is called by the term ṣarāḥat al-lafẓ (explicitness of expression). For this reason I appended it to my book Uṣūl al-Inshā' wal-Khaṭāba (The Foundations of Composition and Oratory) after its copies had been scattered in printing. A parallel to this will come in the beginning of surah al-Hadid.

Since among the states of what is on the earth are the deeds and conditions of people, including beliefs and conduct, and among what ascends to the sky is righteous action and good speech, He followed this with His saying ﴿And He is the Most Merciful, the Oft-Forgiving﴾, that is, the One of vast mercy and vast forgiveness. This is a general statement intended to urge people to seek the causes of the mercy and forgiveness that are desired, for whoever desires to obtain something searches for the means of obtaining it and strives toward them. Within it is also an allusion to the polytheists, urging them to repent of polytheism, so that He may forgive them what they have committed before.

﴿And those who disbelieve say, "The Hour will not come upon us." Say, "Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come upon you."﴾ Mentioning what enters the earth and what comes out of it implies the state of the dead as they enter their graves and as they are raised from them, as the Exalted says: ﴿Did We not make the earth a receptacle, for the living and the dead?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 25-26], and He says: ﴿the Day the earth splits open from them, swiftly. That is a gathering easy for Us﴾ [Qaf: 44]. Mentioning what descends from the sky and what ascends into it alludes to the ascent of the souls at the separation from the bodies and the descent of the souls to be returned to the bodies that will be restored on the Day of Resurrection. This, together with the earlier words ﴿And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter﴾ [Saba': 1], was a suitable occasion for the transition (al-takhallus, a smooth shift of topic) to the denial of the resurrection by the polytheists, because refuting their claim is among the most important aims of this surah. So the transition came with His words ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "The Hour will not come upon us."﴾ The waw here is parenthetical (al-waw al-i'tiradiyya), used for digression (al-istitrad). It is originally the waw of conjunction joining a parenthetical sentence to what precedes it. Since it conveys only a joining in mention without a joining in ruling, it is called the parenthetical waw. It is not here a waw of conjunction, because there is no connection of meaning between the two sentences. The connection comes only from parts of the first sentence, so the second became a digression and a parenthesis. It has already been mentioned earlier that this saying was the occasion of revelation of the surah.

The defining of the subject by the relative pronoun is because this relative (alladhina) has become like a proper name designating the polytheists, in the terminology of the Qur'an and the common usage of Muslims.

Al-Sa'a (the Hour) is a proper noun by predominance in the Qur'an for the Day of Resurrection and the hour of gathering.

He expressed the negation of its occurrence by the negation of its coming, by way of metonymy (kinaya), because if it were occurring it would have come, since its occurrence is its coming.

The pronoun of the speaker in the plural (we, "our") is meant to include all people.

God taught His Prophet (ﷺ) the answer to the words of the disbelievers with an emphatic refutation, in keeping with the Qur'an's practice of seizing opportunities to convey beliefs.

Bala (بَلى, "yes") is a particle of response specific to contradicting a negation. It is therefore a particle of affirmation for what a preceding statement negated. It is like bal (بَلْ) or composed of bal and an added alif, or it is an alif of feminine marking merely for feminizing the word, like the added tā' of feminine in thamma and rubba. But bala is a particle specific to affirming a negation, so it is not conjunctive, whereas bal is used to answer both affirmation and negation and is conjunctive. The discussion of bala was given earlier at His words ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾ [al-Baqara: 81] in Surat al-Baqara.

He reinforced what bala required, namely the affirmation of the coming of the Hour, by an oath upon it, to show the speaker's confidence that it is coming. This is not for persuading the addressees, and it is an emphasis that terrifies the listening deniers.

The coming (ityan) is made transitive to the pronoun of the addressees from among all people, rather than "it will come to us," and rather than being left without an object, because what is meant is the coming of the Hour, at which their punishment occurs. As one says, "The enemy has come upon you" and "The pursuers have come upon you," its attachment to the pronoun of the addressees is an indication that it is a metonymy for the coming of something disagreeable in which there is punishment.

The verb atā (أتى, "to come") often occurs in the sense of the descent of what is disagreeable, like ﴿The command of God has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1], ﴿So the punishment came to them﴾ [al-Zumar: 25], and ﴿The day when some of the signs of your Lord come﴾ [al-An'am: 158], and the saying of al-Nabigha:

"Verily poems shall come to you, and there shall drive toward you an army whose front ranks are the forelegs of the riding-camels."

And his saying:

"It came to me, may you not be cursed, that you blamed me."

From this usage they move to making the verb atā transitive with the preposition 'ala (على), so they say: atā 'ala kadha, meaning he destroyed it entirely. The verb jā'a (جاء) is used much more frequently in other senses, and it may also be used for what is disagreeable, like ﴿And the waves came to them from every place﴾ [Yunus: 22].

﴿Knower of the unseen; not escaping from Him is an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, nor anything smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear Record.﴾

﴿Knower of the unseen (ʿĀlim al-Ghayb)﴾ is a second predicate of the divine name in His words ﴿And He is the Wise, the All-Aware﴾ [Saba': 1], according to the reading of whoever reads it in the nominative. It is an adjective of "my Lord" (rabbī), the thing sworn by, according to the reading of whoever reads it in the genitive. The context of confirming the coming of the Hour required its mention, since its time and its circumstances are among the matters hidden from people's knowledge. In this attribute there is completion, showing the vastness of His knowledge. After the mention in Surat al-Baqara of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of existing things, apparent and hidden, great and minute, it is followed here by the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of what will be, that it will be and when it will be.

The unseen (al-ghayb) was discussed earlier at His words ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqara: 3], with meanings mentioned there.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Ruways from Ya'qub read ʿĀlimi al-ghayb (عالِمُ الغَيْبِ) in the form of the active participle, with ʿĀlimu in the nominative, by way of resumption (al-qat', breaking off into a new predicate). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Khalaf, and Rawh from Ya'qub read it also in the form of the active participle, but in the genitive, as an adjective of the divine name in His saying "my Lord."

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ʿAllāmi (عَلّامِ), in the intensive form, in the genitive as an adjective. The mention of the Hour has repeatedly been followed in the Qur'an by mention of His sole knowledge of it, because the deniers of it made lack of knowledge of it a sophistic (sufsatā'ī, specious) proof that it is not going to happen. For this reason the Qur'an named it "the Event" (al-wāqi'a) in His words ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 1], ﴿there is no denial of its occurrence﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 2].

[p. 141]

Al-ʿUzūb means concealment. Its root revolves around meanings of distance from sight. In its present tense there is both a damma and a kasra on the ʿayn. The majority read the zāy with a damma, and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra. The meaning of ﴿does not escape Him﴾ is: it does not escape His knowledge. It was mentioned in Surat Yunus: ﴿Nor does anything escape your Lord, of an atom's weight on earth or in heaven﴾ [Yunus: 61]. The "weight of a grain" was mentioned in Surat al-Anbiya': ﴿even if it were the weight of a grain of mustard seed﴾ [al-Anbiya': 47]. By His words ﴿an atom's weight﴾ He pointed to bringing closer the meaning of the possibility of resurrection, because the deniers rejected it on the ground that bodies turn to dust and earth, so their restoration is impossible. They were alerted that God's knowledge encompasses their parts.

The places of those parts in the heavens and on earth, and His knowledge of them in detail, entail the power to subject them to be gathered and joined, each to its counterpart, until bodies are reassembled from the atoms that composed them at the last moments of life, after which death came and the body ceased, through death, to acquire new parts. When the earth passes over the parts of that body and tears it into every torn piece, God is knowing of every part, since existing things do not have their atoms annihilated. So it is possible to restore new bodies that spring from the atoms of the first bodies, and their souls are breathed into them. God is powerful to subject them to gathering through forces that God creates to join the scattered, or through the subjection of angels to gather them from the farthest directions in earth, air or heaven according to their dispersion. Or some of them may be fit to split open into bodies, as a seed splits open into the root of a tree. Or through the creation of a special attraction that draws those atoms toward one another, and then forms from them its body. To this meaning points His saying: ﴿It is He who originates creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27]. Then those bodies grow quickly until they become in the forms of their origins that they had in the worldly life.

Consider His saying ﴿On the Day when the caller calls to a dreadful thing﴾ [al-Qamar: 6], ﴿with eyes humbled, they will emerge from the graves as if they were scattered locusts﴾ [al-Qamar: 7], in Surat Iqtarabat al-Sa'a, and His saying ﴿the Day when people will be like scattered moths﴾ [al-Qari'a: 4], in Surat al-Qari'a. The moth (al-farāsh) is the young of the locust, which arises from eggs like a worm, then does not remain long before it becomes a locust and flies. For this reason God named that resurrection a "creation" (nash'a), because in it there is a new origination and a renewed creation, namely the forming of those parts

[p. 142]

into the form in which they were joined at death, then the return of each body's soul to it after its formation, by what is called breathing. He said ﴿and that it is He who produces the later creation﴾ [al-Najm: 47], and He said ﴿Were We wearied by the first creation? Rather, they are in doubt about a new creation﴾ [Qaf: 15], ﴿And We have certainly created man﴾ [Qaf: 16], and the verse. That is, this resembles the creation of Adam from the dust of the earth, its shaping, and the breathing of the spirit into him. This is a convincing demonstration for the one who reflects, if they had set themselves to reflect.

By His words ﴿nor anything smaller than that or greater﴾ He pointed to what none knows but God, of the elements and the subtle forces whose parts are minute and whose effects are great, and their movements, including the spirits that dwell in bodies and the powers that God deposits in them.

**[Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 34, verses 4–5]**

﴿So that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds. For those there is forgiveness and generous provision.﴾ ﴿And those who strove against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them, for those there is a painful punishment of a grievous kind.﴾

The *lam* of causation (*lam al-ta'lil*, the "lam" of purpose) is connected to the verb *(la-ta'tiyannakum)* ("it will surely come upon you"). It does not restrict the coming to the addressees specifically. Rather, what is meant includes them and others, because the reward of those who believed has no connection to the addressees. It is as if it were said: "The Hour will surely come, so that He may reward those who believed and reward those who strove against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them." The addressees are the latter. The pronoun in *(yajziya)* ("He may reward") refers back to "the Knower of the Unseen."

The meaning is that the wisdom in bringing about the Hour, for resurrection and gathering, is the reward of the righteous for the soundness of their belief and deeds, that is, a good reward of a similar kind. The reward of the corrupters is an evil reward. The type of reward is understood from the description of the two groups mentioned in the context. The use of the demonstrative *(ulā'ika)* ("those") for each group serves to draw attention to the fact that the one indicated deserves what follows the demonstrative, because of the qualities that precede it.

Thus the sentence *﴿ulā'ika lahum maghfiratun﴾* ("for those there is forgiveness") is a independent (*ibtida'iyya*) parenthetical sentence placed between the two coordinated items.

The sentence *﴿ulā'ika lahum 'adhābun min rijzin﴾* ("for those there is a punishment of a grievous kind") is also an independent sentence.

Page 143

His saying *﴿wa-alladhīna sa'aw﴾* ("and those who strove") is coordinated with *alladhīna āmanū* ("those who believed"). The implied sense of the sentence is: "so that He may reward those who believed and those who strove, each according to what befits each group."

The meaning is that the human world contains righteous people whose righteousness varies in degree, and corrupt people whose corruption varies in degree. People have benefited from the righteousness of the righteous and have been harmed by the corruption of the corrupters. Sometimes these corrupters nullify the benefits of those righteous people, and those righteous people correct the corruption of these corrupters. Each group has passed away according to what it did. The good-doer did not receive a reward for his goodness, nor did the corrupter receive the recompense for his corruption. Therefore, the wisdom of the Creator of people required that He inform them of what He wanted from them and obligate them to strive in the earth for righteousness. It also required that He store up the reward for both groups. Thus, among its requirements was bringing both groups forward to be recompensed for their deeds. Since it has been observed that this did not occur in this life, we know that after this life there is an everlasting life accompanied by just recompense, because that is what is fitting to the wisdom of the One who guides the wise, exalted is He. This is something that sound reason indicates, and the Creator of creation has informed us of it through the tongue of His Messenger and Messengers (ﷺ). Thus reason and transmitted revelation agree, and falsehood and deception are nullified.

The reward of those who believed was made to be forgiveness, that is, their sins are overlooked, and *rizqan karīman* ("generous provision"), which is what they are given of bliss, according to the differences in their ranks in bliss and the beginning of its duration. They will surely attain forgiveness and generous provision.

It was described as *karīm* ("generous"), that is, precious in its kind, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, exalted is He, *﴿kitābun karīmun﴾* ("a noble book") [al-Naml: 29], in Surah al-Naml.

*﴿alladhīna āmanū wa-'amilū al-ṣāliḥāt﴾* ("those who believed and did righteous deeds") is contrasted with *﴿wa-alladhīna sa'aw fī āyātinā﴾* ("and those who strove against Our signs"), because striving against the signs of God is equivalent in meaning to disbelieving in them. Thus it includes the doing of evil deeds, which is one of the evil deeds. Do you not see that He afterwards described them with His saying: *﴿wa-qāla alladhīna kafarū hal nadullukum 'alā rajulin﴾* ("And those who disbelieved said: 'Shall we direct you to a man?'") [Saba': 7], etc.

The meaning of *﴿sa'aw fī āyātinā﴾* ("strove against Our signs") is that they exerted effort by turning people away from them and attempting to invalidate them. So *al-sa'y* ("striving") is used metaphorically for earnest effort in some action. Its explanation was already given earlier, at His saying, exalted is He, *﴿wa-alladhīna sa'aw fī āyātinā mu'ājizīna ulā'ika aṣḥābu al-jaḥīm﴾* ("And those who strove against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them, they are the companions of the Blazing Fire") [al-Hajj: 51], in Surah al-Hajj. The signs of God here are the Qur'an, as His subsequent saying indicates: *﴿alladhī unzila ilayka min rabbika huwa al-ḥaqq﴾* ("And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth") [Saba': 6].

Page 144

*(Mu'ājizīn)* ("seeking to frustrate") is an intensive form of *mu'jizīn*, and it is a figurative depiction (*tamthīl*): their state in their scheming against the Prophet (ﷺ) is likened to the state of one who walks swiftly in order to outpace another and frustrate him. *Al-'adhāb* ("punishment") is the punishment of Hell. *Al-rijz* ("grievous kind") is the worst of punishments, and it was explained earlier at His saying, exalted is He, *﴿fa-anzalnā 'alā alladhīna ẓalamū rijzan mina al-samā'i bimā kānū yafsuqūn﴾* ("So We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment from the sky because they were defiantly disobeying") [al-Baqarah: 59], in Surah al-Baqarah. *(Min)* ("of") is explanatory (*bayāniyya*), because the punishment itself is a *rijz*.

The majority of readers read *(mu'ājizīn)* in the form of *mufā'ala* (with the *alif*), as a figurative depiction of their state of thinking they would be saved and escape God's punishment of them, through their denial of resurrection and prophethood, in the state of one who competes with another and tries to outpace him, that is, tries to make him unable to catch up.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr alone, read it *(mu'ajjizīn)* in the form of the active participle from *'ajjaza*, with the *jim* doubled. Its meaning is: discouraging people from following the signs of God, or making those who believe in the signs of God unable [to proceed] through slander and disputation.

The majority of readers read *(alīm)* in the genitive case as an adjective of *rijz*. Ibn Kathir, Hafs, and Ya'qub read it in the nominative case as an adjective of *(adhāb)*. The two are the same in meaning.

Thus reason and transmitted revelation agree, and falsehood and deception are nullified.

The reward of those who believed was made to be forgiveness, that is, their sins are overlooked, and *rizqan karīman* ("generous provision"), which is what they are given of bliss, according to the differences in their ranks in bliss and the beginning of its duration. They will surely attain forgiveness and generous provision.

It was described as *karīm* ("generous"), that is, precious in its kind, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, exalted is He, *﴿kitābun karīmun﴾* ("a noble book") [al-Naml: 29], in Surah al-Naml.

*﴿alladhīna āmanū wa-'amilū al-ṣāliḥāt﴾* ("those who believed and did righteous deeds") is contrasted with *﴿wa-alladhīna sa'aw fī āyātinā﴾* ("and those who strove against Our signs"), because striving against the signs of God is equivalent in meaning to disbelieving in them. Thus it includes the doing of evil deeds, which is one of the evil deeds. Do you not see that He afterwards described them with His saying: *﴿wa-qāla alladhīna kafarū hal nadullukum 'alā rajulin﴾* ("And those who disbelieved said: 'Shall we direct you to a man?'") [Saba': 7], etc.

The meaning of *﴿sa'aw fī āyātinā﴾* ("strove against Our signs") is that they exerted effort by turning people away from them and attempting to invalidate them. So *al-sa'y* ("striving") is used metaphorically for earnest effort in some action. Its explanation was already given earlier, at His saying, exalted is He, *﴿wa-alladhīna sa'aw fī āyātinā mu'ājizīna ulā'ika aṣḥābu al-jaḥīm﴾* ("And those who strove against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them, they are the companions of the Blazing Fire") [al-Hajj: 51], in Surah al-Hajj. The signs of God here are the Qur'an, as His subsequent saying indicates: *﴿alladhī unzila ilayka min rabbika huwa al-ḥaqq﴾* ("And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth") [Saba': 6].

Page 144

*(Mu'ājizīn)* ("seeking to frustrate") is an intensive form of *mu'jizīn*, and it is a figurative depiction (*tamthīl*): their state in their scheming against the Prophet (ﷺ) is likened to the state of one who walks swiftly in order to outpace another and frustrate him. *Al-'adhāb* ("punishment") is the punishment of Hell. *Al-rijz* ("grievous kind") is the worst of punishments, and it was explained earlier at His saying, exalted is He, *﴿fa-anzalnā 'alā alladhīna ẓalamū rijzan mina al-samā'i bimā kānū yafsuqūn﴾* ("So We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment from the sky because they were defiantly disobeying") [al-Baqarah: 59], in Surah al-Baqarah. *(Min)* ("of") is explanatory (*bayāniyya*), because the punishment itself is a *rijz*.

The majority of readers read *(mu'ājizīn)* in the form of *mufā'ala* (with the *alif*), as a figurative depiction of their state of thinking they would be saved and escape God's punishment of them, through their denial of resurrection and prophethood, in the state of one who competes with another and tries to outpace him, that is, tries to make him unable to catch up.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr alone, read it *(mu'ajjizīn)* in the form of the active participle from *'ajjaza*, with the *jim* doubled. Its meaning is: discouraging people from following the signs of God, or making those who believe in the signs of God unable [to proceed] through slander and disputation.

The majority of readers read *(alīm)* in the genitive case as an adjective of *rijz*. Ibn Kathir, Hafs, and Ya'qub read it in the nominative case as an adjective of *(adhāb)*. The two are the same in meaning.

[Page 145]

﴿And those who have been given knowledge see that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, and it guides to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) with ﴿so that He may reward those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [Saba': 4]. It is the counterpart of the reward of those who believe and do righteous deeds. Therefore, by ﴿those who strove against Our signs﴾ is meant those who disbelieved. He departed from making the relative pronoun's referent "those who disbelieved" so that the sentence could serve as a preparation for refuting the statement of the polytheists about the Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿Has he invented a lie against God, or is there madness in him?﴾ [Saba': 8]. Their saying that is a metaphor (kināya) for the falsity of what he brought them of the Qur'an, in their claim. So it was fitting that it be prepared for refuting it by the testimony of the people of knowledge that what the Messenger brought is the truth, unlike the falsehood of the ignorant polytheists. Thus the conjunction of this sentence is a conjunction of purposes (ʿatf al-aghrāḍ). This is a method of refuting the doubts of the misguided and the heretics: one presents before mentioning the doubts what opposes them in refutation of them. Perhaps the people of disputation (ahl al-jadal) followed another method, which is to present the doubts and then to attack them with refutation. This is the method of ʿAḍud al-Dīn in the book al-Mawāqif. Some of our shaykhs used to relate the criticism of many people of knowledge of his method, and for this reason al-Taftazānī opposed it in his book al-Maqāṣid.

The truth is that both methods are valid, and both have been followed in the Qur'an.

It is also possible that the sentence ﴿and those who have been given knowledge see﴾ is a conjunction with the sentence ﴿and those who strove against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them﴾ [Saba': 5]. After the sentence ﴿and those who strove﴾ [Saba': 5] was introduced to correspond to the sentence ﴿so that He may reward those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [Saba': 4], etc., it was regarded as intended from another aspect. So it needed to have its content answered by the sentence ﴿and those who have been given knowledge see﴾, to indicate that those who strove against the signs are people of ignorance. Its mention after it is therefore a follow-up to the doubt with what refutes it, which is the other method.

The seeing here is intellectual (ʿilmiyya). The verb "see" was chosen here instead of "know" (yaʿlamu) to point out that it is a certain knowledge, of the same standing as knowledge of visible things whose knowledge is necessary. The two objects of "see" are ﴿what has been sent down﴾ and ﴿the truth﴾. The pronoun "huwa" (he/it) is a separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl) that conveys restriction of the truth to the Qur'an in a relative restriction (ḥaṣr idāfī), meaning not what the polytheists say, which they use to oppose the Qur'an. It may also convey an absolute restriction in a claimed sense (qaṣr ḥaqīqī idʿāʾī), meaning that truthfulness is confined to it in its pure form, because the truth of other books has been mixed with falsehood.

As for ﴿those who have been given knowledge﴾, some exegetes (mufassirūn, Qur'an commentators) interpreted it as the scholars of the People of the Book among the Jews and Christians. In that case this is a report about what is in their hearts, as in His saying, exalted is He, concerning the monks: ﴿And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they recognise﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 83]. This is then a challenge to the polytheists and a consolation to the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers. It is not an argument based on their silence against it in the early days of Islam, before the Prophet (ﷺ) invited them and argued against them with the good tidings of their messengers and prophets concerning him. Then most of them obstinately opposed it, following their common people.

By this you will see that the intention of the scholars of the People of the Book from this verse does not require that it was revealed at Medina, so that those who imagined that this verse is an exception from the Meccan verses of the sūrah would have that imagination, as has preceded.

The more evident view is that by ﴿those who have been given knowledge﴾ is meant those among the people of Mecca who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), because they were given the Qur'an. In it is a great knowledge, of which they are the knowers, despite their differing levels in understanding it and deriving rulings from it. The man from Mecca would be harsh and coarse, until when he embraced Islam his heart softened, his breast filled with wisdom, he was expanded to the laws of Islam, and he was guided to the truth and to the straight path. The first and most famous and most excellent example of these was ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, given the great distance between his two states in the Jāhiliyya and Islam. This is what the saying of Abū Khirāsh al-Hudhalī expressed, mixing seriousness with jest:

"The young man returned like a grown man, saying nothing but justice,
and the blamers rested."

When they met the Prophet (ﷺ), the lights of prophethood shone upon them and filled them with wisdom and piety. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to one of his companions: "If you were in your houses as you are with me, the angels would shake hands with you with their wings." By this virtue they governed the community, conquered kingdoms, established justice among people, Muslim and protected (dhimmī) and treaty-bound alike, and filled the eyes of the kings of the earth with awe. On this interpretation ﴿those who have been given knowledge﴾ in the sūrah of al-Ḥajj is understood, and it is supported by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And those who have been given knowledge and faith said﴾ [al-Rūm: 56] in the sūrah of al-Rūm.

The sentence ﴿and it guides to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾ stands in the position of a conjunction with the second object of "see". The meaning: they see that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, guiding to the Mighty, the Praiseworthy. This is a conjunction of a verb with a noun in which lies the root of derivation, which is "the truth", since the verbal noun is in the force of a verb, because it is either derived or is the origin of derivation. The shift from the descriptive to the present-tense verb form is to imply the renewal and recurrence of guidance. The choice of the two attributes ﴿the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾ here, rather than the rest of the Most Beautiful Names, is an allusion to the fact that the rest of the believers, when they believe that the Qur'an is the truth and guidance, sense from faith that it is a path by which they reach honour, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Honour belongs to God, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn: 8]; and it reaches praiseworthiness, that is, the qualities that make one deserving of praise, which are perfections of virtues and bounties.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verses 7–8 (part 1 of 2):

[p. 147]
﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you that when you have been completely torn apart, you will indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ ﴿Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?" Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in punishment and far-off error.﴾

This is a transition to another statement from the ugliness of the polytheists, joined by conjunction to ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "The Hour will not come upon us"﴾ [Saba destination: 3]. This statement serves as evidence for the first statement, because their saying "The Hour will not come upon us" is a claim, and their saying ﴿Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you that when you have been completely torn apart, you will indeed be in a new creation?﴾ is the basis of that claim. For this reason it is related in the same style in which the claim was related, in the predicate and the predicated subject.

They have also incorporated into the argument an expression of wonder at the one who brings the opposite of their proof, then followed that wonder with a disparagement of the one they wonder at.

The addressee of their saying "Shall we direct you" is not mentioned, because the purpose of the verse is to draw attention to the ugliness of the statement, and there is no aim concerning those to whom it is said. So it may be that this saying was a mutual talk among them, or that some of them said it to others, or that their leaders said it to their common people and masses. It may also be that it was the saying of the Meccan unbelievers to those who came to them during the season (of pilgrimage). This is what the verb "we direct you" (nadullukum) indicates, namely that it is addressed to those who had not yet heard the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The interrogation is used in the sense of offering (al-'ard), like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So say: "Would you like to purify yourself?"﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18], and it is an offer used as a metaphorical expression of wonder, meaning: "Shall we direct you to a marvel of a man who will tell you this impossible news?"

The meaning is: you would hear from him what we have heard from him, and thereby you would recognise our excuse for opposing him with enmity. The polytheists had prepared an answer for the tribal delegations arriving among them during the season who would ask about the news of this one who had appeared among them, claiming that he is a messenger of Allah to mankind, and about the revelation he conveys from Allah. This is as reported in the account of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, when he said to Quraysh: "This season has come, and the delegations of the Arabs will come to you in it, and they have heard about the affair of your companion. So agree upon one opinion concerning him, and do not differ, lest some of you contradict others and your statements refute one another." They said: "So you, O Abu 'Abd Shams, say and establish for us an opinion which we may adopt." He said:

[p. 148]
"Rather, you say, and I will listen." They said: "We say he is a soothsayer (kahin)?" He said: "No, by Allah, he is not a soothsayer. We have seen soothsayers, and he is not like the murmuring of the soothsayer nor his rhymed prose." They said: "Then we say he is possessed?" He said: "He is not possessed. We have seen possession and known it, and he is not like its choking, its convulsion, or its whispering." They said: "Then we say he is a poet?" He said: "We have known all poetry, and he is not poetry." They said: "Then we say he is a sorcerer?" He said: "He is not like its spitting or its knotting." They said: "What then shall we say, O Abu 'Abd Shams?" He said: "The closest saying about him is that you say: he is a sorcerer; he has brought a speech which is sorcery, which separates a man from his father, a man from his brother, a man from his wife, and a man from his clan."

Perhaps the polytheists used to receive those arriving at Mecca with this saying: ﴿Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you that when you have been completely torn apart, you will indeed be in a new creation?﴾, hoping that it would turn people away from considering the call, by giving the impression of the impossibility of this new creation.

This is supported by the conclusion of the statement with the interrogation ﴿Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?﴾

Then, if the speaking was among the polytheists themselves, the expression of the Messenger (ﷺ) as "a man" (rajul) in indefinite form, despite his being known among them and among the people of their city, is because they intended by its indefiniteness that he is not recognised, out of feigned ignorance. Al-Sakkaki said: "It is as if they did not know of him anything beyond that he is a certain man."

And if the saying of the polytheists was addressed to those coming to Mecca during the season, then the expression "a man" follows what the context requires, because the arrivals do not know the Prophet (ﷺ) or his call. It is like the saying of Abu Dharr before his conversion to his brother: "Go and find out for us the news of this man who claims to be a prophet." The meaning of "we direct you" (nadullukum) is "we inform you and guide you." The original sense of dalalah (guidance) is guiding to the road that leads to a sought place. The usual use of this verb is guiding one who seeks knowledge. Accordingly, the verse indicates that this saying was said to those who asked them about the news of a man who had appeared among them claiming prophethood, and so they say: "Shall we direct you to a man who claims such-and-such", i.e., he is not a prophet but rather a fabricator or a madman. So the object of the interrogation is what is contained in their saying ("when you have been completely torn apart, you will indeed be in a new creation" and "Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?"), that is, do you

[p. 149]
want us to direct you to one whose description is this, meaning: and it is not among his attributes that he is a prophet; rather he is either a liar or someone without reason.

Al-naba' (the news/announcement) is informing about a great matter, and the greatness of this saying in their view is the greatness of the boldness of its speaker in claiming the occurrence of what they see as impossible to occur.

The clause ﴿you will indeed be in a new creation﴾ is the thing announced. Since al-inba' (announcing) has the sense of saying, because it is informing, it is correct that what follows it be from the speech of the announcer. So the grammatical estimate in terms of meaning is: he says, "you will indeed be in a new creation." For this reason the emphatic "inna" with a kasra on the hamza was used rather than the one with a fatha, in observance of the reporting of speech.

This is a report of what he announced, because the announcer only announced that people would be in a new creation.

As for the prepositional phrase, namely His saying ﴿when you have been completely torn apart﴾, it is not part of what the man announced; rather it is an interjection in the speech of those relating, to draw attention to the impossibility of what this man says, on the basis that it entails the new creation for all the dead. "Idha" (when) does not function here as a conditional establishing that the new creation is conditioned by it, because it is not necessary for the new creation to be preceded by decay; rather what is meant is that decay would be an obstacle to the new creation announced.

The placing of this interjection first is for the sake of emphasis on it, so that it may be fixed in the minds of the listeners, because it is the basis of the impossibility in their claim. The restoration of life to the dead occurs after the non-existence of the parts of bodies, and after their scattering into a state near to non-existence, and after some dispersal, and while the bodies remain in their state with varying hardness and moisture. They denied the restoration of life in all these circumstances, but in their speech they specified the restoration as after being torn apart completely, i.e., after the bodies have dissolved or been severely scattered, because of the greater strength of the impossibility of returning life to them after that.

Tamzeeq (tearing apart) is the separation of tightly joined parts from one another so that they become distant pieces.

Al-mumazzaq is a mimi (noun of place/manner) verbal noun from mazzaqahu, like al-musarrah for tasrih (sending free).

And "kull" (every) in both respects is used in the sense of multiplicity, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And even if every sign came to them﴾ [Yunus: 97], and the saying of al-Nabighah:

[p. 150]
"by them is every ... "

This has been mentioned more than once before.

Al-khalq al-jadid (the new creation): that which is recently come into existence, i.e., in a creation other than the first creation which time has worn out. Jadid is on the pattern fa'il from jadda, meaning "cut." The original meaning of jadid is "cut," and it was originally an attribute of the cloth which the weaver weaves; when he finishes it he cuts it from the loom. It was meant that by the recency of its cutting it became a metaphor for its not having been worn, then this spread so that jadid became an attribute meaning "recent," and the passive sense was forgotten, so it became an attribute with an active meaning. One says: "the cloth became new with patches," meaning: it was recently woven. It is likely that jadda intransitive is the intransitive counterpart (mutawi') of jaddahu transitive, just as jabara al-'azm (the bone was set) was the intransitive counterpart of jabara, as in the saying of al-'Ajjaj:

"Allah has restored the religion, so it was restored."

By this, the combination is justified between the view of the Basrans, who regarded jadid as fa'il in the sense of fa'il, and the view of the Kufans, that it is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul. On these two considerations it may be said: "a jadid garment," as He said, ﴿Indeed the mercy of Allah is near﴾ [al-A'raf: 56].

The description of the new creation as jadid, on account of the fact that the verbal noun functions like a generic noun, would be "old" (qadim); so it means "that which is obtained by the verbal noun." And it would be jadid, in which case it is like the active participle, so it is described as jadid to make it definitively one of its two possibilities. The adverbial sense in His saying ﴿in a new creation﴾ is figurative, in the sense of being strongly involved with the new creation, a involvement like that of the contained in the container.

The clause ﴿Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?﴾ is in the position of a second description of "a man." They brought it in interrogative form in order to associate the addressees with them in oscillating the man between these two states.

The hamza of the verb "aftara" was dropped, because it is a hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamza), and it falls away because the interrogative hamza was joined to the verb, so the connecting hamza drops in continuous speech.

They made the Messenger's (ﷺ) condition revolve between lying and madness, on the basis that if what he said about resurrection was said by him deliberately and with sound reason, then in their view he is a fabricator, because they claim that it does not correspond to reality, since it is impossible in their limited view. And if he said it with his tongue while his reason was disordered, then he is mad, and the speech of a madman is not described as fabrication. They only divided his condition between the two matters on the basis that he reported receiving revelation from Allah, so no third possibility remained, namely that he be mistaken or erring, as is not hidden.

Al-Jahiz used this verse as evidence for his view that Arabs describe speech as truthful if it corresponds to reality together with the speaker's belief in it, and as false if it does not correspond to reality nor to belief. Whatever is other than these two kinds is described neither as truthful nor false, but is an intermediate state between them: it is that which contradicts reality yet agrees with the speaker's belief, or contradicts belief while matching reality, or contradicts both, or the speaker has no belief at all. Of this last kind is the speech of a madman.

It is not valid that this verse be evidence for him, because it relates the speech of the polytheists in a context of their obfuscation and error or their misleading; so it is sophistry. Furthermore, fabrication (iftira') is more specific than lying (kadhib), because fabrication, if it is deliberate, its contrast with madness does not imply that the speech of a madman is not lying; rather, it is simply not fabrication.

Al-iftira' is inventing and producing a report that has no informant. It was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 103] in Surat al-'Uqud.

Allah has refuted their argument by indicating that they are astray or misleading, and deluded or deluding, so He nullified their claim entirely with the particle of retraction (bal), then with the clause ﴿Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in punishment and far-off error.﴾ He matched what they attributed to the Messenger (ﷺ) with two descriptions: that they are in punishment, which corresponds to their saying "Has he invented a lie against Allah," because one who lies against Allah has His punishment imposed upon him; and that they are in far-off error, which corresponds to their saying "or is there madness in him?"

He turned away from saying "Rather, you are in punishment and error" to "those who do not believe in the Hereafter," as an incorporation of their threat.

Dalal (error) is the deviation from the road leading to the intended goal. "Far-off" (ba'id) is described of error

[p. 152]
on account of its being an attribute of the road of the one who has gone astray, so the attribution of the description to error is metaphorical, because it is the attribute of the place of error, namely the road which swerved from the intended place; for the one who is astray, the further he goes along the misleading road, the more distant he becomes from the intended goal, so his error becomes severe and his escape difficult. This, in addition, is a supporting element (tarshih) for the metaphorical attribution.

His saying ﴿in the punishment﴾ is an incorporation by which their state in the Hereafter is described together with the description of their state in this world.

In the sense of preparation for them, so two figurative usages arise in the particle of location: the torment and the misguidance are treated as though they both occurred together, because of their mutual necessity, so this is the use of what is designated for the actual occurrence in what has not yet occurred, as an alert to the certainty of its occurrence.

And if the saying of the polytheists was addressed to those coming to Mecca during the season, then the expression "a man" follows what the context requires, because the arrivals do not know the Prophet (ﷺ) or his call. It is like the saying of Abu Dharr before his conversion to his brother: "Go and find out for us the news of this man who claims to be a prophet." The meaning of "we direct you" (nadullukum) is "we inform you and guide you." The original sense of dalalah (guidance) is guiding to the road that leads to a sought place. The usual use of this verb is guiding one who seeks knowledge. Accordingly, the verse indicates that this saying was said to those who asked them about the news of a man who had appeared among them claiming prophethood, and so they say: "Shall we direct you to a man who claims such-and-such", i.e., he is not a prophet but rather a fabricator or a madman. So the object of the interrogation is what is contained in their saying ("when you have been completely torn apart, you will indeed be in a new creation" and "Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?"), that is, do you

[p. 149]
want us to direct you to one whose description is this, meaning: and it is not among his attributes that he is a prophet; rather he is either a liar or someone without reason.

Al-naba' (the news/announcement) is informing about a great matter, and the greatness of this saying in their view is the greatness of the boldness of its speaker in claiming the occurrence of what they see as impossible to occur.

The clause ﴿you will indeed be in a new creation﴾ is the thing announced. Since al-inba' (announcing) has the sense of saying, because it is informing, it is correct that what follows it be from the speech of the announcer. So the grammatical estimate in terms of meaning is: he says, "you will indeed be in a new creation." For this reason the emphatic "inna" with a kasra on the hamza was used rather than the one with a fatha, in observance of the reporting of speech.

This is a report of what he announced, because the announcer only announced that people would be in a new creation.

As for the prepositional phrase, namely His saying ﴿when you have been completely torn apart﴾, it is not part of what the man announced; rather it is an interjection in the speech of those relating, to draw attention to the impossibility of what this man says, on the basis that it entails the new creation for all the dead. "Idha" (when) does not function here as a conditional establishing that the new creation is conditioned by it, because it is not necessary for the new creation to be preceded by decay; rather what is meant is that decay would be an obstacle to the new creation announced.

The placing of this interjection first is for the sake of emphasis on it, so that it may be fixed in the minds of the listeners, because it is the basis of the impossibility in their claim. The restoration of life to the dead occurs after the non-existence of the parts of bodies, and after their scattering into a state near to non-existence, and after some dispersal, and while the bodies remain in their state with varying hardness and moisture. They denied the restoration of life in all these circumstances, but in their speech they specified the restoration as after being torn apart completely, i.e., after the bodies have dissolved or been severely scattered, because of the greater strength of the impossibility of returning life to them after that.

Tamzeeq (tearing apart) is the separation of tightly joined parts from one another so that they become distant pieces.

Al-mumazzaq is a mimi (noun of place/manner) verbal noun from mazzaqahu, like al-musarrah for tasrih (sending free).

And "kull" (every) in both respects is used in the sense of multiplicity, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And even if every sign came to them﴾ [Yunus: 97], and the saying of al-Nabighah:

[p. 150]
"by them is every ... "

This has been mentioned more than once before.

Al-khalq al-jadid (the new creation): that which is recently come into existence, i.e., in a creation other than the first creation which time has worn out. Jadid is on the pattern fa'il from jadda, meaning "cut." The original meaning of jadid is "cut," and it was originally an attribute of the cloth which the weaver weaves; when he finishes it he cuts it from the loom. It was meant that by the recency of its cutting it became a metaphor for its not having been worn, then this spread so that jadid became an attribute meaning "recent," and the passive sense was forgotten, so it became an attribute with an active meaning. One says: "the cloth became new with patches," meaning: it was recently woven. It is likely that jadda intransitive is the intransitive counterpart (mutawi') of jaddahu transitive, just as jabara al-'azm (the bone was set) was the intransitive counterpart of jabara, as in the saying of al-'Ajjaj:

"Allah has restored the religion, so it was restored."

By this, the combination is justified between the view of the Basrans, who regarded jadid as fa'il in the sense of fa'il, and the view of the Kufans, that it is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul. On these two considerations it may be said: "a jadid garment," as He said, ﴿Indeed the mercy of Allah is near﴾ [al-A'raf: 56].

The description of the new creation as jadid, on account of the fact that the verbal noun functions like a generic noun, would be "old" (qadim); so it means "that which is obtained by the verbal noun." And it would be jadid, in which case it is like the active participle, so it is described as jadid to make it definitively one of its two possibilities. The adverbial sense in His saying ﴿in a new creation﴾ is figurative, in the sense of being strongly involved with the new creation, a involvement like that of the contained in the container.

The clause ﴿Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?﴾ is in the position of a second description of "a man." They brought it in interrogative form in order to associate the addressees with them in oscillating the man between these two states.

The hamza of the verb "aftara" was dropped, because it is a hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamza), and it falls away because the interrogative hamza was joined to the verb, so the connecting hamza drops in continuous speech.

They made the Messenger's (ﷺ) condition revolve between lying and madness, on the basis that if what he said about resurrection was said by him deliberately and with sound reason, then in their view he is a fabricator, because they claim that it does not correspond to reality, since it is impossible in their limited view. And if he said it with his tongue while his reason was disordered, then he is mad, and the speech of a madman is not described as fabrication. They only divided his condition between the two matters on the basis that he reported receiving revelation from Allah, so no third possibility remained, namely that he be mistaken or erring, as is not hidden.

Al-Jahiz used this verse as evidence for his view that Arabs describe speech as truthful if it corresponds to reality together with the speaker's belief in it, and as false if it does not correspond to reality nor to belief. Whatever is other than these two kinds is described neither as truthful nor false, but is an intermediate state between them: it is that which contradicts reality yet agrees with the speaker's belief, or contradicts belief while matching reality, or contradicts both, or the speaker has no belief at all. Of this last kind is the speech of a madman.

It is not valid that this verse be evidence for him, because it relates the speech of the polytheists in a context of their obfuscation and error or their misleading; so it is sophistry. Furthermore, fabrication (iftira') is more specific than lying (kadhib), because fabrication, if it is deliberate, its contrast with madness does not imply that the speech of a madman is not lying; rather, it is simply not fabrication.

Al-iftira' is inventing and producing a report that has no informant. It was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 103] in Surat al-'Uqud.

Allah has refuted their argument by indicating that they are astray or misleading, and deluded or deluding, so He nullified their claim entirely with the particle of retraction (bal), then with the clause ﴿Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in punishment and far-off error.﴾ He matched what they attributed to the Messenger (ﷺ) with two descriptions: that they are in punishment, which corresponds to their saying "Has he invented a lie against Allah," because one who lies against Allah has His punishment imposed upon him; and that they are in far-off error, which corresponds to their saying "or is there madness in him?"

He turned away from saying "Rather, you are in punishment and error" to "those who do not believe in the Hereafter," as an incorporation of their threat.

Dalal (error) is the deviation from the road leading to the intended goal. "Far-off" (ba'id) is described of error

[p. 152]
on account of its being an attribute of the road of the one who has gone astray, so the attribution of the description to error is metaphorical, because it is the attribute of the place of error, namely the road which swerved from the intended place; for the one who is astray, the further he goes along the misleading road, the more distant he becomes from the intended goal, so his error becomes severe and his escape difficult. This, in addition, is a supporting element (tarshih) for the metaphorical attribution.

His saying ﴿in the punishment﴾ is an incorporation by which their state in the Hereafter is described together with the description of their state in this world.

In the sense of preparation for them, so two figurative usages arise in the particle of location: the torment and the misguidance are treated as though they both occurred together, because of their mutual necessity, so this is the use of what is designated for the actual occurrence in what has not yet occurred, as an alert to the certainty of its occurrence.

The fa' here introduces what follows as a consequence of His saying, ﴿Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in punishment﴾ [Saba': 8], etc., because seeing the creatures of God in the heavens and the earth is, by its nature, something that would guide them if they reflected upon it as they should.

The interrogative is one of wonder mixed with rebuke for their failure to reflect on what is before them and behind them of the heavens and the earth, that is, the great creatures that show that the One who was able to create those creatures from nothing is able to re-create man after he has become nothing.

The seeing is visual, as indicated by its being followed by (ila, "to"). The question about the negation of this seeing on their part means the negation of its effects, namely drawing inference from the states of the heavenly and earthly beings to the possibility of resurrection. So the existence of seeing is likened to its non-existence, and the particle of negation is borrowed for it (istiʿarah). The purpose is to urge them to contemplate and reflect, so that they may make up for the knowledge they have neglected. This is like His saying, ﴿Have they not reflected within themselves? God did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth and for a specified term. Indeed, many of mankind are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾ [Rum: 8].

Page 153

By (what is before them) is meant what each of them faces of the heavenly and earthly beings, and by (what is behind them) is meant what lies behind each of them of these beings. For if they willed, they could look at it by turning to what is behind them. This is like looking at the northern half of the celestial sphere at night and then looking at its southern half, whereupon they would see shining stars, some rising from their place of rising and some descending toward their place of setting, and a moon of varying shapes according to the days; and in the daytime, by looking at the sun rising and setting, along with what accompanies that of brightness, evening and twilight. Likewise is looking at the mountains of the earth, its seas, its valleys, and what is upon them of kinds of animals and the variety of their species.

The (min) in His saying (min al-samaʾ wa al-ard) is partitive (tabʿidiyyah).

The (heaven) and (earth) are used to denote what they contain, just as (the town) is used for its people in His saying, ﴿and ask the town﴾.

The clause ﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) of threat. So the connection of the rebuking wonder is with what reminds them of the power of the Maker of those great created things to punish those who associated others with Him, and who restricted the vastness of His power and denied His Messenger ﷺ. It comes to their minds to mention the peoples who were struck by punishment by means of something from the terrestrial beings, such as the swallowing up, or from the celestial beings, such as the falling of fragments from celestial bodies, like what befell Qarun of the swallowing up and what befell the people of al-Aykah of the falling of fragments.

Al-Kisa'i alone read (nakhsibbihim), with the assimilation of the fa' into the ba'. Abu ʿAli said: "This is not permissible, because the ba' is weaker in sound than the fa', so the fa' is not assimilated into the ba'. Although the ba' is assimilated into the fa', as in your saying, idrib fulanan (strike so-and-so), this is like the ba' being assimilated into the mim, as in your saying, idrib malikan, but the mim is not assimilated into the ba', as in your saying, idmum bakran, because the ba' falls short of the mim by the loss of the nasalization (ghunnah) that is in the mim." This is a rejection of a transmitted reading by analogy, and that is usurpation.

Al-Kisf, with a kasrah on the kaf and a sukun on the sin in the reading of the majority, is a piece of a thing.

Page 154

It has already been mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿or you cause the heaven to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed﴾ [al-Isra': 92], in Surat al-Isra'.

The majority read (nakhsif) and (nusqit) with the nun of majesty (nun al-ʿaẓamah). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read them with the ya' of the third-person absent, by way of iltifat (shift) from the station of speaking to the station of absence. The referents of the two pronouns are known from the context of the discourse. The clause ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for every servant who turns back in repentance﴾ is a cause-giving explanation (taʿlil) of the rebuking wonder, in view of what it contains of urging contemplation and reflection, as has been stated just before. So the position of the emphasizing particle here is merely for the sake of explanation, like the saying of Bashshar:

Indeed that success lies in early rising

It is also possible to make the clause a concluding summation (tadhyil). The one referred to is what is before them and behind them of the heavens and the earth, that is, of the creatures in them.

The (ayah) is the proof. The definiteness is generic, so the singular definite is equivalent to the plural, that is, many signs. The (munib) is one who returns with his thought to investigating what contains his soul's perfection and the goodness of his final destination in the Hereafter. He appraises admonitions at their true worth and receives them with doubt about the condition for which he was admonished, so he repeats his looking until he is guided, and does not reject the counsel of advisers and the guidance of guides, wrapping himself in the cloak of the arrogant. Thus he does not fail to look at the signs of God's power, and among the greatest of those who turn back in repentance are the believers together with their Messenger.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verses 10–11:

﴿And We certainly bestowed upon Dawud (David) grace from Us: "O mountains, echo the praises with him, and the birds." And We made iron pliable for him,﴾ ﴿"Make full coats of mail and measure well the links, and work righteousness. Indeed, I am Seeing of what you do."﴾ The connection of transition from the preceding discourse to the mention of Dawud is hidden. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Allah mentioned His blessing upon Dawud and Sulayman as an argument for what He granted Muhammad, meaning: do not consider this improbable, for We have indeed favoured Our servants before.

Page 155
Al-Zamakhshari, on the verse ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for every servant who turns back (in repentance)﴾ [Saba: 9], said: because the one who turns back does not fail to reflect on the signs of Allah, that He is capable of everything, including the resurrection and the punishment of those who disbelieve in it. End quote. Al-Tibi said: In it is an indication toward explaining the arrangement of this verse with His saying ﴿And We certainly bestowed upon Dawud grace from Us﴾; for it serves as a transition (takhallus) from it to that, because he is among those who turn back, the ones who reflect on the signs of Allah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength; indeed, he was one who often turned back (to Allah)﴾ [Sad: 17]. End quote. Al-Tibi means that Dawud is among the most famous examples of those who turn back, through what he was known for: the transformation of his condition after having been a rough shepherd, until Allah chose him as a prophet and a righteous king reforming a great nation. He is thus the model of those who turn back, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength; indeed, he was one who often turned back﴾ [Sad: 17], and He said: ﴿So he asked forgiveness of his Lord and fell down bowing and turned in repentance﴾ [Sad: 24]. Because of his turning back and his returning, Allah bestowed upon him the blessings of this world and the Hereafter, and blessed him and blessed his offspring. In mentioning his grace there is a lesson for people regarding the good care of Allah for those who turn back, with an implicit contrast to those who did not take heed of the signs of Allah. In this there is also an allusion to the good tidings to the Prophet ﷺ that after the denial of his people and the straitness of his condition from them, his affair would end in great honour and the establishment of the rule of a great nation, just as the condition of Dawud ended. This allusion is clearer in His saying ﴿Be patient over what they say and remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength; indeed, he was one who often turned back﴾ [Sad: 17], in Surah Sad. Al-Tibi named this transition to the mention of Dawud and Sulayman a takhallus, but the proper term is istitrad or i'tiraD (digression), even if it is lengthy, since the return to the mention of the states of the polytheists after the story of Dawud, Sulayman and Saba' indicates that refuting the condition of the people of polytheism is the aim of this surah, as we shall point out at His saying ﴿And Iblis had already confirmed his assumption about them﴾ [Saba: 20].

Dawud, peace be upon him, was introduced at His saying ﴿And We gave Dawud a Zabur﴾ [al-Nisa': 163] in Surah al-Nisa', and at His saying ﴿and of his descendants, Dawud﴾ [al-An'am: 84] in Surah al-An'am.

The "min" in His saying "minna" (from Us) is for origin, connected to "ataynā" (We gave), meaning: from Our presence and from Our side, and this is an honouring of the grace that Dawud was given, like His saying ﴿a provision from Our presence﴾. The indefiniteness of "fadlan" (grace) is for magnifying it: it is the grace of prophethood, the grace of kingship, the grace of care for the reform of the nation, the grace of judging with justice, the grace of courage in war, the grace of abundant blessing upon him, the grace of making him self-sufficient from people through what he was inspired to make of coats of mail, the grace of giving him the Zabur, giving him a beautiful voice, long life in righteousness, and other than that.

Page 156
The clause ﴿O mountains, echo the praises with him﴾ is the object of an omitted verb of saying, and omitting the verb of saying is a common usage; the omitted verb of saying with its clause is a resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani) explaining the clause ﴿We gave Dawud grace from Us﴾.

In this style in which the verse is composed there is grandeur, the majesty of the Creator, the great status of Dawud, abundance of meanings, brevity of expression, and the conveying of the meaning of accompaniment by the waw, rather than had it been a conjunction particle.

The imperative in "awwibī ma'ahu" (echo with him) is an imperative of creation and subjection.

Al-ta'wib means tarjī' (modulating the voice). It was said that al-ta'wib in the sense of tasbih (glorification) is a Ethiopian word, so it is among the words arabicized into the Arabic language. The mention of the mountains glorifying with Dawud has already been mentioned in Surah al-Anbiya'.

"Al-ṭayr" (the birds) is in the accusative by coordination with the vocative, because a definite conjoined noun after a vocative may be in the accusative or the nominative, and the accusative is preferred according to Yunus, Abu 'Amr, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, and al-Jarmi, and it is more apt. It is also permitted that "wal-ṭayr" be an object of accompaniment for "awwibī", the meaning being: echo with him and with the birds, which indicates that the birds also echoed with him.

The softening of iron: its subjection to his fingers when he bends the rings of coats of mail and presses the rivets.

"An" (that) is explanatory for what is in "alanā lahu" (We made pliable for him), in the sense of: We made him aware of the subjection of iron so that he would proceed to its working; thus in "alanā" there is the meaning of: We inspired to him: "Make full coats of mail."

Iron: a metallic earth which, when smelted by fire, its parts merge together and become soft and can be hammered and shaped; when it cools, it hardens. It was mentioned at His saying ﴿Say: be stones or iron﴾ [al-Isra': 50] in Surah al-Isra'.

"Sabighat" (full) is an adjective of an omitted noun, its being evident from the context, since the description of coats of mail as "sabighat" and "sawabigh" became widespread, so that when this description is mentioned they dispense with mentioning the described noun.

Page 157
The meaning of "qaddir" is: make it according to a measure, and "taqdir" is making a thing according to a specific quantity.

"Al-sard" is the making of a coat of mail, i.e., the assembling of its rings and its rivets that bind the plates of the mail to one another like the stitching of a garment. A coat of mail is described as "masrudah" just as it is described as "sabighah." Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali said:

And upon them two are masrudah coats, which Dawud judged or made, and the sabigh of Tubba'

And the maker of coats of mail is called "sarrad," with the sin and the zay. Al-Ma'arri, describing a coat of mail, said:

And Dawud, smith of the full coats, dragged them, and that is a mould which the man Tubba' preserved

Since Allah subjected to him what was difficult for others, He followed it with His command to thank Him by doing righteousness, because thanks is given by action that pleases the one thanked, the Benefactor.

The pronoun in "i'malu" (work) is for Dawud and his family, like His saying ﴿Enjoin your family to prayer and be steadfast in it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 132], or for him alone as a form of honour.

His saying "Indeed, I am Seeing of what you do" — the placement of "inna" here is in the position of the fa' of causation, like the saying of Bashshar:

Indeed, that success is in early rising

And this has been mentioned more than once.

"Al-baṣīr" means the one who is aware and knowing, and here it is a metonymy for the recompense for righteous action.
