And upon them two are masrudah coats, which Dawud judged or made, and the sabigh of Tubba'

And the maker of coats of mail is called "sarrad," with the sin and the zay. Al-Ma'arri, describing a coat of mail, said:

And Dawud, smith of the full coats, dragged them, and that is a mould which the man Tubba' preserved

Since Allah subjected to him what was difficult for others, He followed it with His command to thank Him by doing righteousness, because thanks is given by action that pleases the one thanked, the Benefactor.

The pronoun in "i'malu" (work) is for Dawud and his family, like His saying ﴿Enjoin your family to prayer and be steadfast in it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 132], or for him alone as a form of honour.

His saying "Indeed, I am Seeing of what you do" — the placement of "inna" here is in the position of the fa' of causation, like the saying of Bashshar:

Indeed, that success is in early rising

And this has been mentioned more than once.

"Al-baṣīr" means the one who is aware and knowing, and here it is a metonymy for the recompense for righteous action.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 12:

﴿And to Solomon the wind, its morning course was a month's journey and its evening course was a month's journey. And We caused a spring of molten copper to flow for him, and among the jinn were those who worked before him by the permission of his Lord. And whoever of them deviates from Our command, We will make him taste the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ This is a continuation of the virtue of Solomon upon the virtue of David, for the sake of taking lesson from what Solomon was given of grace, honouring his father for his repentance (inabah) and honouring Solomon for his righteous upbringing in the presence of his father. So the conjunction is upon ﴿And We had certainly given David from Us bounty﴾ [Saba': 10], and the connection is like the connection of the mention of David, for Solomon was described with repentance; the Exalted said (then he repented) in Surah Sad.

And (al-rih, "the wind") is coordinated with (al-hadid, "the iron") in His saying (and We made iron soft for him), by supplying a verb indicated by (wa-alannā, "and We softened"). The sense is: "And We subjected the wind to Solomon," in the manner of the poet's saying:

"Girt with a sword and a spear"

That is: "and carrying a spear." The lam in His saying (li-Sulayman, "for Solomon") is the lam of reinforcement (lam al-taqwiyah), because when the verb was omitted, owing to what preceded it, the first object was linked to the lam of reinforcement, since the need for the lam of reinforcement when the verb is omitted is greater than the need for it when the verb is placed after the object. And (al-rih, "the wind") is the second object.

The meaning of His subjecting the wind to him is: the creation of a wind suited to the course of his ships for raiding or trade. So God made for his anchorages on the shores of Palestine seasonal winds that blow for a month heading east, so that his ships go out during that season, and blow for a month heading west, so that his ships return to the shores of Palestine, as the Exalted said: ﴿And to Solomon the wind, running by his command to the land which We had blessed﴾ [al-Anbiya': 81] in Surah al-Anbiya'.

Thus ghuduw ("morning course") is used for departing and setting out from a place, by analogy with the going forth of livestock to pasture in the morning, which is the time of their going out, or by analogy with people's going forth in the morning.

And rawah ("evening course") is used for returning from the errand for which one went out, as in the saying of Abu Rabi'ah:

"Are you going out in the morning from the family of Nu'm, or early? A morning on the morrow, or returning in the evening, or late?"

Because their custom was that the evening return of livestock took place in the evening, so it is derived from raha, when one returns to his abode.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (﴿And to Solomon the wind﴾) with the singular form (al-rih) and with the accusative case of (al-rih), taking it as coordinated with al-hadid in His saying (and We made iron soft for him). Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read (al-rihu) in the nominative, taking it as coordination of sentences, with (al-rihu) as the subject and (li-Sulayman) as the predicate placed first. Abu Ja'far read (al-riyah) in the plural form, in the accusative.

Al-qitr, with a kasra on the qaf and a sukun on the ta', is melted copper. It was mentioned in His saying (He said: "Bring me, that I may pour upon it molten copper") [al-Kahf: 96] in Surah al-Kahf.

Al-isalah is making a thing flowing, that is, spread out upon the earth like the course of a valley.

"A spring of copper" (ayn al-qitr) is not a literal spring, but is a metaphor for the outlet from which the melted copper is poured in his workshops, so that the molten copper flows out of channels and similar pipes as water flows from a spring, owing to the intensity of smelting copper and its continuous smelting, so that it never ceases to flow, in order that he may fashion from it vessels, weapons and shields. This was nothing but melting and smelting that broke the customary order, by a divine power. He likened the smelting to electricity or to bluish fiery tongues. This is what no king of his time had been given.

It is also possible that the flowing is a metaphor for an abundance of copper, an abundance resembling the abundance of water of springs and rivers, as the saying of Kuthayyir: "And the valleys flowed beneath the necks of the mounts." And (asalna, "We caused to flow") would also be a further development (tarshih) of the metaphor of applying the name "spring" to the meaning of molten copper; the point of resemblance is abundance.

His saying ﴿And among the jinn were those who worked before him﴾ may be a coordination with the clause (We caused a spring of molten copper to flow for him), so that His saying (those who worked before him) is the subject and His saying (by the permission of his Lord) is the predicate. The min in (min al-jinn, "among the jinn") is an explanation of the vagueness of (man, "those who"), placed before what it explains for the sake of emphasis on its strangeness; it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). You may also take (man ya'malu, "those who worked") as coordinated with (al-rih, "the wind") in His saying (and to Solomon the wind), meaning: We subjected to him those among the jinn who work before him; and the clause (And We caused a spring of molten copper to flow for him) would then be an interjected parenthesis between the coordinated and that to which it is coordinated.

The meaning of (ya'malu bayna yadayhi, "works before him") is: serves him and obeys him. It is said: "I am before your hands," meaning: obedient.

This does not require that his workers be the jinn alone; rather it requires that some of them were workers. In the verse of al-Naml: ﴿from the jinn and mankind and the birds﴾ [al-Naml: 17].

Al-zaygh is going beyond the limit and the path. The meaning: whoever disobeys Our command, conveyed through the tongue of Solomon.

The mention of the jinn among Solomon's host, peace be upon him, has preceded in Surah al-Naml.

"The punishment of the Blaze" means the punishment of the Fire, as a comparison: that is, a punishment like the punishment of Jahannam. As for the punishment of Jahannam, it will be literal only on the Day of Reckoning.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 13:**

﴿They made for him whatever he willed: sanctuaries (maharib), statues (tamathil), basins like cisterns (jawab), and fixed cooking pots. Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude. But few of My servants are truly grateful.﴾ The clause ﴿They made for him whatever he willed﴾ explains the earlier clause ﴿they worked before him﴾.

And ﴿from sanctuaries﴾ specifies what ﴿whatever he willed﴾ refers to.

The word *maharib* is the plural of *mihrab*, which originally meant a fortress from which the enemy or the attacker of a city is fought, or because weapons (*harib*) are thrown from its battlements. Then it was applied to a strong palace. The palaces of Ghumdan in Yemen were called "Ghumdan's maharib." This is the meaning intended in this verse. Later, *mihrab* was applied to the place where one withdraws for worship, so it is like a private mosque. God the Exalted said: ﴿Then the angels called to him while he was standing in prayer in the mihrab﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39], which has been discussed in the commentary on Surat Al 'Imran. David had a mihrab in which he sat for worship. God the Exalted said: ﴿Has there come to you the news of the litigants, when they climbed over the wall of the mihrab?﴾ [Sad: 21], discussed in the commentary on Surat Sad.

As for the use of *mihrab* for the place in the mosque where the imam stands to lead the people, it is made like a non-penetrating niche reaching to the floor of the mosque in the qibla wall, under which the imam stands. Calling this a *mihrab* is a recent designation, and I have not found the time when the name *mihrab* began to be applied to this position. The adoption of *mihrabs* in mosques occurred in the second century (AH), and it is presumed that it began at its beginning, during the lifetime of Anas ibn Malik, because it was narrated from him that he refrained from sitting in the *mihrabs*. They called it *al-taq* or *al-taqa* (the niche/arch), and sometimes they called it *al-madhbah* (the altar). I have not seen that they called it *mihrab* at that time. They used the term *mihrab* for the place where sacrifices were slaughtered in the church. 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a said:

"A statue by a monk, a priest; they made it in the altars of the mihrab."

The *madhbah* (altar) and the *mihrab* were borrowed from the Jews, as is well known from the branching of Christianity from Judaism. What is related from Anas ibn Malik, if it is authentic, refers to a special room for prayer.

I have seen the application of *mihrab* to the niche in the mosque in the speech of al-Farra', that is, in the middle of the second century. Al-Jawhari transmitted from him that he said: "*al-mahārib* are the fronts of assemblies, and from it the mihrab of the mosque is named," because by then *mihrab* was no longer applied absolutely to the place of worship.

Among the errors is that in the Prophet's Mosque (ﷺ), at the place where the Prophet (ﷺ) is likely to have prayed, they made a separate *mihrab*-shaped structure which they call "the mihrab of the Prophet (ﷺ)." In fact it is only a sign marking the place where he stood.

What appears is that the Muslims began by making small niches to indicate the qibla, so that someone entering the mosque to pray would not go astray, since that happens often. Then they gradually enlarged them until they made them in the form of a small half-corridor in the qibla wall, large enough for the imam's position. I suppose the first placement of this was when the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus was built. Then the caliph al-Walid ibn 'Abd al-Malik ordered that it be placed in the Prophet's Mosque when he expanded and rebuilt it, during the governorship of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz over Medina, as al-Samhudi mentioned in his book *Khulasat al-Wafa bi-Akhbar Dar al-Mustafa*.

*Al-tamathil* is the plural of *timthal* with a kasra on the *ta'*. Its pattern is *tif'al*, because the *ta'* is an augment. It is one of a number of nouns that came in the pattern *tif'al* with a kasra on the *ta'*. The regular pattern of this type, and most of it, has a fatha on the *ta'*. The nouns that came in this pattern include verbal nouns (*masadir*) and other nouns. Most verbal nouns have a fatha on the *ta'*, except two: *tibyan* and *tilqa'* (meeting). Among the nouns, about fourteen are attested with a kasra, among them *timthal*, which Ibn Durayd enumerated. Ibn al-'Arabi, in *Ahkam al-Qur'an*, added nine from his teacher al-Khatib al-Tabrizi, making them twenty-five.

*Al-timthal* is the depicted image, i.e., the three-dimensional form resembling some bodily thing. The sculptors made for Solomon various images, such as imagined forms of angels and animals, like lions. Solomon's throne was surrounded by fourteen lion statues, as described in chapter ten of the First Book of Kings. He had also placed in the Temple a great basin of polished bronze, raised upon twelve bronze bull figures.

Three-dimensional statues were not forbidden in earlier religious laws, but Islam prohibited them because Islam was thorough in cutting off the roots of idolatry from the souls of the Arabs and others. Most idols were statues, so Islam forbade making them for that reason. The prohibition was not because they are corrupt in themselves, but because they were a means to idolatry. The jurists agreed on the prohibition of making living beings with shadows, if they are complete in the limbs without which a living being cannot live, and on the reprehensibility of anything other than that, such as partial statues, images on walls, papers, and embroidery on cloth, or what is sat upon and trodden. The ruling on making them follows the ruling on possessing them. An exception was allowed for dolls that girls play with, for the benefit of accustoming them to household work.

*Al-jifan* is the plural of *jafna*, which is a large bowl in which water is poured. The *jafna* in the Torah is said to hold forty *bath* (a unit of measure). We do not know the amount of the *bath* among them, but there is no doubt it is a unit of measure. The *jifan* were compared in their size and capacity to the *jawabi*. The *jawabi* is the plural of *jabiya*, which is a great, wide, deep basin in which water is collected for watering trees and crops. Al-A'sha said:

"A jafna that repelled blame from the people of al-Muhallaq, like the cistern of the Iraqi shaykh, overflowing."

That is, the *jafna* in its capacity was like the cistern of the Iraqi man, and the people of Iraq were people of vineyards and plantings, so they gathered water for irrigation.

The *jifan* mentioned were in the Temple known to us as the Temple of Jerusalem, for placing water in which they washed what they offered of burnt offerings, as in chapter four of the Second Book of Chronicles.

In the Mushaf it is written *(kalajawab)* without a *ya'* after the *ba'*. The majority read it without a *ya'* both in continuous recitation and in pause. Ibn Kathir read it with the *ya'* in both states. Warsh, from Nafi', and Abu 'Amr read it with the *ya'* in continuous recitation and without it in pause.

*Al-qudur* is the plural of *qidr*, which is a vessel in which food is placed to be cooked, of meat, oil, fats, and spices. Al-Nabigha said about al-Nu'man ibn al-Harith al-Julahi:

"In front of his house is a great black cauldron, which swallows the joints of the lean camel.

A remnant of a cauldron, inherited by the family of al-Julah, elder after elder."

That is, it is large enough to hold a camel's legs when placed in it to cook broth or the like.

These are the pots in which food was cooked for Solomon's army, for the keepers and servants of the Temple, and their followers. The mention of pots occurs in general in the sixteenth verse of chapter four of the Second Book of Chronicles.

*Al-rasiyat* are those fixed in the ground, which are not lifted from above their supports, because cooking is continually done in them, morning and evening.

The clause ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude﴾ is a quoted speech of a verb that is omitted, i.e., "We said: Work, O family of Dawud." The object of *i'malu* (work) is omitted, indicated by *shukran* (gratitude). Its estimate is: "Work righteousness," as was mentioned just before, "work for the gratitude of God the Exalted." So *shukran* is in the accusative as a *maf'ul li-ajlihi* (object of purpose, i.e., "for the sake of gratitude"). The address is to Solomon and his family.

It is concluded with ﴿But few of My servants are truly grateful﴾, which is part of the quoted speech, and in it there is an exhortation to be concerned with righteous deeds. It is possible that this concluding statement is a new utterance that came in the Qur'an, i.e., "We said that to the family of Dawud, but few of them acted and most did not act, and Solomon was among the first of the small group."

*Al-shakur* means one who is very grateful. Since work is gratitude, it indicates that those who work are few.

[Page 164]

﴿Then when We decreed death for him, nothing showed them his death except a creature of the earth eating away at his staff. So when he fell, the jinn realized that had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri'') of His words ﴿And among the jinn were those who worked before him ... and cooking pots set firmly in place﴾, meaning that their labor for him continued until he died. Then ﴿When We decreed death for him﴾ and so on. There is no doubt that this did not last long, because a man of such greatness of kingdom must be missed by his followers. The clause ﴿nothing showed them his death﴾ and so on is the answer to ﴿When We decreed death for him﴾.

The pronoun in ﴿showed them﴾ refers to something known from the context, namely the people of his court.

Al-dalalah (indication, showing) is informing about a hidden matter. It was discussed earlier at His words ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "Shall we direct you to a man..."﴾ [Saba': 7] in the preceding verse.

Dabbat al-ard (the creature of the earth) is al-aradah, with three fatha vowels, which is al-sirfah (with a damma on the sin, a sukun on the ra', a fatha on the fa', and a feminine ta'), meaning a worm that gnaws wood. So "al-ard" here is the verbal noun of "aradat al-sirfah al-khashab" (the woodworm gnawed the wood), from the pattern of "daraba". God had subjected many woodworms to the staff (minsa'ah) of Sulayman, so they hastened to gnaw it.

The clause ﴿So when he fell﴾ is a consequence of the clause ﴿nothing showed them his death﴾. The clause ﴿the jinn realized﴾ is the answer to ﴿So when he fell﴾. Al-minsa'ah, with a kasra or a fatha on the mim, and with a hamzah after the sin, which may be softened so that it becomes an alif, is the great staff. It is said that it is a word from the language of Abyssinia (Habasha).

Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read it with an alif after the sin. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub, Khalaf, and Hisham on the authority of Ibn 'Amir read it with a fathah hamzah after the sin. Ibn Dhakwan on the authority of Ibn 'Amir read it with a sukun hamzah after the sin, as a lightening, and this lightening is rare.

The majority of readers (al-jumhur) read ﴿the jinn realized﴾ with a fatha on the ta' (first letter), the ba' and the ya'. Ruways on the authority of Ya'qub read it with a damma on the ta', a damma on the ba', and a kasra on the ya', in the passive voice, meaning that the people realized the jinn. The clause ﴿that had they known the unseen﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from "the jinn" according to both readings.

His words ﴿the jinn realized﴾ are an ambiguous predication, which is explained by His words ﴿that had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment﴾.

[Page 165]

The ﴿an﴾ is a verbal particle (masdariyyah), and the verbal noun formed from it is a substitute of inclusion from "the jinn", meaning: their affair became clear, that they do not know the unseen; that is, the lack of their knowledge of the unseen became clear. The evidence for the deleted element is the conditional clause and its answer.

Al-'adhab al-muhin means the humiliating punishment, that is, the one that degrades, or the painful and exhausting one. For had they known the unseen, their knowledge of what had already occurred would have been eternal (azali), and this refutes the belief of the common people at that time and what the polytheists believed, that the jinn know the unseen. For this reason the polytheists used to seek knowledge of hidden matters from soothsayers (kuhhan, sing. kahin, one who claims knowledge of the unseen). They claimed that every soothsayer had a jinn who came to him with news of the unseen, and they called it a ra'iy (familiar spirit). For if they knew the unseen, it would have been easier for them to know the death of Sulayman.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 15:

﴿Indeed there was for Sheba in their dwelling a sign: two gardens, one on the right and one on the left. "Eat of the provision of your Lord and be grateful to Him. A good land and a Forgiving Lord."﴾ The account of Sulayman, peace be upon him, led on to the mention of Sheba because of the connection between the kingdom of Sulayman and the kingdom of Sheba through the story of Bilqis, and because the condition of the people of Sheba is the opposite of the conditions of Dawud and Sulayman. Those two were examples of the bestowal of blessings upon the grateful, while those people were an example of the removal of blessings from the disbelievers. In it there is also an admonition to the polytheists, for they were in the midst of abundant blessing, and then when a messenger came to them from the One who had bestowed blessing upon them, reminding them of their Lord and warning them that they were sinners in worshipping other than Him, they denied him and turned away from reflecting on the indication of that blessing upon the Benefactor who alone deserves divinity.

Ibn 'Atiyya said, in commenting on the words of Allah the Exalted ﴿And We had certainly given Dawud bounty from Us﴾ [Saba': 10]: "When the parable for Muhammad ﷺ was completed, the parable returned to them, i.e., the polytheists, that is, their condition with Sheba and what befell them of destruction because of disbelief and insolence." End of quote. This story is thus a parable of one nation with another and one land with another, and that is a means of analogy and lesson. It is also the benefit of recording history and the vicissitudes of nations, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah presents an example: a town that was secure and at rest, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place, but it denied the favors of Allah, so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they had been doing. And there had certainly come to them a messenger from among themselves, but they denied him, so the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers﴾ [an-Nahl: 112-113]. So the course of this story is an allusion to those like Sheba. The meaning: there was for Sheba, in the condition of their dwellings and the order of their land, a sign.

Page 166
The sign here is the indication and proof through the change of conditions and the alternation of times. It is a sign of Allah's disposal and His blessing upon them. But they were not guided by that sign, so they associated others with Him, though in His bestowal upon them there was what is evidence of His existence and then of His oneness.

The emphasis by the oath-lam and the particle of confirmation is to treat the addressees, who were being alluded to with this story, as one who doubts this, because they did not take warning from the condition of a people from among the inhabitants of their own lands. The verb kāna is left without feminine marking because its subject is not truly feminine and because a separating prepositional phrase intervenes. The lam in li-Saba' is related to āyah. Al-masākin: the lands in which they dwell, as indicated by His saying "two gardens, on the right and on the left." Al-masākin means the abodes of residence. The discussion of Saba' was already presented at His saying "and I have come to you from Saba'" in Surat an-Naml. The name Saba' is applied to the nation, as here, and to their land, as in the verse of an-Naml, and its detail has been mentioned earlier.

Al-Jumhur read fī masākinihim in the plural form of maskan. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ḥafs and Khalaf read it in the singular form "fī maskanihim," except that Ḥamzah and Ḥafs opened the kāf, while al-Kisa'i and Khalaf kasra'd the kāf. This is contrary to analogy, because the present-tense form of it does not have a kasra on its ʿayn, so the proper form of the noun of place from it is a fatha on the ʿayn. Forms like their saying masjid for a place of prayer are anomalous. "Jannatān" is a substitute (badal) for "āyah," by considering it as completed with what is connected to it of the complement and the implied saying. "Jannatān" is an eloquent metaphor: in their dwellings there is something resembling two gardens, in that it is a plantation of trees bearing fruit, joined one part to another, like what is known of the condition of gardens. The dual "two gardens" is by consideration that what is on the right of the walker is like one garden and what is on his left is like one garden. It has been said that each man had in his dwelling, i.e., his house, two gardens: a garden on the right of the dwelling and a garden on its left, and they would enjoy their shade morning and evening and pick their fruits of palm, grapes and others. The construction then is distributive, meaning each dwelling had two gardens, like the saying "the people mounted their animals." This is suitable to His saying "in their dwellings," rather than saying "in their lands" or "their abodes." It is also possible that what is meant is that their city, which was Ma'rib, was surrounded on its right and left by a forest of gardens, where they spent the summer and exploited them, like the Ghouta of Damascus. This fits His saying after "And We replaced their two gardens with two gardens" [Saba': 16], because its apparent meaning is that what was substituted was two gardens, unless one makes it distributive, matching the plural with the plural.
The meaning: they were people of gardens planted with fruitful trees and vines.

Their city was Ma'rib (with a silent hamza after the mim), which lay between San'a' and Hadramawt. It has been said that a traveller on its roads, if he placed a basket on his head, would find it filled with fruits that fell from the trees under which he walked. Perhaps there is some exaggeration in this saying, but it indicates abundance. This was by means of a plan that Allah inspired in them for storing the waters that came down in the seasons of rain, through the great dam they built at Ma'rib.

The clause "Eat of the provision of your Lord" is a speech being said, either by the indication of the tongue of the state, as in the saying: "The pool was full and said: 'Enough for me.'" Or they were informed of it through the tongues of prophets sent among them. It was said that twelve prophets were sent among them, such as Tubba' As'ad, for it was related that he was a prophet, as indicated by Allah's saying "and the people of Tubba'" [Qaf: 14]. Or it was from others, as Allah said: "Among them are those We have related to you and among them are those We have not related to you" [Ghafir: 78]. Or it was from what Sulayman said to Bilqis, or from what the righteous messengers of Sulayman said to Sheba. In placing "two gardens" in the structure of the speech in place of "a sign" there is a metonymy for the goodness of the soil of their lands. It has been said they used to sow three times each year.

Al-ṭayyibah: good in its kind, suitable to those who work it and exploit it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they sailed with them with a good wind and rejoiced in it; there came to it a violent wind﴾ [Yunus: 22]. He said: ﴿So We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [an-Nahl: 97]. He said: ﴿And the good land its vegetation comes out by the permission of its Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 58]. He said: ﴿My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring﴾ [Al 'Imran: 38]. And in the hadith of Abu Talha concerning his charity of the garden of Bi'r Ha': "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ would enter it and drink from its good water." Al-ṭayyib is the opposite of al-khabith. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾ [an-Nisa': 2]. He said: ﴿He makes lawful for them the good things and forbids for them the evil things﴾ [al-A'raf: 157].

Its derivation is from al-ṭīb, with a kasra on the ṭa', in the pattern fiʿl, which is the thing from which a pleasant fragrance spreads.

The clause "a good land" is part of the speech and is a resumed sentence within the quoted speech, meaning "a good land for you." The indefiniteness of "baldah" is for magnification. "Balda" is the subject, "ṭayyibah" is an adjective of "balda," and its predicate is omitted, its estimate being "for you." He turned away from annexing "balda" to their pronoun so that the clause would be light on the tongue and would function like a proverb.

The clause "and a Forgiving Lord" is coordinated with the clause "a good land."

The indefiniteness of "Rabb" is for magnification. It is the subject with its predicate omitted, on the pattern of "a good land," and the estimate is: "and a Lord for you," that is, "your Lord is Forgiving."

The turning away from annexing "Rabb" to the pronoun of the addressees to indefinite "Rabb," with the estimate of the lam of particularity, is for the purpose of honouring them with this particularity, and so that the clause is on the pattern of the one before it, seeking lightness, and so that harmony occurs between the two phrases, so that they proceed as a proverb.

The meaning of "Ghafur" is: one who overlooks you, that is, their disbelief in which they were before the belief of Bilqis in the religion of Sulayman, peace be upon him. The duration of their remaining upon faith is not known.

[Page 169]

This is a continuation (*tafri'*, a consequence) of His saying "and give thanks to Him," and it falls as a parenthetical interruption (*i'tiraḍ*) within the parts of the story, the remainder of which is His saying ﴿And We placed between them and the towns...﴾ (Qur'an 34:18), and so on. It is a parenthesis introduced by *fa* (therefore), like His saying ﴿That, so taste it, and that for the disbelievers is the punishment of the Fire﴾ (Qur'an 8:14), which was discussed in Surat al-Anfal.

"Turning away" (*i'rāḍ*) presupposes that a messenger or prophet had issued a call earlier. The meaning is: they turned away from responding to the call to monotheism, returning to the worship of the sun, after they had given it up in the time of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. Perhaps the Queen of Sheba had turned them away only from sun-worship, since peoples used to follow the religions of their kings. It has been said that the Queen did not live long after her visit to Solomon, only a few years.

[Page 169 continues]

*Al-irsāl* (sending) means release, the opposite of confinement. Its construction with the preposition *'alā* (upon) indicates that it was a sending of punishment. The Flood of al-'Arim was held back by the dam at Ma'rib, and they would release from it only the amount with which they watered their gardens. When they disbelieved in God after the call to monotheism, God decreed for them a punishment by determining the causes of the collapse of the dam, so that the water it contained was released. It became a danger to them and destroyed livestock and trees. Then it was followed by drought, through the disruption of the regular pattern of rainfall and the absence of water at the time of need. This was a recompense for their turning away and their polytheism.

*Al-'Arim* may be a descriptive term derived from *al-'arāma*, meaning severity and abundance, in which case the annexation of "the flood" to "al-'Arim" is an annexation of a qualified noun to its qualifier (*iḍāfat al-mawṣūf ila al-ṣifa*). It may also be that *al-'Arim* is the name of the flood that poured into the dam, in which case the annexation is of the named to the name, i.e., "the great flood" (*al-sayl al-'arim*).

The valleys and watercourses in the land of the Arabs had names, such as the torrent of Mahzur and Mudhaynib, from which the gardens of Medina were irrigated. This meaning is supported by the words of al-A'sha:

*And Ma'rib, al-'Arim has effaced its traces.*

It has also been said that *al-'Arim* is the plural name of *'aramah* (on the pattern of *shajarah*), and it has been said there is no singular from its own form. It means what is built to hold back water. It is a Yemeni and Abyssinian term, and it is *al-masnāh* in the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. *Al-masnāh*, on the pattern *maf'alah*, which is the name of an instrument, is derived from *sanaytu* meaning "I watered," and from it the water-wheel is called *sāniyah*, and *sāniyah* is the bucket by which water is drawn. The annexation in both of these senses is original.

The meaning is: We released the flood that had been stored behind the dam.

The people of Saba' had a great dam near the region of Ma'rib (Ma'rib is one of the districts of Yemen). It was the greatest of the dams in the land of Yemen, where there were many scattered dams. They had made these dams for storing the water that came with the floods during the rains of summer and autumn. They would go to the passageways of the floods between the mountains and build in the path of the water a wall of stones, built in a solid construction. They would pour pitch into the cracks between the stones until they sealed, so the water falling there was held back. When the reservoir was full, they constructed beside it great spillways into which the water would pour, overflowing from the top of the dam. In this way they secured as much as they could of the stored water.

The dam of Ma'rib, in which the Flood of al-'Arim was held, was begun by Saba', the first king of this nation, but he did not complete it, and his son Himyar completed it. As for what is said, that the Queen of Sheba built it, this is a confusion, since perhaps the Queen built other subsidiary reservoirs around it, or repaired its structure with a restoration that was called "building." They used to maintain these dams with repair and restoration every year, so that they would withstand the force of the floods that fell upon them.

They would make closed outlets in the dam, which they opened by removing the blockage when they wanted to release water to the various places they watered from it, since they had made their gardens clustered around the dam. Seventy valleys poured into the dam of Ma'rib.

They made this dam between two mountains, both known as al-Balaq, so they were al-Balaq al-Aymanu (the right Balaq) and al-Balaq al-Aysaru (the left Balaq).

The greatest of the valleys that poured into it was named "Idhnah." They said that the valleys used to come to Saba' with trees and valleys of Yemen.

This dam is a wall whose length from east to west is eight hundred cubits, its height is some ten cubits, and its width is one hundred and fifty cubits.

al-Hasan al-Hamdani saw it and described it in his book called *al-Iklil*. He belonged to the people of the early fourth century (AH), and I have heard its essentials. The French traveller Arnaud described it in the year 1883, and the French traveller Glaser also described it.

The time of the collapse of this dam is not known, nor the causes of that. The apparent reason for its collapse is that their kings were occupied with internal wars among themselves, which diverted them from attending to its maintenance until it was ruined. Or perhaps some enemy who fought them destroyed it. As for what is mentioned in the stories, that rats destroyed the dam, that is among the fables.

Regarding al-'Arim, al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said:

*Of Saba' the dwellers, Ma'rib, when they built, instead of guarding against its flood, al-'Arim.*

[Page 171]

*Al-tabdīl* (exchange) is substituting one thing for another. It transitively takes the object taken directly, and the object given with the preposition *bi-*, which is the preposition of exchange (*bā' al-'iwaḍ*), as was discussed in His saying ﴿and do not exchange the bad for the good﴾ (Qur'an 4:2) in Surat al-Nisa'.

The meaning is: We gave them trees of *khamt*, *athl* and *sidr* in place of their two gardens. That is, their land became a barren desert with nothing in it but thorny trees and desert shrubs. Between these two states there were great conditions that befell them, and they suffered thirst and the loss of fruit until they were forced to leave those homelands. When this final state indicated those conditions, the earlier mention was omitted and it was limited to ﴿And We exchanged for them their two gardens for two gardens bearing bitter produce...﴾ to the end of the verse.

The application of the name "two gardens" to these growing places is a figure of speech (*mushākalah*) for mockery (*tahakkum*), like the saying of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

*We hosted you, and hastened your hospitality, before dawn, with a ground and pounded meal.*

and His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿So give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾.

Al-A'sha described this state, at its beginning and its end, with his words:

*In that is a lesson for those who are observant, and Ma'rib, al-'Arim has effaced its traces.*

*Marble which Himyar built for them, which does not shift when its flood comes.*

*It watered their crops and their vines, despite the abundance of their water when it was distributed.*

*So they lived by that in prosperity, until a torrent overwhelmed them, routing.*

*It drove away the herds and their pastures, into a barren waste with a mirage that deceives.*

*They fled swiftly, and could not obtain from it enough to drink for a weaned child.*

*Al-khamt* is the tree of the *arak* (toothbrush tree). *Khamt* is also applied to anything bitter. *Al-athl* is a great tree among the thorny trees, resembling the tamarisk (*al-ṭarfā'*). *Al-sidr* is also a thorny tree, with thorns resembling those of the *'unnāb* (jujube). All of these grow in the wastelands.

*Al-sidr* is the most shady and the most beneficial of them, because its leaves are used to wash with water, which cleanses, and it has a pleasant fragrance. For this reason it is described here as "few," to indicate that most of their trees were of no benefit. The fewness is intensified by mentioning the word *shay'* (a thing), which in itself indicates paucity. One says "a thing of such-and-such" when it is little.

In the Qur'an: ﴿...and what will not avail you against God in any way...﴾.

*Al-ukul*, with a *ḍamma* on the *hamza* and a *sukūn* on the *kāf*, and also with a *ḍamma* on the *kāf*, means the edible produce. Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read it with a *ḍamma* on the *hamza* and a *sukūn* on the *kāf*. The rest of the ten readers read it with a *ḍamma* on the *kāf*. The majority read *ukulin* with tanwin, in the genitive. If *khamt* is intended to mean the tree called *khamt*, then *khamt* cannot be an adjective of *ukulin*, because *khamt* is a tree, nor can it be a substitute (*badal*) for *ukulin* in the same way, nor an appositive (*'aṭf al-bayān*) as Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) assumed, because an appositive is like a matching substitute. Therefore it is determined that *khamt* here is an adjective, as one says: "a thing *khamiṭ*" when it is bitter.

Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read *ukuli* with annexation to *khamt*. In that case *khamt* refers to the *arak* tree, and its *ukul* is its fruit, which is the *bariru* (its berry), and it has a bitter taste.

The meaning of *dhawatay ukulin* is "two possessors of produce." *Dhawāt* is the plural of *dhāt*, which means "possessor" (feminine), and it is the feminine of *dhū* meaning "possessor." The original of *dhāt* is *dhawāh*, with the feminine *tā' marbūṭa* like *nawāh*, and its form is *fa'alah* with two *fatḥas*, and its final radical is a *wāw*. So its original is *dhawawah*. When the *wāw* moved after a *fatḥa*, it was changed to an *alif*. Then in the singular they lightened it by deleting the middle radical, and they said *dhāt*. Its form is then *fal-t* or *fal-h*. Al-Jawhari said: The original of the *tā'* in *dhāt* is a *hā'*, like *nawāh*, because when you stop on it in the singular, you say *dhāh* with the *hā'*, but when they joined it to what follows by annexation, it became a *tā'*. What indicates that the original is a *hā'* is that in the diminutive one says *dhuwayhah* with the feminine *hā'*. End of quotation. The lexicographers did not explain the reason for this substitution, and perhaps it is because the word was built on one letter with an *alif* which is the lengthening of the *fatḥa*, so pronouncing the *hā'* after them was heavy in pause. Then, when they formed the dual, they returned it to its original, because the dual returns things to their roots. So they said *dhawātā kadhā* (two possessors of such-and-such), and the *nūn* was dropped because of the obligation of its annexation. Its original form is *dhuwayyātun*. The *yā'* was changed to an *alif* because it moved and the preceding letter was open. Its form is *fa'alatān*, and after the change its form became *fa'ātān*. When they make the plural, they return to deletion and say *dhawātu kadhā* with the meaning of "possessors" (feminine plural). Its original is *dhuwayyātun*, so the *yā'* was changed to an *alif* because it moved and the preceding letter was open. So the original form of *dhawātay* is *fa'alātun*, then after the change its form became *fa'ātin*, and it is among what is attached to the sound feminine plural, because its *tā'* in the singular originally is a *hā'*. As for its *tā'* in the plural, it is a *tā'* that became a substitute for the *hā'* of the singular, according to the custom of the plural with *alif* and *tā'*.

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 34, verse 17**

﴿That We requited them for their disbelief; and do We requite anyone but the ungrateful?﴾ This is an explanatory resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf bayani) arising from His words "So We sent against them the flood of al-ʿArim," and so it is part of the parenthetical digression (iʿtiraḍ).

The demonstrative noun (ism al-ishara) may be in the accusative position, serving as a substitute for the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq) that specifies the type of requital. This is explanation by way of indication: that is, "We requited them the requital indicated," namely what preceded of the exchange of their two gardens for two other gardens. Its placement before its governing verb serves to emphasise the severity of that requital.

Its evocation by the demonstrative noun is because of the magnitude of its terror.

It is also permissible for the demonstrative noun to be in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), with the indication referring to what preceded, from His words "So We sent against them the flood of al-ʿArim" up to His words "of a few lote-trees." The clause "jazaynahum" (We requited them) is then the predicate (khabar), and the connecting pronoun is a deleted pronoun, its estimated form being: "jazaynahumuh" (We requited them it).

The preposition ba in "bi-ma kafaru" indicates cause, and ma is a verbal-noun (masdariyya) particle; that is, "because of their disbelief."

Disbelief here is disbelief in God, that is, denial of His divinity, since they were worshippers of the sun.

The interrogative in "wa-hal yujazi" is a denial in meaning (istifham inkari fi ma'na al-nafy), as the exception indicates.

Al-kafur: one who is intensely ungrateful and disbelieving, because they did not know God and worshipped the sun; thus they were in a worse state than the people of polytheism.

The meaning is: that requital is only requited to the ungrateful, because that requital is great in its kind, that is, the kind of punishments, for punishment is of the same genus as requital, and reward is also of the same genus as requital. Therefore, when it was said "That We requited them for their disbelief," it became clear that what is meant is: "And is requited the like of their requital only the ungrateful?" So it should not be supposed that this implies that the non-ungrateful are not requited for their deeds, nor that reward is not called requital, nor that the believing sinner is not requited for his disobedience, because all of these suppositions are dispelled by what the demonstrative noun contains of specifying the type of requital, for total annihilation and the like does not apply to believers.

صفحة ١٧٤

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read "yujazi" with the ya of the third person and the passive form, with "al-kafur" in the nominative case.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azama), the active form, and "al-kafura" in the accusative case.

The continuation of the story, mentioning one blessing after another. What was mentioned before concerned the blessing of ease, delight, and the pleasantness of residence, while what is mentioned here concerns the blessing of security, the facilitation of journeys, and the flourishing of their lands.

By "the towns that We had blessed" is meant the towns of the land of Sham (Greater Syria). When they set out from Ma'rib toward the Shami lands with caravans for trade and the sale of food, they took the route through Tihama, then the Hijaz, then the outskirts of Sham, then the land of Sham. Whenever they had covered a stage of the journey, they found a village, a town, or a dwelling where they could rest, and they rested and replenished their provisions. For this reason they did not carry provisions with them when they left Ma'rib.

As for these "visible towns," it is possible that they came into being through the efforts of people living along the sides of the road traveled by caravans between Ma'rib and Jillaq, seeking to benefit from the caravans' stopping among them, to buy provisions from them, and to supply those towns with the goods and fruits they needed. This is the nature of civilization (al-'umran).

It is also possible that the Sabaeans established buildings where they would take shelter at each stage of their journeys, dug wells and reservoirs (masani') there, and appointed men to guard them, who would be present to receive them when they stopped. This would be among the means of civilization and security for caravans that their kings had firmly established. The establishment of these stations may also have attracted those who lived around them and wished to deal with the caravan when it passed by.

In either case, the attribution of making these towns to God, exalted is He, is because He is the One who inspires people and kings, or because He created for them a good soil whose produce is abundant enough for the needs of the inhabitants, thus permitting them to seek to market it in other lands.

The description "visible" (zahirah) means that they were close to one another, such that some of them were visible to others and some could be seen from others. It was also said: "visible" means that they could be seen by the traveler from a distance, in that the towns were built on hills and elevations which the traveler could observe, so he would not lose his way to them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "What appears to me is that the meaning of 'visible' is that they lay outside the cities, being on the outskirts of cities. From this is the saying of people: 'We alighted at the outskirts (zahir) of such-and-such city,' meaning outside of it. So His saying 'visible' is like people's naming them 'desert settlements' (badiyah) and 'suburbs' (dahiyah)." From this is the verse of the poet, which the lexicographers have recited:

"Even if a band of Quraysh witnessed me, the Quraysh of the open valleys (al-Bitah), not the Quraysh of the outskirts (al-Zawahir)."

And in the hadith of the prayer for rain: "The people of the outskirts (al-Zawahir) came complaining of drowning." End of quote. And this is a beautiful interpretation. In His saying "visible" on this reading, there is a metonymy (kinayah) for the abundance of towns, such that all the villages are visible from among them.

The meaning of "We appointed the journey therein by measure" is that their distances were arranged in measure and balance, such that no distance exceeded one stage. So the one who set out in the morning would take a midday rest in one village, and the one who set out in the afternoon would spend the night in another. Thus the meaning is: We measured the distances of travel among the towns, that is, their intervals. The phrase "therein" (fiha) is connected to the verb "qaddarna" and not to "al-sayr," because the measuring applies to the towns and their intervals, not to the journey itself, since the measuring of the journey follows from the measuring of the intervals.

The clause "Travel therein by night and by day, secure" is a quoted statement of an omitted saying. The clause of saying is an explanation of the clause "qaddarna," or a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for it.

This saying is the saying of creation (qawl al-takwin), namely, making them travel therein; the imperative form is for creation. The pronoun in "therein" refers to the towns, and the locative sense derived from the adverbial particle is a figurative imagery (takhyil) of a metaphor (makniyyah): the towns, because of their close proximity, were likened to a container, the comparison term was omitted, and it was indicated by the locative particle. The meaning is: travel among them.

They used to travel in the morning and evening, so they would journey in the morning, then a village would lie in their path and they would rest there and take a midday break, and they would journey in the evening, and a village would lie in their path where they would spend the night. So the meaning of His saying "Travel therein by night and by day" is: travel however you wish. The mention of nights before days in this context of enumerating blessings is because travelers have more need of security at night than during the day, since in the night highwaymen and beasts of prey encounter them.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 19 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿They said, "Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys far apart," and they wronged themselves. So We made them into tales, and We scattered them completely. Indeed, in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful person.﴾

The fa' in His words "fa-qalu Rabbana" (﴿So they said, "Our Lord..."﴾) indicates that this statement came immediately after the blessing bestowed on them, namely the nearness of the towns and the ease of travel. Sequence (ta'qib) is understood according to what suits each thing. When the blessing was complete, they became insolent toward it, and the causes of its removal came upon them. Among the greatest causes of the disappearance of a blessing is ingratitude for it. Shaykh Ibn 'Ata' Allah al-Iskandari said: "Whoever does not give thanks for blessings has exposed them to disappearance, and whoever gives thanks for them has tied them down with their cord."

In my view, the more apparent meaning is that they uttered this statement as a response to the admonitions of their prophets and righteous men, when those men forbade them from associating partners with God. The prophets would remind them that God had bestowed upon them that comfort, and they would answer with this statement, seeking to silence the callers to good among them. This is similar to the statement of the disbelievers of Quraysh:

﴿O God, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment.﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:32)

Before this, [the verse says] "fa-a'radu" (﴿they turned away﴾), since turning away implies that they were being called to something. This meaning is strengthened by the phrase "wa-zalamu anfusahum" (﴿and they wronged themselves﴾) following the report of their statement. It may be coordinated with the clause "fa-qalu," meaning: they then followed that with ingratitude for the blessing and with associating partners with God. The wronging of oneself is frequently used in the Qur'an to mean associating partners with God, and polytheism is nothing other than the greatest ingratitude for the blessing of the Creator.

It is also possible that the clause "wa-zalamu anfusahum" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), with the wa' being the wa' of circumstance. That is, they said this while they had wronged themselves by associating partners with God, so their statement accompanied their polytheism.

On both interpretations, the punishment was caused by two causes, as is clearly stated in His words:

[p. 177]

﴿So they turned away, and We sent upon them the flood of al-'Arim, and We replaced their two gardens with two gardens...﴾ (Saba' 34:16), up to His words "﴿...none but the ungrateful?﴾" (Saba' 34:17).

The consequence of disbelief is their total destruction, which is the meaning of His words "fa-ja'alnahum ahadith," as you will know. The consequence of ingratitude for the blessing of the nearness of the lands is their being torn apart, "kulla mumazzaq," that is, their dispersal. Thus the structure of the speech follows the pattern of laff wa nashr (enumerating two things and then matching each with its corresponding result), which is an arrangement that arouses curiosity.

The exegetes have customarily held that they supplicated God with this request. This is contradicted by the apparent fact that they were not affirming God. If we follow the view that they recognized God and made this supplication, then it was because they did not appreciate His great blessing as it deserved. So they asked God to remove those populated towns so that they could travel through the wastelands and carry provisions of food and water.

Furthermore, it is possible that the people who uttered this statement were among those who had experienced a time when travel distances in their lands were great, before their land developed into that civilization. Or they were among those who heard stories of past journeys in their lands or the journeys of nomadic peoples, and those conditions appealed to them. This is one form of ingratitude for blessings, arising from corruption of taste in perceiving benefits and their opposites.

The verb form "al-mubā'adah" (distancing), in the pattern of mufā'alah, takes the place of the causative hamza and the doubling (of the middle radical). So the meaning is: "Our Lord, make far away between our journeys." The Prophet ﷺ said: "O God, distance between me and my sins as You have distanced between the east and the west."

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) recited "bā'id." Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amr recited "ba''id" with a fatha on the ba' and a shadda on the 'ayn. Ya'qub alone recited "Rabbuna" in the nominative and "ba'ada" in the past tense with a fatha on the 'ayn and on the dal, the clause being the predicate of the subject. The meaning is that they were dissatisfied with that prosperity, found it too small, and asked that the lands become even closer. This is from the insolence of blessing, seeking what is impossible at that time.

The construction gives the meaning "make the distance between our journeys." Since "bayn" requires plural objects, it is determined that the meaning is: "Make distance between one journey and another of our journeys." This means extending the stages, since each stage is considered a journey. That is, "Make distance between the stages of our journeys."

The meaning of "fa-ja'alnahum ahadith" is: We made those who were in the gardens and in the abundance of life into "ahadith" (tales), meaning that none of them remained. Their existence came to be only in reports and stories. God annihilated them when they scattered after the flood of al-'Arim, and this destruction spread rapidly among them through exile in the land, poverty, and the attacks of raiders upon them on the roads, as we shall know. The verb "ja'ala" (to make) implies change, and since it was connected to their persons, they were transformed from visible beings into reported narratives heard by people. The meaning is that they perished and people spoke about them. This is similar to the expression "they entered into the report of kana" (i.e., they became a matter of narrative and past history). Otherwise, no person or group is free from being the subject of conversation. It may also be used in praise, as in the poet's words:

"These are their graves, and those are their palaces,
and their talk is a repository for the pages."

Or it may be meant as: "We made them tales of admonition and warning," meaning: "We struck them with a strange matter that is fit for people to speak of." In this case, "ahadith" is described by an implied adjective indicated by the context, like His words: "﴿...who seizes every ship by force﴾" (Al-Kahf 18:79), meaning every sound ship, as indicated by His words: "﴿...so I wished to damage it﴾" (Al-Kahf 18:79).

Al-tamziq (tearing) means cutting cloth into pieces. It is used here figuratively for dispersion, likening the scattering of a people's unity in disorder to the tearing of cloth into pieces.

"Kulla" is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), since it means "all of its tearing." Through its being annexed to the verbal noun, it acquired the sense of the absolute object.

The meaning of "kulla" here is "much tearing," because "kull" often occurs in the sense of "many," not in the sense of "all." God says: "﴿...and even if every sign came to them...﴾" (Yunus 10:97), and al-Nabigha said:

"With it is every one who drags its skirts."

The verse alludes to the well-known dispersion that befell the tribe of Saba', when the ruin of the dam and the barrenness of the land led them to leave those homelands, a departure and scattering that the Arabs used as a proverb: "They went, or they scattered, 'aydi Saba'," or "ayadi Saba'," with the hamza of Saba' lightened to lighten the proverb. In the lexicon Lisan al-'Arab, under the root y-d-y, al-Ma'arri said: "They did not pronounce the hamza in Saba' because they treated it together with what precedes it as one unit." He said this, but perhaps it is a confusion or a distortion. Al-Ma'arri only mentioned the non-manifestation of the fatha on the ya' of "ayadi" or "aydi," as the reasoning requires, because the reasoning requires that the fatha on the hamza of Saba' be maintained, as is the case with a compound construction of attribution (murakkab mazji).

[p. 179]

The Lisan al-'Arab says: "Some of them give it tanwin when they lighten it." Dhu al-Rummah said:

"Alas for a dwelling whose people were scattered,
the 'aydi Saba' from it, and their departure was prolonged."

But most do not give it tanwin. Kuthayyir said:

"'Aydi Saba', O 'Azza, I was not after you
so the two eyes have not been pleased with a sight since you departed."

The word "al-ayadi" and "al-aydi" here is the plural of "yad" (hand). "Yad" also means a path.

The meaning is that they went off in various directions, taking routes from which they proceeded to many regions, as in His words: "﴿...we were in various ways (tara'iqa qiddan)﴾" (Al-Jinn 72:11). It has been said that "al-ayadi" is the plural of "yad" in the sense of "blessing," because the wealth of Saba' was lost.

The tribe of Saba' was a great people, divided into ten branches: al-Azd, Kinda, Madhhij, al-Ash'ariyyun, Anmar, Bajila, 'Amila, who are Khuza'a, Ghassan, Lakhm, and Judham.

When they left their homelands, the first six scattered in Yemen, and the last four went out to distant regions. Al-Azd joined 'Uman, Khuza'a joined Tihama in Makkah, al-Aws and al-Khazraj joined Yathrib, and perhaps they are counted among Lakhm. Ghassan joined Busra and al-Ghuwayr in the lands of al-Sham, and Lakhm joined Iraq.

The storytellers have mentioned a cause for this dispersion that is more like fables, so I have turned away from mentioning it, though it exists in the books of biographies and histories. In my view, that was a forsaking by God, the Exalted, who took from them the capacity to reflect on consequences. So Satan made their intellects light, and they grew anxious at the reversal of their condition. They did not clothe themselves with patience when the blessing was taken from them, and they did not turn to God in repentance. So anxiety, rebellion, obstinacy, and the bad management of their leaders drove them to leave their homelands, instead of gathering their scattered affairs and mending their breach, and so they were dispersed in the earth. It is not hidden what they encountered in that: fatigue, hunger, loss of persons, camels, provisions, and settling among peoples who did not pity their condition nor allow them to share their wealth, so they were left as dependents among them.

[p. 180]

The sentence "﴿Indeed, in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful person﴾" is a concluding remark (tadhyil), which is why it is separated (from the preceding clause). Its opening with the emphatic particle "inna" is for emphasis on the importance of the lesson. What is indicated by "dhalika" (that) is what preceded it in His words: "﴿Indeed there was for Saba' in their dwellings a sign﴾" (Saba' 34:15).

It appears that this concluding remark marks the end of the story, and that what follows this sentence is connected to the first purpose, which relates to the statements of the polytheists, and moves from it to the lesson drawn from Dawud and Sulayman, with the condition of the polytheists illustrated by the condition of the people of Saba'.

"Al-Ayat" (the signs) is in the plural because that story contains many signs and lessons. The condition of their dwellings is a sign of God's power, His mercy, and His bounty. In it is a sign that He is the One who disposes of affairs; in the sending of the flood upon them is a sign of His singular disposal of affairs, and that He is the Avenger, and that He is One. Therefore He punished them for associating partners with Him. In the reversal of their condition from ease to hardship is a sign of the alternation of conditions and the changing of the world, and a sign of the attributes of states belonging to God, the Exalted: creation, provision, giving life, and causing death. In that is a sign of the impossibility of feeling secure that a state of good or evil will endure. In what existed of the prosperity of their region and the expansion of their villages up to the lands of al-Sham is a sign of the extent of prosperity and the greatness of authority among the signs of divine dispositions, and a sign that security is the foundation of prosperity. In their wish for the removal of that is a sign of the degree of decline that the intellects may reach, leading to the disruption of a nation's affairs and the loss of its greatness. In what they came to of displacement from their homelands and dispersal in the earth is a sign of what necessity compels people to, of undertaking dangers and hardships, as the proverb says: "Fever has nursed me to you."

The combination of "sabbar" (steadfast) and "shakur" (grateful) in the description is to convey that the duty of the believer is to adorn himself with both qualities: patience in the face of hardships, and gratitude for blessings. These people spoken of did not give thanks for the blessing, so they became insolent toward it, and they did not endure patiently what befell them when it was removed. So their souls were disturbed and anxiety overtook them, and they left their homes and scattered in the earth. Do not ask about what they suffered in that of ruin and humiliation.

The steadfast person takes lessons from those conditions, knowing that patience in the face of hardships is better than anxiety, and chooses the lesser of two harms. Anxiety does not make him light-headed so that he throws himself into dangers without looking at consequences.

[p. 181]

The grateful person takes lessons from the blessings he has been given, so he increases in gratitude to God, the Exalted, does not become insolent toward the blessing, and does not transgress, lest he be punished by having it taken away as it was taken from them. Beyond that, God may deprive them of success and cast them, through abandonment, into the crooked paths.

The verse clearly indicates that securing the roads, facilitating communication, and bringing lands closer together for the easy exchange of benefits and the procurement of livelihoods from here and there, is a divine blessing and a legislated objective that God loves for whomever He wishes to show mercy among His servants. As He, the Exalted, said: "﴿And when We made the House a place of return for people and a sanctuary﴾" (Al-Baqarah 2:125), and He said: "﴿and He gave them security from fear﴾" (Quraysh 106:4). Therefore He says here: "﴿And We placed between them and the towns that We had blessed other visible towns, and We determined the travel between them: 'Travel through them by night and by day in security.'﴾" (Saba' 34:18)

Also, excessive neglect in rendering a blessing its due thanks exposes it to loss and to the reversal of circumstances. God, the Exalted, says: ﴿God presents a parable: a city that was secure and tranquil, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place, yet it denied the favours of God, so God made it taste the garment of hunger and fear, because of what they used to do.﴾ [al-Nahl: 112].

Because of all of this, it was a duty upon the rulers of the affairs of the Ummah to strive with all their effort to secure the lands, guard the roads, facilitate travel, and establish security in all regions of the country, both great and small, by every available means. This was among the most important purposes on which the wealth of the Muslims is spent, and on which the people of goodness among the affluent expend their wealth as aid toward this end. This is part of the mercy toward the people of the earth, in accordance with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Show mercy to those on the earth, and He who is in heaven will show mercy to you."

It was also a duty upon the people of knowledge and religion to guide the leaders and the Ummah to the path of goodness, and to draw attention to the landmarks and routes of that path in detail rather than in generalities, for the Ummah has become in need of action and has grown weary of mere words.

[Page 182]

﴿And Iblis indeed found his assumption about them to be true, so they followed him, except for a group of the believers.﴾ ﴿He had no authority over them, except that We might know who believes in the Hereafter from one who is in doubt about it. And your Lord is Guardian over all things.﴾

The more apparent view is that this is a conjunction (ʿatf) with His saying, ﴿And those who disbelieved said: Shall we direct you to a man who...﴾ (verse 7), and that what lies between them, the narratives presented for the purpose of admonition as already mentioned, stands as a digression (istitrad) and parenthetical insertion (iʿtirad). Accordingly, the pronoun in ʿalayhim ("concerning them") refers to those who disbelieved in His saying, ﴿And those who disbelieved said: Shall we direct you...﴾ and so on. What the exegetes have commonly followed is that the pronoun in ʿalayhim refers to Saba', the people spoken of. However, there is no escape from the fact that His saying after this, ﴿Say: Call upon those whom you claimed besides God...﴾ and the verses that follow, returns to the argument against the polytheists, from which the discourse had shifted to the story of Dawud and Sulayman and the people of Saba'. The suitability of the verse to both interpretations arises from its position, and this is among the eloquence of the Qur'an, which is derived from the arrangement of the verse's placement.

The purpose, then, is to alert the believers to the schemes of Satan and the evil outcome of his followers, so that they may beware of him, remain vigilant against his cunning, and not fall into the snare of his whispering.

The meaning is: Satan embellished for the polytheists, or embellished for those by whom the condition of the polytheists is exemplified, associating others with the Bestower of blessings, and made attractive to them the opposite of gratitude, until they came to desire it. He perceived in them a readiness to be deceived by him, so he cast his whispering upon them and made the counsel of the righteous among them hateful to them. Thus his surmise about them proved correct: that they would take up his call. They accepted it and turned away from its opposite, and so they followed him.

In His saying ﴿Iblis indeed found his assumption about them to be true﴾ there is concision by ellipsis (ijaz hadhf), because the truth of the assumption, from which their following derives, requires that he had called them to something while assuming that his call would be answered.

The majority of readers recited ṣadaqa with a light dal, so Iblis is the subject (fāʿil) and ẓannahu ("his assumption") is in the accusative by removal of the preposition (naṣb ʿalā nazʿ al-khāfiḍ), meaning "in his assumption." ʿAlayhim ("concerning them") is connected to ṣadaqa, by implying the sense of awqaʿa ("to inflict") or alqā ("to cast"), meaning he inflicted his assumption upon them, and it proved true concerning them. The sense of ṣidq here is correctness in assumption, since correctness corresponds to reality, and so it belongs to the category of truth. Abu al-Ghul al-Tuhawi, one of the poets of the Hamasa (anthology of poetry), said:

"My soul and what my right hand possesses are ransom for the horsemen concerning whom my assumptions proved true."

[Page 183]

ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾi and Khalaf read ṣaddaqa with a doubled dal, meaning he made his assumption concerning them come true when they were deceived by his whispering. When he whispered to them, he assumed that they would obey him, so he persisted in whispering until he overpowered them, and thus he made his assumption concerning them come true.

In ʿalā ("concerning") there is an indication that Iblis's action was of the kind of domination and overpowering over them.

His saying ﴿so they followed him﴾ is a consequence and sequel (tafrīʿ wa taʿqīb) to the act ﴿Iblis indeed found his assumption about them to be true﴾, meaning: his assumption was realized when they yielded to the act of his whispering, and they hastened to act upon what he called them to of association and ingratitude.

The phrase ﴿except for a group﴾ is an exception (istithnāʾ) from the pronoun of the nominative in ﴿so they followed him﴾. It is a connected exception (muttaṣil) if the pronoun in ittabaʿūhu refers to the polytheists. If it refers to the people of Saba', then it may be connected if there were believers among them, otherwise it is a disconnected exception (munqaṭiʿ), meaning that none disobeyed him in that matter except a group of believers, who were those among the people of Mecca who believed, or those among the people of Saba' who believed. Perhaps among them there was a group of believers who were saved before the sending of the flood of al-ʿArim (Sayl al-ʿArim).

Firqa ("group") means a company in general. Its being made an exception from the plural pronoun indicates that they were few in comparison with the rest. Otherwise, firqa applies to a large multitude, as in His saying, ﴿a group He guided, and a group upon whom misguidance was decreed﴾ [7:30].

The definite article in al-muʾminīn is for comprehensiveness (istighrāq), and min is partitive (tabʿīḍiyya), meaning: except for a group that are some of the communities of believers across times and lands.

His saying ﴿He had no authority over them﴾ means that Satan had no authority over those who followed him.

The verb kāna in negation, together with min which indicates total comprehensiveness in negation, implies the absence of authority, meaning dominion and control, for Satan. That is, he has no inherent power by which he is independent and with which he disposes of the world as he wills, because that power belongs exclusively to God, exalted is He.

The exception in ﴿except that We might know﴾ is an exception from causes (istithnāʾ min ʿilal). It implies that his influence over them through whispering was by God's empowerment. That is, We made Satan a cause that reaches their intellects and wills, so his whispering penetrates them. Thus a group is affected by it and a group is saved from it, according to the strength of being affected and resisting that God placed in these and those, in accordance with the laws God placed in created beings.

It is also permissible that the exception be from the general scope of authority (sulṭān), with the excepted item omitted and indicated by its cause. The estimated meaning is: except an authority by which We might know who believes in the Hereafter. This indicates that it is an authority granted to him by God's appointment, supported by the fact that its cause is attributed to the pronoun of the Majesty (ḍamīr al-jalāla).

Refer to what we said at His saying, ﴿Indeed My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the misguided﴾ [al-Hijr: 42], in Surat al-Hijr, and add it to what we have said here.

Whoever gave the reason for empowering Satan with authority limited it to distinguishing between those who believe in the Hereafter and those who do not, in consideration of the condition of those to whom admonition was previously addressed, namely the people of Saba', who were the disbelievers of Quraysh. This is because their denial is coupled with polytheism and equivalent to it, for if they believed in the Hereafter they would believe in its Lord, who is the one Lord with no partner. Otherwise, the causes for making Satan a source of whispering are many, and they return to distinguishing disbelievers from believers and the God-fearing from those who turn away.

"We know" (nuʿlim) is used as a metonymy (kināya) for making the distinction between the two states apparent, because manifestation in custom entails knowledge. Qabisa al-Ta'i, one of the men of the battle of Dhi Qar, said:

"I advanced while the spear swayed between us, that I might know which of them is the coward and which the brave."

He meant that the coward would be distinguished from the brave, so that people would know it, for his principal aim was to display the courage of his own self, out of confidence in it, not to test the courage of his rivals. Otherwise he would have been hesitant in advancing. The meaning therefore is: that there may become manifest one who believes in the Hereafter and be distinguished from one who is in doubt about it, so that whoever knows it will know it. Our knowledge is connected to this in a particular (juzʾī) way at the time of its occurrence, upon which reward is consequently based. We mentioned earlier that there is no escape from considering a realizing connection (taʿalluq tanjīzī) to God's knowledge. I saw in the al-Risala al-Khaqaniyya of ʿAbd al-Hakim al-Salkuti that some scholars affirmed this connection but did not specify who said it.

The composition differs between the two relative clauses. The clause ﴿who believes in the Hereafter﴾ is verbal (fiʿliyya), while the clause ﴿who is in doubt about it﴾ is nominal (ismiyya). This is because belief in the Hereafter is something that arose after their previous disbelief, renewed and increasing moment by moment, so the situation required that the verb be placed in the relative clause of its adherents. As for their doubt about the Hereafter, it is, unlike that, something rooted within them, so the nominal clause was brought for its adherents.

[Page 184]

[Page 185]

The particle of location (ḥarf al-ẓarfiyya) "in" (fī) is used to indicate that doubt encompasses their souls. The phrase ﴿about it﴾ (minhā) is connected to "doubt" (shakk). The clause ﴿And your Lord is Guardian over all things﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyīl). Al-Ḥafīẓ is the one from whose power nothing under his guard escapes. It implies knowledge and power, since the reality of guarding is constituted by both together. For this reason guarding is often followed by knowledge, as in His saying, ﴿Indeed I am a Guardian, Knowing﴾ [Yusuf: 55]. The pattern faʿīl indicates the strength of the act. The generality of ﴿all things﴾ indicates that nothing among existing beings escapes His knowledge. Thus this concluding clause stands in the position of a safeguard against any meaning other than the implicit meaning of His saying ﴿that We might know who believes in the Hereafter from one who is in doubt about it﴾, that is, so that this may become manifest to everyone, and the proof will stand for them and against them.
