[p. 186]

The story of Sheba (Saba') had been presented as an example and a lesson for the polytheists of Quraysh. Their circumstances resembled those of the polytheists in the security of their land, the ease of their provision, and the safety of their routes on their journeys. This is indicated by His saying ﴿Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary, to which the fruits of every thing are brought?﴾ [al-Qasas: 57], and His saying ﴿For the covenant of the Quraysh﴾ [Quraysh: 1], through to the end of the surah. Then [the lesson concerns] how they met God's blessing with association (shirk) and ingratitude for His blessing, and how they confronted with hostility those who called them to good, those who were inspired from Him to call them. When the account of them was concluded, the discourse moved on to applying the lesson to those intended to take heed from it. This transition is clearly connected. It is also a return to refuting the claims of the polytheists, and the speech directed at them contains a rebuke for their errors. Furthermore, since the Shaytan (Satan) had misled the people of Sheba and they followed him, and since the Shaytan is the source of misguidance and the essence of association, the discourse mentioned him, followed by mention of his branches and his allies.

The speech opens with the command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to say to them what follows in the rest of these consecutive verses, with the word "say" (qul). He was commanded to speak, renewing the meaning of conveying the message, which is the mission of the whole Qur'an.

[p. 187]

The imperative in His saying "call upon" (ud'ū) is used for reproach and rebuke, meaning: continue in your calling [upon them].

"Those whom you claimed besides God" means "those whom you claimed to be lords." The two objects of the verb "claimed" are omitted. The first is omitted because it is an attached pronoun in the accusative governed by the verb, omitted for the sake of lightening the connection with its complements. The second is omitted because its qualifier indicates it, namely "besides God."

"Besides God" is a qualifier of an omitted noun, whose estimate is: "you claimed them to be allies."

The meaning of "besides God" is that they start from a direction other than the direction of God, i.e., you claimed them to be gods, taking them from a source other than God. This is because when they worship them, they are occupied with their worship and neglect the worship of God, who alone deserves worship, and they exceed the right of His divinity in many states and at many times.

The clause "they do not possess" explains the rebuke contained in "call upon those whom you claimed." The utmost lowliness is denied of them: they do not possess even what equals an atom's weight in the heavens and the earth.

The "atom" (dharra) is the egg of an ant, which appears as a small white grain. This was discussed at His saying ﴿And not an atom's weight is hidden from your Lord﴾ [Yunus: 61] in the surah of Yunus. By "the heavens and the earth" is meant their substance and essence, with what they contain of existing things, since the polytheists do not claim that their substance holds any dominion for their gods. As for "mithqal": it is either a name for the weights with which things are weighed, so it was applied figuratively by metonymic usage (majāz mursal) to the equivalent; or it is a noun of measure (maṣdar mīmī) by which the weight is named, and then it was applied figuratively to the equivalent. "Mithqal" was discussed at His saying ﴿even if it be the weight of a grain of mustard seed﴾ in the surah of al-Anbiya'.

The "mithqal of the atom" is what equals an atom, by which the scale is weighed down; that is, they possess nothing of the heavens or the earth. The repetition of the negative particle is for emphasis, to draw attention to it.

Then He denied that they have any helper (ẓahīr) from among them, that is, one who assists God, the Exalted. His saying "in submission to His word" means in fear and awe. His saying "fear is removed from their hearts" means that dread is lifted from their souls.

That does not mean it is what is intended in the verse of Surah Saba', but rather this is the manner in which the angels receive God's command in this world and the next, so their words follow one single pattern.

Al-Bukhari's and al-Tirmidhi's transmission of this hadith in the discussion of the interpretation of Surah Saba' does not mean that it is related concerning that; rather, they intend that among the forms of its meaning is what is mentioned in Surah Saba'. This spares you from resorting to the artificial constructions that some have strained to use in interpreting this verse and connecting it to what precedes it.

This is indicated by His saying ﴿Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary, to which the fruits of every thing are brought?﴾ [al-Qasas: 57], and His saying ﴿For the covenant of the Quraysh﴾ [Quraysh: 1], through to the end of the surah. Then [the lesson concerns] how they met God's blessing with association (shirk) and ingratitude for His blessing, and how they confronted with hostility those who called them to good, those who were inspired from Him to call them. When the account of them was concluded, the discourse moved on to applying the lesson to those intended to take heed from it. This transition is clearly connected. It is also a return to refuting the claims of the polytheists, and the speech directed at them contains a rebuke for their errors. Furthermore, since the Shaytan (Satan) had misled the people of Sheba and they followed him, and since the Shaytan is the source of misguidance and the essence of association, the discourse mentioned him, followed by mention of his branches and his allies.

The speech opens with the command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to say to them what follows in the rest of these consecutive verses, with the word "say" (qul). He was commanded to speak, renewing the meaning of conveying the message, which is the mission of the whole Qur'an.

Know that it is reported regarding the manner in which the angels receive revelation that whoever among the angels receives revelation asks the One who conveys it to him with words like these, as in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and others: that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) said: "When God decrees a matter in the heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His word, like a chain upon a smooth rock. And when fear is removed from their hearts, they say: 'What has your Lord said?' They say: 'The truth,' and He is the Most High, the Great." End of quote.

So His saying in the hadith, "decrees," means that the command of creation proceeded from Him, which the angels are charged with carrying out. His saying in the hadith, "in the heaven," is connected to "decrees" in the sense of conveying His decree to the heaven, where the angels dwell. His saying "in submission to His word" means in fear and awe. His saying "fear is removed from their hearts" means that dread is lifted from their souls.

In the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas from al-Tirmidhi: "When our Lord decrees a matter, the bearers of the Throne glorify Him, then the people of the heaven nearest to them glorify Him, and so on, then the people of each heaven," and so on, the hadith.

That does not mean it is what is intended in the verse of Surah Saba', but rather this is the manner in which the angels receive God's command in this world and the next, so their words follow one single pattern.

Al-Bukhari's and al-Tirmidhi's transmission of this hadith in the discussion of the interpretation of Surah Saba' does not mean that it is related concerning that; rather, they intend that among the forms of its meaning is what is mentioned in Surah Saba'. This spares you from resorting to the artificial constructions that some have strained to use in interpreting this verse and connecting it to what precedes it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 24:

﴿Say: "Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?" Say: "Allah. And indeed we or you are either upon guidance or in manifest error."﴾ This is a transition from crushing the polytheists by showing the weakness of their gods and the uselessness of those gods for them in this world and the Hereafter, to obligating them to acknowledge the falsehood of worshipping them, because they do not deserve worship. The one who deserves worship is the one who provides for His servants, since worship is gratitude, and only the Benefactor deserves gratitude.

[p. 192]
This is an argument by rational proof: that Allah is the Provider necessarily entails that He alone is God, since it is not permissible for Him to be singled out for some attributes of divinity while being shared in others. Divinity is a reality that does not accept division or partition.

The command "say" is repeated to increase attention to what is said, for the original command to "say," in the context of confronting the delivery of the message, already indicates attention, and repeating that command adds to the attention.

"Man" (مَنِ) here is an interrogative used to draw attention to an error. Therefore it is followed by the answer from the questioner's side in His words, "Say: Allah," because it is established that they do not deny that answer, as in His exalted saying, "Say: Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth, or who owns hearing and sight?" up to His saying, "They will say: Allah," in Surah Yunus. The beginning of this verse has a parallel in Surah al-Ra'd.

Coordinating with the interrogative is the presentation of the purpose in a subtle manner that brings the opponent into the trap of defeat. This is done by dividing the two groups' states between the state of guidance and the state of error. Since the state of each group is the opposite of the state of the other group, between conformity with the truth and non-conformity, it is determined that the matter of error and guidance revolves between the two states and does not exceed them. For this reason the particle "or" (أوْ), which indicates division derived from doubt, was used.

This style of speech is called "the equitable speech" (al-kalam al-munsif), which is that the disputant does not leave his opponent anything that provokes anger and heated contention in the debate. In the science of debate (ilm al-munazara) it is called "loosening the reins for the debater." Nevertheless, the indication of their being bound by the proof is a clear indication.

Among its subtleties here is that it contains an allusion to preferring one side over the other in one of the two possibilities, by way of contrasting the two sides in the arrangement of the two states through lafv wa nashr (a rhetorical device in which two or more things are mentioned together and then their corresponding counterparts are mentioned in order), which is the original form of lafv.

He mentioned the pronoun of the speaker's side and his group, and the side of the addressees. Then he mentioned the state of guidance and the state of error in the order of mention of the two sides. Thus he indicated that the first are directed toward guidance and the latter are directed toward manifest error, especially after the interrogative indication. This is also an allusion (ta'rid), which is more effective than explicit statement, especially in bringing down the opponent's bird (i.e., in drawing the opponent's mind down to the desired conclusion).

It also contains tajahul al-'arif (feigned ignorance by one who knows, a rhetorical device in which the speaker pretends not to know what he knows). Thus three embellishments of rhetorical art (badi') and a point of eloquence (bayan) came together in this sentence, and it included four distinctive features.

[p. 193]
For the side of the people of guidance, the particle of elevation (حرف الاستعلاء, "upon") was used, borrowed to signify control, as a representation of the state of the one who is guided by the state of one who manages his horse, driving it wherever he wishes, one who has control over something by which he reaches his goal. This is a state similar to the state of the one who is guided with insight, for he retrieves the paths of truth from every direction, with broad vision and an open breast. Therefore there is in it a metaphorical representation (tamthiliyya makniyya) and a subordinate one (tab'iyya).

For the side of those who are astray, the particle of inclusion (حرف الظرفية, "in") was used, borrowed to signify the intensity of being engulfed by the attribute, as a representation of their state in which error encompasses them, by the state of a thing in a container surrounding it, which does not leave it, does not separate from it, and does not allow it to see beyond what it is in of narrowness that clings to it. Therefore there is also in it a subordinate metaphorical representation. This relates to His exalted saying, "Whoever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam; and whoever He wills to lead astray, He makes his breast constricted and tight," ﴿Surah al-An'am 6:125﴾.

Thus there occurred in the verse four metaphors (isti'arat), three embellishments of rhetorical art, a rhetorical style (uslub bayani), and an established proof. This is a wondrous inimitability (i'jaz badi').

The description of error as "manifest" (مُبِين) rather than describing guidance as "manifest" is because the reality of guidance is predicated univocally (بالتواطؤ, i.e., applying equally to all instances). This is the meaning of the statement of our companions, the Ash'ariyya (the followers of al-Ash'ari, the school of Sunni theology): faith does not increase or decrease in its essence, and its increase is only through the abundance of acts of obedience. As for disbelief, it occurs by denying some of the beliefs and by denying all of them, and all of this is truly called disbelief. For this reason it is said: "disbelief is of one degree below another." So He described their disbelief as the most intense disbelief, for "manifest" means clear within its genus, reaching the utmost extent of its limit.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 25:

﴿Say: You will not be questioned about what we committed in sin, nor will we be questioned about what you do.﴾ The command is repeated, that he should say to them another statement, as a renewed emphasis (li-ziyadat al-ihtimam), as was mentioned just before, and as a summons to the ears of the addressees to listen to it.

Since this statement contains an elucidation (bayan) of the statement that precedes it, the clause of the command "say" is disconnected (fusilat) from its sister clause, for an elucidation (al-bayan) is not joined to what it elucidates by a conjunctive particle (harf al-nasq). When he (the speaker) had placed the matter of the two groups between one being upon guidance and the other being in error, and error brings about sin (al-ijram), the debate expanded. So it was said to them: If we have committed sin, you are not held accountable for our sin, and if you have done a deed, we are not held accountable for it. That is, each group is held accountable alone for its own deed; so it is more profitable for both groups that each look at its own deeds and the deeds of its opponent, so that it may know which of the two groups is more deserving of success and salvation with God.

Also, the clause was separated so that this sentence would stand independently by itself, so that the listener would single it out for reflection on its meaning. Thus it may be regarded as a fresh independent beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i), and yet with that it is a clear interjection (i'tiraD bayyin) in the midst of the argument.

So the meaning of "You will not be questioned, nor will we be questioned" is that each group has its own particular fate (khuwayyisatuhu).

And "questioning" (al-su'al) is a metonymy (kinaya) for its effect, which is the reward for a righteous deed and the requital for sin with its like, as is in the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

"It was said that you are one who is blamed and one who is held to account (mas'ul)."

He meant "and one who is held to account (mu'akhadh) for what came from you before," in reference to his previous line:

"That is more awe-inspiring to me, when I speak to him..."

The attribution of sin to the side of the speaker and those with him is based on the claim of the addressees. And God, Exalted, said: "And when they see them they say: Indeed, these are surely astray" (83:32). The polytheists used to rebuke the believers for being sinners in avoiding the worship of their people's idols.

This is the subtle point of phrasing it in the past tense (sigha al-madi), because it is established by the claim of the polytheists. And what the polytheists do is phrased in the present tense (al-mudari'), because they are awaiting from them a deed, as an allusion (ta'rid) that they will do a deed other than what they had done, that is, that they will believe in God after their disbelief.

This is a kind of courtesy (mushaaraka wa-muwada'a) and a conciliatory approach, so that they may be alone with themselves and consider their situation, and so that the disputation of the believers does not distract them from reviewing and taking account of themselves. They attributed the action in its unrestricted sense to the side of the addressees, because reflection and contemplation after that reveals the reality of both actions.

This verse has no connection to the matter of participation in fighting (mushaarakat al-qital), so it is not to be regarded as abrogated (mansukha) by the verses of fighting.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 26:

Page 195
﴿Say: Our Lord will gather us together, then He will judge between us with truth, and He is the Judge, the All-Knowing.﴾ The repetition of the verb "Say" (qul) is due to what you have learned in the preceding sentence of the increased emphasis on these disputations, so that each argument stands on its own, not conjoined by a conjunction; thus this sentence is an initial resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i).

Also, it stands in the position of an explanation (bayan) of the preceding sentence, because the negation of the questioning of each party about the deeds of the other implies that there is a questioning about one's own deeds. So it clarifies that the One who asks people about their deeds is God Most High, and that He is the One who separates the two parties with truth when He gathers them on the Day of Resurrection, the day whose occurrence they deny. So consider what their state will be on the day when what they denied comes to pass.

Here the disputation progressed from allusion to a near indication, close to explicit statement, because affirming the Day of Reckoning and the questioning carries the implication of plainly declaring that they are the misguided. This progression is called by the people of disputation "al-taraqqi" (ascent).

Al-fath means judgment and separation with truth, as in His saying, ﴿Our Lord, judge between us and our people with truth, and You are the best of judges﴾ [al-A'raf: 89]. It is derived from opening a small window (kuwwa) to reveal what is behind it.

The sentence ﴿and He is the Judge, the All-Knowing﴾ is a concluding appendage (tadhyil) describing Him, may He be exalted, with abundance of judgment, its strength, and the comprehensiveness of knowledge. For this reason it is a concluding appendage to the sentence ﴿Our Lord will gather us together, then He will judge between us with truth﴾, which contains a particular judgment, so it is concluded with a general attribute. He follows al-Fattah with al-'Alim only to indicate that His judgment is pure justice, because He is All-Knowing, and no causes of error or injustice arising from ignorance and incapacity, or from following psychological weakness arising from ignorance of circumstances and outcomes, surround His judgment.

[Page 196]

﴿Say: Show me those whom you have joined with Him as partners. Nay! Rather, He is Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ The command to speak has been repeated for the fourth time, for the sake of greater emphasis. This returns to the point that the argument against the falsity of polytheism is, in effect, a conclusion drawn from the earlier sentence: ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?﴾

The imperative in "Show me" (arūnī) is used to express incapacitation (ta'jīz, the challenge that the opponent cannot meet). It is a challenge to the polytheists to produce any proof for their association of partners. It is a transition from arguing against the divinity of the idols by means of analogy, as in "Say: Who provides for you," to refuting it by means of what is self-evident (badāha). Among the methods of disputation (jadal), the method of questioning (istifsār) is, according to the terminology of the dialecticians, normally placed before the other methods of debate. It is placed here instead because it would have resulted in the complete refutation of the opponent's claim, so it was deliberately delayed, so that the exposure of the opponent through the preceding proofs would not be lost, thereby spreading out the ground of the argument, so that every proof calls out against the opponents' error and falsehood. The exposure of error is among the aims of the debater whose argument is upheld.

The "showing" (ird'a) here is from visual seeing (al-ru'yah al-baṣariyyah), and so it takes two objects: one directly, and the second by means of the transitivizing hamza.

The intended meaning is: "Show me their persons, so that we may see whether there is on them anything that befits the attribute of divinity." That is, anyone who looks upon the idols for the first time will realise that they are devoid of the attributes of divinity, for he sees stones that neither hear, nor see, nor understand. The absence of divinity from the idols is self-evident, and it requires no more than seeing their state, as in the words of al-Buhturi:

"That one who sees should see, and that one who hears should be aware."

The expression of the thing seen by means of a relative construction (al-mawṣūliyyah) serves to alert the addressees to their error in making them partners with God in lordship, in the manner of the words of 'Abdah ibn al-Ṭabīb:

"Verily, those whom you see as your brothers, their burning hearts will be soothed by your being struck down."

In making the relative clause "you have joined" (alḥaqtum) indicates that those idols were not described with divinity as a true, essential attribute, but that the polytheists attached them to God, Most High. That is a title of honour which the people of caprice have conferred upon them. This state contradicts the attribute of divinity, since divinity is an essential, eternal attribute. This attachment was invented for them by 'Amr ibn Luḥayy, and it was not known among the Arabs before him. The pronoun in "with Him" (bihi) refers to the Divine Name (ism al-jalālah) in the phrase ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth? Say: Allah﴾.

The word "partners" (shurakā'a) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the relative pronoun. The meaning is: partners to Him.

[Page 197]

Since he turned away from delving into the consequences of this showing, it is understood that they will be exposed at that showing, so it is assumed as already accomplished. The request for its realisation is followed by the affirmation of its effect, which is the restraint from believing in their divinity, and the nullification of it for them by affirming it for God alone. Therefore he combined the two particles of restraint and negation (al-radc and al-ibṭāl), then moved to specifying the true God, in the manner of His words: ﴿Nay! Rather, you do not honour the orphan﴾.

The pronoun in "He is Allah" (huwa Allāh) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n). The sentence following it is an explanation of the meaning of the matter. "The Mighty" and "the Wise" are two predicates. That is: "Rather, the important matter is: Allah, the Mighty, the Wise, not your gods." So in the sentence there is a restriction of might and wisdom to God, Most High, as a metonymy for restricting divinity to Him, Most High, in a restriction of exclusivity (qaṣr ifrād).

It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the God understood from the phrase "those whom you have joined with Him as partners," in which case it is a subject (mubtada'), and the sentence after it is its predicate. It is also permissible for it to refer to the one present in the mind, which is Allah. Its explanation is His saying "Allah," so the Divine Name is an appositive (ʿaṭf bayān). "The Mighty" and "the Wise" are two predicates of the pronoun. The difference between this aspect and the first aspect appears in the difference in the referent of the detached pronoun, the difference in the position of the Divine Name after it, and the difference in the position of the sentence after that.

Might (al-'izzah) is independence from others. The Wise (al-ḥakīm) is an adjective derived from wisdom (al-ḥikmah), which is the furthest extent of knowledge, or from ordering (al-iḥkām), which is the perfecting of workmanship; the term is widely used for both meanings. This is an affirmation of the deficiency of their idols and the absence of knowledge from them. This is the saying of Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees, nor avails you at all?﴾

[Page 198]

This is a shift from refuting the polytheists' error concerning lordship (rububiyyah) to refuting their error concerning the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ.

The style of address changed from arguing with the polytheists to informing them of the Prophet's ﷺ mission, honouring him by directing this information to him concerning this great blessing. The refutation of the polytheists' claims is achieved by way of allusion (ta'ridh).

In this verse there is an affirmation of the mission of Muhammad ﷺ and an affirmation of its universality against those who deny it among the Jews.

"Kaffatan" is one of the words of generality (alfaz al-'umum). It occurs here as a circumstantial accusative (hal) of "al-nas" (mankind), an exception from the general category of states. It is a hal placed before its referent (sahibuha), which is the genitive noun governed by the preposition. Discussion of it has already passed at the words of the Exalted, ﴿يا أيها الذين آمنوا ادخلوا في السلم كافة﴾ [al-Baqarah: 208] in Surat al-Baqarah, and at His words ﴿وقاتلوا المشركين كافة﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36] in Surat Bara'ah. We mentioned that the correct view is that "kaffatan" may be applied to a rational being and to other than a rational being, and that it admits the various grammatical cases (wujuh al-i'rab), as preferred by al-Zamakhshari (al-Zamakhshari), and as the Qur'an and usage confirm, contrary to Ibn Hisham in Mughni al-Labib (Mughni al-Labib), and that what was used to stress the indefiniteness according to al-Zamakhshari is an exaggeration and a restriction in permissibility. The sense of this verse is: "And We have not sent you to mankind except comprehensively." He placed the hal before its referent to give it prominence, because it encompasses all those who disbelieved in his mission.

Placing the hal before the genitive noun is permissible according to the view of the verifying scholars among the grammarians, although al-Zamakhshari rejected it here and treated it as equivalent to placing the genitive before the preposition. So he made "kaffatan" a qualifier (na't) of a deleted noun, meaning "his sending comprehensively," i.e., generally. Ibn Malik (Ibn Malik) refuted him in al-Tashil (al-Tashil) and said: "Abu 'Ali al-Farisi (Abu 'Ali al-Farisi) and Ibn Kaysan (Ibn Kaysan) permitted it in this verse." I say: Ibn 'Atiyyah (Ibn 'Atiyyah) and al-Radi (al-Radi) also permitted it. Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj) made "kaffatan" here a hal of the kaf in "arsalnaka" and interpreted it as meaning "gathering mankind in warning and conveying," and Abu al-Baqa' (Abu al-Baqa') followed him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The tා' (ta' marbuta) in this interpretation should be for emphasis (mubalaghah), like the ta' in 'allamah' and 'rawiyah,' and likewise the placing of the excepted element first is also for this purpose."

Al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari here both agreed in removing "kaffatan" from the meaning of description by conveying comprehensiveness, which is a partial comprehensiveness with respect to a specific purpose, to the meaning of total collective inclusiveness derived from that. This is like one who aims at "kull" (all) and says: "Innaka kullun lil-nas," meaning "you are one who gathers mankind." Or one who aims at "'ala" (on), which indicates partial elevation, and uses it in the sense of total elevation, saying: "Iyyaka wa 'ala," meaning "beware of arrogance (al-isti'la')."

"Al-bashir al-nadhir" (the bringer of good news and the warner) has already been discussed in the words of the Exalted, ﴿إنا أرسلناك بالحق بشيرا ونذيرا﴾ [Fatir: 24] in al-Baqarah.

[Page 199]

The structure "wa ma arsalnaka illa kaffatan lil-nas" (We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind) conveys the restriction (qasr) of the universality of the mission to the second-person pronoun (kaf al-khitab) in "arsalnaka." It is a relative restriction (qasr idafi), meaning: not restricted to the people of Makkah, or to the Arabs, or to those who come to you seeking faith and guidance, as 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul (Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul) said to the Prophet ﷺ when he came to a gathering in which he was present and recited the Qur'an to them. Ibn Ubayy said: "Nothing you say is better than this, O man, but sit in your place, and whoever comes to you, recite to him."

This requires the affirmation of his mission by implication (dalalat al-iqtida'), since that restriction is true only if the basic fact of his mission is established. Thus it entails a refutation of all those who deny it, both those who deny his mission from its origin and those who deny its universality and claim it is restricted.

The function of the corrective contrast (istidrak) in the words "wa lakinna akthar al-nas la ya'lamun" (but most people do not know) is to remove what might be suspected: that one might be deceived by the large number of those who deny his mission, thinking that their multitude should deceive the reflective person. Rather, they do not know.

The object of "ya'lamun" (know) is deleted, because what precedes it indicates it. The meaning is: they do not know what you have given good news of to the believers and what you have warned the disbelievers about; that is, they consider the good news and the warning untrue.

It is also possible that the verb "ya'lamun" is treated as equivalent to the negated state of knowledge, the intent being to negate the attribute of knowledge from them, in accordance with the Exalted's words, ﴿قل هل يستوي الذين يعلمون والذين لا يعلمون﴾ [al-Zumar: 9], meaning: but most people are ignorant of the value of the good news and the warning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 29–30:

﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you should be truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say, "For you is an appointment of a Day from which you will not remain behind an hour, nor precede [it]."﴾ The resurrection and the raising (al-ba'th) were among the greatest things the Messenger (ﷺ) brought that they denied. For this reason, the refutation of their claim in denying the message is followed by the refutation of their claim in denying the resurrection. The sentence is conjoined to the predicate of "but" (lakinna). The implied sense is: "But most people do not know the true meaning of good tidings and warning, and they mock, so they ask about the time of this promise, which is the very manifestation of good tidings and warning." It is also permissible for the sentence to be resumed (mustaʼnafa), with the waw being for resumption (li-l-istiʼnaf).

The pronoun in "yaqulun" refers to the disputing polytheists from whom this statement proceeded. The form of the present tense in "yaqulun" conveys astonishment at their statement, as in His saying, Exalted is He, "He disputes with us concerning the people of Lot" (11:74), together with conveying the repetition and renewal of that saying from them.

The sentence "Say, 'For you is an appointment of a Day...'" to its end is placed in the position of an answer to their statement, and for this reason it is detached and not conjoined, in the manner of relating dialogues in the Qur'an. This answer follows the method of the wise style (al-uslub al-hakim), meaning that what is most important for people of intellect is that their aspirations be directed toward the realization of the occurrence of the promise at the time Allah has appointed for it, and that nothing delays it or hastens it. What made this style fitting is that their question was intended only as a metonymy for the non-occurrence of it.

In this answer there is an oblique allusion to threat, so it corresponds to the intent of the interrogative. For this reason the word "lakum" ("for you") was added to the answer, indicating that this appointment is directed at them primarily.

The pronoun of the plural addressee in "in kuntum sadiqin" ("if you are truthful") refers either to the Messenger (ﷺ), in consideration that with him is a group who report this promise, or the address is directed to the Muslims.

The demonstrative in "hadha al-wa'd" ("this promise") is for belittling and disparagement, as in the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"Whenever this death comes, no need of my soul will remain except that I have fulfilled its fulfilment."

The answer to "in kuntum sadiqin" is indicated by the question, meaning: "If you are truthful, then specify for us the appointed time of this promise." This is speech issuing from ignorance, because truthfulness in reporting something does not necessitate that the reporter know the time of its occurrence, even in the past, so how much more so in the future. The expected form of the answer was departed from: instead of using the pronoun of the promise that occurred in their speech, the answer uses an explicit noun, "appointment of a Day," because of the ambiguity in this indefinite noun, which directs the minds of the listeners to every possible meaning of that expression: that it is the Day of Resurrection, or another day in which the punishment of the leaders of disbelief and the chiefs of the polytheists descends, namely the Day of Badr. Perhaps those who were killed on that day were the ones who uttered the saying "When is this promise, if you are truthful?" The indefiniteness of "a Day" conveys awe and magnification, by the context of the situation.

"Mi'ad" is a mimi noun meaning "promise," so its annexation to its time-expression is explicative (bayaniyya). It is also permissible for it to be used in the sense of time, and its annexation to "the Day" is explicative, because the appointment is the Day itself.

The sentence "la tasta'khirun 'anhu sa'ah" is either an attribute of "mi'ad" or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of "lakum."

"Al-isti'khar" and "al-istiqdam" are intensive forms of delay and advance, like "istajaba." The sin and the ta' are for emphasis.

He placed "al-isti'khar" before "al-istiqdam," as a hint that it is an appointment of force and punishment against them, whose nature is that they would wish for its delay. And "wa la tastaqdimun" completes its certainty at its appointed time in the knowledge of Allah.

"Al-sa'ah" is a portion of time, and its indefiniteness is for diminution, by the aid of the context.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 29–30:

﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you should be truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say, "For you is an appointment of a Day from which you will not remain behind an hour, nor precede [it]."﴾ The resurrection and the raising (al-ba'th) were among the greatest things the Messenger (ﷺ) brought that they denied. For this reason, the refutation of their claim in denying the message is followed by the refutation of their claim in denying the resurrection. The sentence is conjoined to the predicate of "but" (lakinna). The implied sense is: "But most people do not know the true meaning of good tidings and warning, and they mock, so they ask about the time of this promise, which is the very manifestation of good tidings and warning." It is also permissible for the sentence to be resumed (mustaʼnafa), with the waw being for resumption (li-l-istiʼnaf).

The pronoun in "yaqulun" refers to the disputing polytheists from whom this statement proceeded. The form of the present tense in "yaqulun" conveys astonishment at their statement, as in His saying, Exalted is He, "He disputes with us concerning the people of Lot" (11:74), together with conveying the repetition and renewal of that saying from them.

The sentence "Say, 'For you is an appointment of a Day...'" to its end is placed in the position of an answer to their statement, and for this reason it is detached and not conjoined, in the manner of relating dialogues in the Qur'an. This answer follows the method of the wise style (al-uslub al-hakim), meaning that what is most important for people of intellect is that their aspirations be directed toward the realization of the occurrence of the promise at the time Allah has appointed for it, and that nothing delays it or hastens it. What made this style fitting is that their question was intended only as a metonymy for the non-occurrence of it.

In this answer there is an oblique allusion to threat, so it corresponds to the intent of the interrogative. For this reason the word "lakum" ("for you") was added to the answer, indicating that this appointment is directed at them primarily.

The pronoun of the plural addressee in "in kuntum sadiqin" ("if you are truthful") refers either to the Messenger (ﷺ), in consideration that with him is a group who report this promise, or the address is directed to the Muslims.

The demonstrative in "hadha al-wa'd" ("this promise") is for belittling and disparagement, as in the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"Whenever this death comes, no need of my soul will remain except that I have fulfilled its fulfilment."

The answer to "in kuntum sadiqin" is indicated by the question, meaning: "If you are truthful, then specify for us the appointed time of this promise." This is speech issuing from ignorance, because truthfulness in reporting something does not necessitate that the reporter know the time of its occurrence, even in the past, so how much more so in the future. The expected form of the answer was departed from: instead of using the pronoun of the promise that occurred in their speech, the answer uses an explicit noun, "appointment of a Day," because of the ambiguity in this indefinite noun, which directs the minds of the listeners to every possible meaning of that expression: that it is the Day of Resurrection, or another day in which the punishment of the leaders of disbelief and the chiefs of the polytheists descends, namely the Day of Badr. Perhaps those who were killed on that day were the ones who uttered the saying "When is this promise, if you are truthful?" The indefiniteness of "a Day" conveys awe and magnification, by the context of the situation.

"Mi'ad" is a mimi noun meaning "promise," so its annexation to its time-expression is explicative (bayaniyya). It is also permissible for it to be used in the sense of time, and its annexation to "the Day" is explicative, because the appointment is the Day itself.

The sentence "la tasta'khirun 'anhu sa'ah" is either an attribute of "mi'ad" or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of "lakum."

"Al-isti'khar" and "al-istiqdam" are intensive forms of delay and advance, like "istajaba." The sin and the ta' are for emphasis.

He placed "al-isti'khar" before "al-istiqdam," as a hint that it is an appointment of force and punishment against them, whose nature is that they would wish for its delay. And "wa la tastaqdimun" completes its certainty at its appointed time in the knowledge of Allah.

"Al-sa'ah" is a portion of time, and its indefiniteness is for diminution, by the aid of the context.

[Page 202]

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "We will never believe in this Qur'an, nor in what came before it."﴾ When the call of Islam took them by surprise and its matter began to spread, the polytheists (al-mushrikun) adopted various methods to suppress that call. Before Islam appeared, they had been indifferent to discussing the earlier revealed laws (al-shara'i'). When the call of Islam struck their ears, their statements became inconsistent. They said, "God has not sent down anything upon any human being," and they said other things. Among these, they turned to the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab), who lived nearby in Medina, Khaybar and Qurayza, to receive from them prepared arguments (mulaqqanat) with which to confound the Prophet (ﷺ). The People of the Book would dictate to them, whenever they met, whatever might serve to confuse the people about the invalidity of the Muhammadan message. Sometimes they would say:

﴿"Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?"﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:48), and at other times they would say:

﴿"We will not believe you until you bring down to us a book we can read."﴾ (Al-Isra' 17:93). They often considered his sharing the ordinary human conditions with people to be incompatible with his being a messenger chosen by God for them. So they said, "What is wrong with this Messenger? He eats food and walks in the markets." They did not argue this way out of conviction in the validity of Moses' message (peace be upon him), but they used it as a means to nullify the message of Muhammad (ﷺ).

When the numerous proofs of the Qur'an, which clearly affirm that Muhammad is no novelty among the messengers and that he brought the same as what the messengers brought, overwhelmed them, He argued against them by saying: ﴿"Say: Then bring a book from God that is better guidance than both of them, and I will follow it, if you are truthful."﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:49), and the rest of the verse. When they found no way to obstinately deny the equivalence of his condition with the condition of the earlier messengers, and they took refuge in clear polytheism, they resorted to denying the messengers altogether, so that the proof would not stand against them through the equivalence of the Messenger's condition with the condition of the earlier messengers. Thus, the final outcome of their position was that they said: ﴿"We will never believe in this Qur'an, nor in what came before it."﴾

The Qur'an had already argued against them that they had disbelieved in what was given to Moses before, as in Surat al-Qasas; that is, their likes among the idol-worshippers, namely the Copts of Egypt, disbelieved in what was given to Moses. This is part of reasoning by analogy of equivalence (qiyas al-musawah) and comparison (al-tamthil).

This is the meaning of their words "nor in what came before it," because they were not being called to disbelieve in a book other than the Qur'an. Rather, this was said in the course of disputation and debate. Their disbelief in the Qur'an is well known and established, and they only intended to cut off the means of dialectical obligation.

This verse is a transition to mentioning the polytheists' attack on the Qur'an, and it is joined (ma'tufah) to the clause "And they say: When is this promise?"

Limiting the report to their statement without following it with what refutes it is an indication that its falsehood is evident to everyone who hears it, since it combines denial of all the books and laws, and this is clear slander.

Reporting their statement here in the past tense indicates that they had ceased from it.

The particle "lan" (never) is used to emphasize the negation of their belief in the revealed books forever, as a way of discouraging the Prophet and the Muslims from hoping for their belief.

The demonstrative "hadha" (this) refers to something present in minds, because discussion of the Qur'an was widespread among people, both supporters and deniers, so it is as if it were witnessed. There is no meaning of belittlement in the demonstrative, because they did not disparage the Qur'an as deficient. Do you not see the saying of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira: "Its top is fruitful and its bottom is abundant," and the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy after that: "There is nothing better than what you say, O man." And that 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited the Qur'an to him and said to him, "Do you see any harm in what I say?", replied: "No, by the blood (of my ancestors)." How could they, when He challenged them to bring a surah like it, and they did not do so? If they had disparaged it as deficient or foolish, they would have said, "We are too exalted to engage in attempting to produce its like."

The meaning of "bayna yadayhi" (what is before it) is what is near it, whether it preceded it, as in His saying: ﴿"He is only a warner to you before a severe punishment."﴾ (Saba' 34:46), and the Prophet's saying, "I was sent before the Hour." Or it came after it, as God related about Jesus (peace be upon him): ﴿"confirming what was before him of the Torah."﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 5:46) in Surat Al 'Imran. It is not intended here, because it is not an assumed or claimed obligation.

* * *

﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord, returning words to one another.﴾

The reports of their statements and disbelief were followed, after the completion of their types, by mention of their recompense and a depiction of its horror, by what is in His saying: "If only you could see when the wrongdoers..." (verse). It is of the vagueness that conveys magnification.

The connection is with what came earlier, His saying: "And they say: When is this promise?" For after He had silenced them with His saying, "Say: For you is an appointed day..." (Saba' 34:30), He followed it with a depiction of their condition on it.

The address in "If only you could see" is to everyone fit to receive address, among those who reach this verse; that is, if the one who sees were to see this time.

The response to "law" (if) is omitted for magnification, and this omission is common. Its estimate is: "You would have seen a wondrous matter." "Idh" (when) is an adverbial clause connected to "tara" (you see); that is, if you were to see at the time when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord.

The wrongdoers (al-zalimun) are the polytheists. God said: ﴿"Indeed, associating partners with God is a tremendous wrong."﴾ (Luqman 31:13). Something close to it came earlier in His saying: ﴿"If only you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire."﴾ (Al-An'am 6:27) in Surat al-An'am. It has been explicitly stated that this is a standing that gathered the polytheists and those who called them to associate partners, in His saying: ﴿"And on the day We gather them all, then We will say to those who associated partners: 'Stay in your place, you and your partners.' Then We will separate them, and their partners will say: 'You did not used to worship us.'"﴾ (Yunus 10:28-29) in Surat Yunus.

The use here of the nominal clause to which the adverbial clause is attached serves to convey the prolonged length of their standing before God, a length that requires impatience and fills hearts with terror. This is what the hadith of Anas and the hadith of Abu Hurayra indicate, concerning the Prophet's (ﷺ) intercession for the people of the gathering:

"The sun will draw near to the heads of the creatures, and its heat will intensify upon them, so they will say: 'If only we could seek intercession with our Lord, so that He may relieve us from our place.'" The hadith...

The clause "returning words to one another" (yarji'u ba'duhum ila ba'din al-qawl) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) either from "the wrongdoers" or from the pronoun in "mawqufun" (made to stand).

The present tense is used in "yarji'u ba'duhum ila ba'din al-qawl" to bring the situation vividly before the mind, like His saying: ﴿"He argues with Us concerning the people of Lot."﴾ (Hud 11:74).

"Raj' al-qawl" (returning speech) means answer, and "raj' al-ba'd ila al-ba'd" (one returning to another) means mutual reply and discourse. This is when one says a statement and the other answers him, and so on. The answer to a statement is likened to returning the statement, as if the answerer returned to the speaker his very words, since he addressed him with his equal and justice. Bashshar said:

"As if the returning of her speech were the breaking of the gardens, unclothed in flowers."

That is, as if her answer was when she replies to him. From this is also said that the answer is "radd." "Raj' al-rashq" in archery is what you return of the volley of arrows shot at you.

* * *

﴿Those who were made weak will say to those who were proud: "Were it not for you, we would have been believers."﴾

This clause and the clauses after it that are reported with verbs of saying are an explanation of the clause "returning words to one another," so that the explanation is like what is explained by it, to bring vividly before the mind the state of the speech, because it is a strange state, due to the boldness of the weak against the proud, and due to the awakening of these from their heedlessness regarding what the proud had been deceiving them with, until they brought them to this predicament.

The "sin" and "ta'" in "istud'ifu" (were made weak) are for reckoning and supposing, that is, those whom people count as weak and of no account. People count them so because they are so. It is known that they consider themselves weak all the more, because they know best what is within themselves.

The weakness here is figurative weakness, which is the state of needing someone to take charge of their affairs, protect them, and direct them as he wills, in important matters.

Among its implications are lowliness and submissiveness, and for this reason it is contrasted with "those who were proud" (alladhina istakbaru), that is, those who considered themselves great. They only considered themselves great because something required their pride, for if they were not so, they would have been described as deluded and falsely self-impressed. For this reason, the passive verb is used for those "who were made weak," and the active verb for those "who were proud," as has been mentioned in Surat Hud.

"Lawla" is a particle of prohibition for existence, that is, a particle indicating the prevention of its answer, meaning the non-occurrence of its answer because of the existence of its condition. It is thus known to be a conditional particle, but they abbreviated the expression. The meaning of "because of the existence of its condition" is its coming into existence. It is one of the particles that must always precede a nominal clause, so it must be followed by a noun and a subject (mubtada'). The predicate of that subject is often omitted in speech, so that only one noun remains of its condition, and this is abbreviation, because the particle lawla indicates that the occurrence of its answer is contingent upon the existence of its condition. Since the noun after it is in the sense of an existing thing, they omitted the predicate for brevity. It is understood from context that the contingency is in reality upon a particular state among the states in which existence is found, which is understood from the context, because mere existence of a thing is not a cause for the existence of something else. Rather, one takes its most specific state that is necessarily tied to its existence.

The grammarians expressed this meaning with the term "absolute existence" (al-wujud al-mutlaq), and this expression is not precise. What they mean is the state of existence most closely tied to it. Otherwise, absolute existence, that is, bare existence, is not suitable to have a condition attached to it.

In this verse, the conditional is linked to the pronoun of "those who were proud," so this implies that all the states of the proud revolved around preventing them from believing. Their existence therefore had no effect except in that prevention. This is what His saying afterward indicates: ﴿"No, rather it is the scheming of night and day, when you order us to disbelieve in God."﴾ (Saba' 34:33), due to their excessive insistence upon them in this, and repeating it at most times. It is as if it occupied their entire existence, because existence is being in times, so their saying here "lawla antum" (were it not for you) is an exaggeration of the intensity of their eagerness for their disbelief. This is a fitting consideration in rhetorical terms, since the requirement of the situation in this verse is the omission of the comparison (al-mushabbah).

Know that by their saying "believers" (mu'minin) is meant the technical title by which Muslims became known. Accordingly, no complement is estimated for "mu'minin."

The verb "qāla" (said) is left without a conjunction (ʿāṭif, a connecting particle), because it comes in the manner of a responsive dialogue (mujāwaba). The rule in such cases is that speech is reported without a conjunction, as we have explained more than once.

The interrogative hamza is used for denial (inkār) of a statement made by the weak ones (al-mustaḍʿafīn) disowning them. This denial is slander and a denial of reality. It was prompted by fear of having the blame placed on them, by excessive anger and regret at their followers' rebellion against them, and by the loss of their standing among them. So they could not restrain themselves from calling them liars and from humiliating them by implicating them.

The subject is placed before the verbal predicate in the context of the denying interrogative, which amounts to negation, in order to restrict the predicate to the subject, in the manner of: "It was not I who said this."

The meaning is: "We did not turn you away from guidance, but something else turned you away," namely what is introduced by "bal" (rather), which is used for annulment (ibṭāl), in His words ﴿rather, you were criminals﴾. That is, criminality had already been established for you before. Your criminality is what turned you away, since you were not near to faith so that we could have turned you away from it. Rather, you turned away and held aloof because of your criminality, and you did not accept the call to faith.

The summary of the meaning: our situation and yours are the same, and each party bears the consequence of its own deeds, for both parties had turned away from faith. This argument is their arrogance, slander and sophistry, for they used to turn the common people away from religion and fabricate excuses for them. Here they only denied that they had diverted them from faith after it had been embraced, and that is not the claim against them.

The locus of the sophistry is their saying ﴿after it came to you﴾, because "coming" here is used in the sense of approaching it and mixing with it.

The "idh" in His words ﴿after it came to you﴾ is stripped of the sense of locative adverb and is purely a time noun, which is its original usage, as mentioned earlier in His words ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I will make on earth a successive authority"﴾ in Surat al-Baqara. Therefore the annexation of "baʿda" (after) to it is valid, since the annexation is an indication that "idh" has been stripped of the locative sense to general time, like their saying "ḥīnaʾidh" (at that time) and "yawmaʾidh" (on that day). The estimate is: after the time of their coming to you. "Bal" is an idrāb (a turning from one statement to another) of annulment from the matter upon which the denying interrogative entered; that is, ﴿we did not turn you away, rather you were criminals﴾.

"Ijrām" (criminality) here means shirk (associating partners with God), and it indicates their deliberate intent to it and their insistence upon it with insight from themselves, without the enticement (taswīl) of any tempter.

[Page 207]

[p. 208]

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 34, verse 33:**

﴿The ones who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant: "Rather, it was your scheming by night and day, when you were ordering us to disbelieve in God and to set up rivals to Him."﴾ The narration of this statement did not follow the pattern of narrating exchanges without a conjunction (*'atf*), which is the common usage in narrating exchanges, as we have inferred from the usage of the Glorious Book, and as we presented it in His saying, "And when your Lord said to the angels, 'I am placing a vicegerent (*khalifa*) on the earth'" (Q. 2:30). Instead, a conjunction particle was used in narrating this statement, although the oppressed had answered with it the statement of those who were arrogant, "Did we turn you away from guidance?" (Q. 34:32). This is for a subtle purpose: to alert that the statement of the oppressed is, in meaning, a completion of their own statement, which the arrogant seized upon, so they hastened to answer it, for the reason we mentioned there. Had they waited for the completion of their speech and let them finish, what it contained would have nullified their statement. But they interrupted their speech out of extreme anxiety lest they be held accountable for what the oppressed were saying.

Their statement was related with the past tense (*fi'l al-madi*) to match the speech of those who were arrogant. Because the statement of those who were oppressed, after having been a completion of their own statement that the arrogant interrupted, turned into an answer to the arrogant's disavowal that they had led the oppressed away from guidance, the statement of the oppressed came to have two positions. One of these positions requires joining it with a *wa* conjunction, while the other position requires attaching it with the particle *bal* ("rather") and with the addition of "scheming by night and day." The original wording of the speech is: "Those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant: 'Were it not for you, we would have been believers, when you were ordering us by night and day to disbelieve in God,' etc." When the arrogant interrupted them with their speech, the particle *bal* was inserted into the speech of the oppressed, as a refutation of the statement of the arrogant, "Rather, you were criminals." By this, it served both to complete the preceding speech and to answer the arrogant's disavowal. Had it not been joined with *wa*, it would only have indicated that it is an answer to the speech of the arrogant alone. This is among the most elegant instances of concision (*ijaz*).

*Bal* here is also for *idrab ibtali* (a retractive transition, which cancels what precedes it), cancelling the implication of restriction (*qasr*) in their statement, "Did we turn you away from guidance?" That statement lies within the scope of a negation, because the interrogative of denial (*istifham inkari*) carries the meaning of negation.

The phrase "scheming of night and day" is an idafa (genitive construction) with the meaning of "in" (i.e., "scheming during night and day"). There is a omitted *mudaf ilayhi* (the second term of the construction) and a omitted *majrur* (the object of the preposition), both indicated by the context. That is, "your scheming against us."

"Scheming" (*makr*) is in the nominative case as a subject (*mubtada'*). The predicate is omitted, indicated by the contrast of this speech with the speech of the arrogant, since it is an answer to it. So the estimate is: "Rather, your scheming turned us away," which yields restriction, meaning: "Only your scheming turned us away." This is a complete negation of their statement, "Did we turn you away from guidance?" and of their statement, "Rather, you were criminals."

*Makr* means deception: to show a deceiver doing an act that is not actually his, so that the one deceived is misled. This was discussed earlier, and in His saying, "And they schemed, and God schemed" (Q. 3:54), in Surat Al 'Imran.

Applying *makr* to their enticement to them to remain in polytheism is based on the fact that they were deceiving them and giving them illusions, such as their saying: "It is the religion of your fathers," and "How can you feel safe from the anger of the gods against you if you abandon your religion?" and the like. Deception does not imply that the deceiver disapproves of the act he is trying to bring about.

The meaning is: their constant scheming night and day, which is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the continuous insistence upon them in adhering to polytheism. "When you were ordering us" is a temporal clause (*zarf*) modifying what is implied in "scheming of night and day," namely "turned us away," i.e., "at the time you were ordering us to disbelieve in God."

*Andad* is the plural of *nidd*, which means an equal, i.e., "we would set up for God equals in divinity."

This is a presumptuous outburst from the oppressed against their arrogant leaders, when they saw how little these had helped them, and they belittled them when they learned of their lying and slander.

A similar case was narrated in His saying, "When those who were followed disavow those who followed" (Q. 2:166), in Surat al-Baqara, in the two verses.

* * *

﴿And they concealed their remorse when they saw the punishment.﴾ This may be a conjunction (*'atf*) to the clause "they will refer the word to one another" (Q. 34:31), in which case it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*). It may also be conjoined to the clause "when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord" (Q. 34:31).

The plural pronoun refers to all those previously mentioned, namely the oppressed and the arrogant. The meaning is: the punishment prepared for them was revealed to them, following the dialogue that had taken place between them. Then they knew that the mutual blame between them had availed neither party anything. At that point they were certain of their failure, and they regretted what had escaped them in the worldly life, and they concealed their remorse within themselves. It seems they concealed their remorse either to preserve the hope of averting that punishment from them, or out of fear of disgrace among the people of the place of standing. They later declared it, as in His saying, "They will say, 'Alas for us, for what we neglected therein'" (Q. 6:31), in Surat al-An'am, and His saying, "If only I had another turn, I would be among the good-doers" (Q. 39:58), in Surat al-Zumar.

Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned that some exegetes interpreted "concealed" (*asarru*) here with the meaning of "displayed" (*azharu*), claiming that *asarra* is a homonym between two opposites (*min al-adad*). Al-Zamakhshari accepted this and did not object to it, whereas al-Zawzani explained *al-israr* with both meanings in the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*I passed through guards to reach her, and a group that were eager against me, were they to conceal my killing.*

Ibn 'Atiyya, however, rejected it and said: "It has never been established in the language that *asarra* is among the homonyms." I say: there is room for scrutiny here. Many lexicographers have counted this word among the homonyms, and Abu 'Ubayda recited the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*When al-Hajjaj drew his sword, the Kharijite who had been concealing (his opposition) concealed it (again).* (Or: *the Kharijite who had hidden it revealed it.*)

In *Kitab al-Adad* by Abu al-Tayyib al-Halabi, Abu Hatim said: "I do not trust Abu 'Ubayda's statement regarding the Qur'an, nor regarding al-Farazdaq's verse, since al-Farazdaq was very confused in his poetry." Abu al-Tayyib reported from al-Tawwazi that someone other than Abu 'Ubayda recited the verse of al-Farazdaq.

What motivated the interpretation of "concealed" as "displayed" here is what requires their public declaration of remorse, in their saying, "Were it not for you, we would have been believers" (Q. 34:31), and in other verses such as His saying, "And on the Day the wrongdoer bites his hands, saying, 'Would that I had taken a way with the Messenger'" (Q. 25:27), etc.

Remorse (*nadama*) is distress over an action whose remedy has passed. It was discussed earlier at His saying, "And he became among the regretful" (Q. 5:31), in Surat al-'Uqud (Surat al-Ma'ida).

* * *

﴿And We have placed shackles on the necks of those who disbelieved. Are they being recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾ This is a conjunction to the clause "when the wrongdoers are made to stand" (Q. 34:31). The estimate is: "If you could see when We placed shackles on the necks of the captive and the like, and they were tied to them with a chain, a strap of leather, or a rope." This was discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Ra'd. Placing shackles on the necks is a sign that they are driven toward what they are trying to flee and escape from. This was discussed at His saying, "Those are the ones with shackles on their necks" (Q. 13:5), in Surat al-Ra'd.

"Those who disbelieved" are the same people whose pronouns were used earlier. The use of the explicit noun and its being a relative clause indicates that this is the recompense for disbelief. For this reason it is followed by the clause, "Are they being recompensed except for what they used to do?" which is an independent (*mustani'a*) sentence, in a explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), as if a questioner found this punishment to be terrible. It is also an implicit reproach directed at them.

The interrogative with *hal* is used for denial, in view of what follows it of an exception (*istithna'*). So the estimate of the meaning is: "Were they recompensed with other than what they used to do?" and the exception is an *istithna' mufarragh* (an exception in which the excluded element is not stated and the sentence is governed by the preceding negation or interrogation).

"What they used to do" is the second object of the verb *yujzawna*, because *jaza* transitively takes a second object directly, as it belongs to the pattern of *a'ta*, just as it takes it through the preposition when it is taken to mean "compensated him."

Their recompense is described as "what they used to do" in the sense of an eloquent comparison (*tashbih baligh*), meaning "like what they used to do." This equivalence is a metonymy for equality in what they are requited for, with the recompense equal to the deeds for which they are requited, so that it is as if it were the deeds themselves, as in His saying, "A recompense in full measure" (Q. 78:26).

Know that its being equal in measure is something known only to the One who measures realities and intentions. As for its being a fitting match in kind, that is because placing shackles on the neck is a restriction on their freedom of movement, just as their idols restrained them, as He said, "Do you worship what you carve?" (Q. 37:95). And their acceptance of being enslaved by their leaders and great ones is what He said, "And they will say, 'Our Lord, we obeyed our masters and our great ones, and they led us astray from the way'" (Q. 33:67).

Among the notable questions is that when Shaykh Ibn 'Arafa was teaching the exegesis lesson and reached His saying, "When the shackles are on their necks and the chains" (Q. 40:71), one of those present asked him: "Is it correct for us to derive from this verse something that supports the action of the rulers, may God set them right, in bringing the warriors and others to them shackled by the neck, along with the position of Malik, may God have mercy on him, that analogy (*qiyas*) is permissible in punishments based on God's action 'in the case of the hadd for indecency'?" The Shaykh answered him that there is no evidence in it, because Malik only permitted analogy to God's action in this world, whereas this is one of God's dealings in the Hereafter, so its permissibility requires a separate proof.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 34:

﴿And We did not send a warner into any town but that its affluent ones said, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that with which you have been sent."﴾ This is an interjection (i'tiraድ) leading to a shift toward consoling the Prophet (ﷺ) for what he was afflicted with from the polytheists of Makkah,

Especially what their chiefs and great ones confronted him with of incitement against him, by reminding him that this has been the custom of the messengers before him, so there is no shame for him in that. For this reason He said in the verse in az-Zukhruf: ﴿And thus We did not send before you a warner into any town but that its affluent ones said, "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and we are following in their footsteps."﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 23], etc. That is, thus is the denial with which the people of this town denied you. And it is an allusion to his people who opposed him, by reminding them of the consequence of those like them from the people of the towns whose inhabitants denied and whose leaders incited them to that.

Al-mutrafun (the affluent): those who were given tarafah (affluence). Tarafah means comfort and abundance of living. It is in the passive form, with the implied meaning: that God made them affluent, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the eminent ones of his people who disbelieved and denied the meeting of the Hereafter, and whom We had given luxury in the worldly life, said...﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 33], in Surah al-Anbiya'.

In its passive form there is an allusion to reminding them of God's blessing upon them, so that perhaps they would be thankful for it and desist from associating partners with Him. Some scholars of the language say its implied meaning is: "Prosperity overcame them," i.e., made them insolent.

﴿Indeed, we are disbelievers in that with which you have been sent﴾ is a quotation in meaning: that is, the affluent ones of every town said to their messenger, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that with which you have been sent." This is from the construction of plural against plural, which is intended to distribute the statement over the individuals of the plural.

Their saying "you have been sent with it" is mockery, evidenced by their saying "disbelievers," and it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been revealed, indeed you are mad!"﴾ [al-Hijr: 6]. Or the meaning is: "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that which you claim you have been sent with."

[Page 213]

﴿They said: "We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished."﴾ ﴿Say: "Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it, but most people do not know."﴾

They followed their open disbelief in the Qur'an and other laws with a statement by which they indirectly denied the reality of Islam, using a sophistical argument (sifsatá'i, sophistic). They made the abundance of their wealth and children a proof that they were people of good fortune with God, Exalted is He. So the pronoun in "They said" refers back to "those who disbelieved" in His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved said: "We will never believe in this Qur'an."﴾ [Saba': 31], and so on. This is a distortion of realities through the accidental circumstances that surround them. They took what accompanied their state of disbelief, namely the abundance of wealth and children, as a proof that they were the object of God's special care and that what they were upon was the truth. This is an insinuation on their part, the opposite of the situation of the Muslims: that the weakness of the Muslims, their small numbers, and their hardship of life are a proof that they are not favoured by God. They did not realise that the conditions of this world are caused by worldly causes that have no connection to the conditions of children. This sophistical, illusory principle is dangerous, and it was found in the misguided beliefs of the people of pre-Islamic ignorance (Jahiliyya) and is widespread among non-Muslims. Muslims are not free from something close to it in their conduct regarding religion, and its root is analogising the unseen (al-ghá'ib) to the seen (al-shahid), an analogy that sometimes hits the truth and sometimes misses it.

Among the greatest errors of the Muslims in this area is the error of resorting to qadar (divine decree) to excuse themselves, and the error of adopting tawakkul (trust in God) as an excuse for their negligence and laziness.

So the clause ﴿They said: "We have more wealth and children"﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿Those who disbelieved said: "We will never believe in this Qur'an"﴾ [Saba': 31], and so on. Their saying ﴿and we will not be punished﴾ is like a conclusion to their saying ﴿We have more wealth and children﴾. The conjunction particle was used here to give preference to the independent benefit over the aspect of imitation (istinsakh) that is suggested by what preceded it, namely their saying ﴿We have more wealth and children﴾. From this structure there results an argument for the validity of their religion and for the refutation of what Islam brought, then boasting of this over the Muslims and belittling the side of the Muslims, through an allusion to an exceptive syllogism (qiyas istithna'i) based on a supposed connection. It is as if they argued from the absence of punishment to their being brought near to God, based on a suppressed analogy of equality (qiyas al-musawat). It is as though they confined the means of nearness to God to the abundance of wealth and children. Without this interpretation, both clauses would be devoid of their most important meanings, and with it the placement of the answer ﴿Say: "Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it"﴾ becomes more closely connected to the meaning. That is, say to them: the extending and restricting of provision is another matter among God's dispositions, which are bound to what He has determined in the order of this world. That is, there is no necessary connection between it and right guidance and error, or between guidance and misguidance. If you considered the causes of provision, you would see that they do not correspond to the causes of error or of being guided. Perhaps God widens provision for the disobedient and narrows it for the obedient, and perhaps He reverses this. So let neither this nor that deceive you, for you do not know.

This is what made His saying ﴿but most people do not know﴾ hit the mark. Most people have affairs confused for them, so they mix them up and do not place their beauty and ugliness in their proper positions.

This indicates that its state does not show God's pleasure with them, nor His displeasure. This refutation is what is called in the science of disputation (ilm al-munazara) a general refutation (naqd ijmali).

The extending of provision (bast al-rizq) means facilitating and increasing it. The word "extending" (bast) is used figuratively for it, since bast originally means spreading out a garment or the like, because what is spread out becomes greater in the area it covers.

The restricting of provision (qadr al-rizq) means the difficulty of obtaining it and the scarcity of what is obtained. The word qadr (measure/restriction) is used figuratively for it, meaning taqdir (measuring), which is limiting, because a small amount is easy to count and calculate. For this reason, its opposite was described as ﴿He provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾ [al-Baqara: 212]. The object of "restricts" (yaqdiru) is omitted, indicated by the object of "extends" (yabsutu). A parallel to this was discussed earlier in Surat al-Ra'd.

The object of "know" (ya'lamun) is omitted, indicated by the context, that is: they do not know that God extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it, in view of the generality of "whom He wills," whether that person is righteous or wicked. Because of their failure to act on this, they imagined that the extending of provision is a sign of nearness to God, and its opposite a sign of the opposite of that. With this, the view of Ahmad ibn al-Rawandi was mistaken:

"How many an intelligent man whose doctrines have baffled him, and how many an ignorant fool you find provided for!

This is the one who left illusions bewildered, and turned the distinguished scholar into a heretic."

If he had been a distinguished scholar, his understanding would not have been bewildered, and he would not have become a heretic because of the narrowness of his way of thinking.
