[p. 215]

It is possible that the clause ﴿And neither your wealth nor your children﴾ is a conjunctive clause (ʿatf) coordinated with the clause ﴿Say: Indeed my Lord extends provision﴾ [Saba', 34:36], and so it is a speech directed from God Most High to those who said ﴿We have more wealth and children﴾ [Saba', 34:35]. In that case the second-person pronouns are directed to those who said ﴿We have more wealth and children﴾ [Saba', 34:35].

It is also possible that it is a conjunction to the clause ﴿Indeed my Lord extends provision to whom He wills﴾ [Saba', 34:36]. Then it would be among the things the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to say to them and convey from God Most High. In the pronoun of ʿindanā ("with Us") there would be an iltifat (shift of grammatical person), and the second-person pronouns would refer back to those who said ﴿We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished﴾ [Saba', 34:35]. There is also a third possibility, which we will point out shortly.

This is an ascent from refuting the implied premise (al-mulāzamah) to arguing that they are not the objects of God Most High's approval, by way of a detailed refutation (al-naqḍ al-tafṣīlī), which is also called al-munāqaḍah in the science of disputation (ʿilm al-munāẓarah).

This is the position of moving from prohibition (al-manʿ) to argumentation, in order to refute the claim of the opponent. The verse has refuted the notion that their wealth and children bring them near to God Most High, and it has established that nothing brings one near to God Most High except faith and righteous deeds.

The negated sentence was phrased in the form of restriction (ḥaṣr), by defining both the subject and the predicate, because the purpose of this sentence is to negate their statement ﴿We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished﴾ [Saba', 34:35], i.e., "not you." Their speech thus amounted to a restriction of nearness to God in abundance of wealth and children, and so all of that was negated entirely.

The repetition of the negative particle (lā) after the conjunction in ﴿wa-lā awlādukum﴾ serves to emphasize that the negation applies to both mentioned items, so that each one is intended by the negation of its being something that brings one near to God and something one turns toward for that purpose.

Since al-amwāl ("wealth") and al-awlād ("children") are broken plurals (jamʿ taksīr), they are treated as feminine singular nouns, so their predicate is introduced by a relative pronoun for the feminine singular, in accordance with interpreting them as the group of wealth and the group of children. Attention was not paid to the predominance of children over wealth, which would have led to referring to both together with alladhīna ("those who") or the like.

The phrase ﴿tuqarribukum ʿindanā﴾ ("bring you near to Us") was used instead of the phrase "bring you near to Us," since nearness here is a metaphor for honor and dignity, not nearness of place.

Al-zulfā is a noun for nearness, like al-rujʿā ("return"), and it is a absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) standing in for the verbal noun, meaning "brings you near as nearness." A parallel is ﴿And God has caused you to grow from the earth as growth﴾ [Nūḥ, 71:17].

His saying ﴿except for those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ is a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), meaning an exception that is not of the same kind as what precedes it. The word illā here has the meaning of lākin (the light form "but"), used for correction (li-l-istidrāk), and what follows it is a resumed statement (kalām mustaʾnaf). This is one of the usages of the disjunctive exception: when what follows illā is not of the same category as what is excepted, the exception is disjunctive. Then, if what follows illā is a single noun, illā is understood as meaning lākin, the sister of inna ("indeed"), according to the people of the Ḥijāz, who put the following word in the accusative, treating it as if it were the subject of lākin. According to the Banū Tamīm, it is understood as the light, coordinating lākin, so the noun after it follows the case of the noun before it. This is what Sībawayh pointed out in the chapter on those exceptions in which the accusative is preferred.

As for the case where what follows illā is a nominal or verbal clause, illā is understood as the light lākin and the clause after it is made a resumed statement. This is found in the Arab saying: "By God, I will surely do such-and-such, except that the lawful way of that is that I do such-and-such." Ibn Mālik said in his commentary on al-Tashīl: the explanation of this exclusion is that you take their saying illā ḥillu dhālika ("except the lawfulness of that") as equivalent to: "I see no nullifier of this contract except the doing of such-and-such." Ibn Kharūf included in this category the verse ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾ [al-Ghāshiyah, 88:22], ﴿except for one who turns away and disbelieves﴾ [al-Ghāshiyah, 88:23], ﴿then God will punish him with the greatest punishment﴾ [al-Ghāshiyah, 88:24], on the basis that man is the subject and "God will punish him" is the predicate, with the fāʾ entering to include in the subject the meaning of the conditional. Ibn Masʿūd said: illā in the disjunctive exception is followed by a resumed statement.

On this basis, His saying here ﴿except for those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ is to be understood as: "But those who believe and do righteous deeds," so that man (man) is a subject including the meaning of the condition, and ﴿for them is a reward of double﴾ is the predicative clause about the subject. The fāʾ was added in the predicate to include in the subject the meaning of the conditional.

Easier than this is to take man as conditional, and the clause ﴿then those, for them is a reward of double﴾ as the response of the condition, joined with the fāʾ because it is a nominal clause. This realizes the meaning of the disjunctive exception and gives an explanation of the verse without strain and without hesitation in the composition.

It is possible that the clause ﴿And neither your wealth nor your children﴾ etc. is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) between the clause ﴿Say: Indeed my Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾ [Saba', 34:36] and the clause ﴿Say: Indeed my Lord extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him﴾ [Saba', 34:39]. In that case the second-person pronouns are directed to all the people addressed by the Qur'an, believers and disbelievers alike. On this reading, His saying ﴿except for those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ etc. is an exception from the second-person pronoun, meaning: "your wealth does not bring you near, except those of you who believe and do righteous deeds." The clause ﴿then those, for them is a reward of double for what they did﴾ is praise of those who believed and did righteous deeds.

The demonstrative (ism al-ishārah) was used in the predication about "those who believe" to honor them and to draw attention to the fact that they deserve what comes after the demonstrative, because of those qualities which preceded the demonstrative, as in the verse ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah, 2:5] and elsewhere. The sense of this is parallel to His saying ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you; it is a brief enjoyment﴾ [Āl ʿImrān, 3:196] up to His saying ﴿But those who fear their Lord, for them are gardens﴾ [Āl ʿImrān, 3:198].

Al-ḍiʿf means what is multiplied and repeated, so it applies to what is repeated once or more. In a hadith: "And a good deed is rewarded tenfold, up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples." This is indicated by His saying ﴿The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of God is like a grain that grows seven spikes, in each spike a hundred grains, and God multiplies for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah, 2:261].

The idafah (genitive construction) of jazāʾ ("reward") to al-ḍiʿf is an explanatory idafah (idāfah bayāniyyah), meaning the reward which is the multiplication of their deeds, i.e., according to what they deserve, as has preceded. Nearness is alluded to by the multiplication of the reward, because that is a sign of the honor of the one rewarded with God, meaning: those draw near in nearness, and so they are rewarded with a double reward for their deeds, not for the abundance of their wealth and children. Thus the disjunctive correction applies to everything the speech of the polytheists implied of false claims and empty pride, to remove the misconception that wealth and children do not bring one near to God in any way. For among the wealth of believers are charities and expenditures, and among their children are helpers in righteousness, strivers, and those who pray for their parents for forgiveness and mercy.

The preposition bi- in His saying ﴿for what they did﴾ may be causal (sababiyyah), in which case it indicates the basis of the multiplication, which is what suits the cause from among the righteous deeds, as in His saying ﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ [al-Raḥmān, 55:60]. It may also be a counter-exchange (ʿiwaḍ), in which case what they did is what is rewarded, as one says: "I recompensed him with a thousand," so there is no supposed omission in His saying "reward of double."

[p. 218]

Al-ghurufāt is the plural of ghurfah, which was mentioned at the end of al-Furqān. It is a raised room, which is the most beautiful in appearance and the most comprehensive in view. ﴿Āminūn﴾ ("secure") is a second predicate, meaning that it casts into their souls security from the cessation of that bounty.

The majority of readers recited ﴿fī al-ghurufāt﴾ with the plural form, while Ḥamzah recited ﴿fī al-ghurfah﴾ with the singular.

The discourse follows the Qur'an's usual practice of pairing encouragement with warning, and the reverse. This verse therefore functions as a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) between the praise of the righteous believers and their guidance to benefit from their wealth in order to draw near to God, with the phrase ﴿Whatever you spend of anything﴾ [Saba': 39] etc. Those who strive against Our signs are the polytheists, by barring others from hearing the Qur'an and by slandering it with falsehood and idle talk when it is recited.

The verb sa'y (striving) is used figuratively for diligent effort in action, as in His words ﴿then he turned away, striving﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 22]. When it is followed by fi ("in"), it generally means striving toward harm. So ﴿those who strive in Our signs﴾ means they exert themselves to nullify them, and mu'jizin (seeking to frustrate) means contending with them and seeking to prove them powerless. A parallel to this appears in His words ﴿And those who strove against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them, those are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Hajj: 51] in Surat al-Hajj.

The demonstrative ulaika ("those") is used to indicate that they deserve the Blazing Fire because of what was mentioned before the demonstrative, like His words ﴿those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. The phrase fi al-'adhab ("in the punishment") is the predicate (khabar) of the demonstrative.

Muhdarun ("brought forth") here is a kinaya (allusion) for constant presence, so it is an escalation in meaning beyond what the locative particle indicates, namely the encompassing of the punishment around them. It is a second predicate (khabar) of the demonstrative, and its complement is omitted, indicated by the adverbial phrase. A parallel to this appears in His words ﴿then those will be brought forth into the punishment﴾ [al-Rum: 16] in Surat al-Rum.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 39:

Page 219
﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it, and He is the best of providers."﴾
He followed the refutation of the idea that wealth and children, in themselves, are a means of drawing near to Allah the Exalted, as a rejoinder to the claims of the polytheists, with something resembling an exception to that refutation: affirming the benefit of wealth for drawing near to the good pleasure of Allah if it is used in seeking His pleasure. This elaborates in detail what had been indicated in general, that this may be a means of nearness to Allah, by His saying ﴿except for one who believes and does righteous work﴾ [Saba: 37], as has preceded.

His saying ﴿Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him﴾ has a close parallel mentioned earlier, as an emphasis on that, and in order that His saying ﴿And whatever you spend of anything...﴾ (the verse) may be built upon it. What came before was a refutation of the polytheists, and what is mentioned here is an encouragement for the believers; the expressions are one, while the purposes differ. This is among the aspects of the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an: that one utterance be suitable for two aims and be directed at two groups.

Since this second part is directed at the believers, attention is drawn to their honour by the addition of His saying "of His servants", that is, the believers. The pronoun in "for him" refers back to "whom", meaning: and He restricts it for whom He wills of His servants. The object of "restricts" (yaqdiru) is omitted, indicated by the object of "extends" (yabsutu).

What preceded was a discourse that He extends provision to non-believers, so they were not blessed with the description "His servants", because the idiomatic attribution (idafa) carries honour for the believers. In this there is a favour upon those to whom He extends provision, in that Allah has combined for them the virtue of faith and the virtue of abundant provision; and a consolation for those whose provision He restricts, in that they have attained the virtue of faith and the virtue of patience over the straitness of life.

In attaching "for him" to "restricts" there is an indication that this restriction is not without benefit to the one whose provision is restricted, namely the benefit of reward for contentment with what has been apportioned to him and of being spared reckoning for it on the Day of Resurrection. In a hadith: "No affliction befalls a believer but that it expiates for him, even the thorn that pricks him."

Were it not for this indication, it would have been said: "and restricts it upon him", as He said ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted, let him spend from what Allah has given him﴾ [al-Talaq: 7]. As for the state of the disbelievers, He bestows provision upon some of them which they will be reckoned for with a severer reckoning

Page 220
on the Day of Resurrection, since they did not thank their Provider; and He restricts it for some of them, so that misery does not reach them. This is a preface to His saying ﴿And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it﴾, as an incitement to spending. What is meant by spending is spending in what the Shari'a has permitted.

This is an instruction to the Muslims that the bliss of the Hereafter does not contradict the bliss of this world. Allah the Exalted said ﴿And among them is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire"﴾ [al-Baqara: 201] ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned﴾ [al-Baqara: 202]. As for the bliss of this world, it is caused by worldly circumstances which Allah the Exalted has arranged and made easy for whom He made easy in His knowledge of the unseen; and as for the bliss of the Hereafter, it is caused by deeds explained in the Shari'a. Many of the righteous attain bliss in this world together with knowledge that they will be blessed in the Hereafter, just as bliss was bestowed upon Dawud and Sulayman, and upon many of the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ, and many of the imams of the religion, such as Malik ibn Anas, al-Shafi'i, Shaykh 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Zayd, and Sahnun.

As for Allah's choosing for His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ the state of asceticism in this world, it was so that he would attain the highest perfections of being wholly devoted to receiving revelation and of beautiful character, and of equality with the majority of his Companions in their conditions. We have explained this at length in the treatise on the food of the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him. He followed this with encouraging the wealthy to spend in the way of Allah, making the promise of replacing what a person spends a metaphor for encouragement to spend, because Allah's promise of its replacement, together with the emphasis of the promise, implies that He loves such spending from the sincere.

He emphasized this promise by the form of a conditional sentence, by making the answer clause nominal, and by placing the predicate-subject before the verbal predicate in His saying "then He will replace it." So in this promise there are three emphases indicating great care in its realization, so that one moves from that to the metaphor that it is what He, the Exalted, desires.

"Of anything" is an explanation of the generality in "whatever" (ma). The clause "and He is the best of providers" is a concluding addition to the encouragement and the promise, with an increase, to show that what He replaces is better than what the spender spent.

"Best" (khayr) here carries the sense of "more excellent" (akhyar), because the provision that reaches one from Him, the Exalted, is only from His bounty, which He causes to flow through the hand of some of His creatures; so when its facilitation is with His pleasure toward the one provided for and with a promise from Him, that is more worthy of blessing and permanence. The apparent meaning of the verse is that the replacement of provision occurs both in this world and in the Hereafter.

By "spending" is meant spending that is encouraged in the religion, such as spending on the poor

Page 221
and spending in the way of Allah by supporting the religion. Malik related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: Allah the Exalted says, "O son of Adam, spend, and I will spend upon you." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "It may be compensated with its like or more, or it may be compensated with reward, or it may be stored up for him, and it is like supplication in the promise of response." End of quote. I say: It may also be compensated with health, and it may be compensated with long life. Allah has secrets in His creation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verses 40–41:

﴿And on the Day We shall gather them all together, then We shall say to the angels, "Did these worship you?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "Glory be to You! You are our Guardian, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them believed in them."﴾

This is a conjunction with the phrase ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord﴾ [Saba': 31], completing the depiction of the horror of their condition on the Day of the Promise, which they denied. It follows what was described of the mutual blame between the arrogant among them and the weak. Here it describes their disgrace through the disavowal of them by the angels and the angels' testimony against them, that they used to worship the jinn.

The pronoun of absence in "nahshuruhum" (We shall gather them) refers back to what the pronoun of ﴿They said, "We have more wealth and children"﴾ [Saba': 35] referred to, which in turn refers to "those who disbelieved" from the words ﴿Those who disbelieved said, "We will never believe in this Qur'an"﴾ [Saba': 31]. The whole discourse is organised around the condition of the polytheists.

The word "jami'" (all) is in the form fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, meaning "gathered." Its use as an adjective became common to convey the comprehensiveness of the individuals, both in their essences and their conditions, to which the verb applies; that is, the speaker gathers them. Labid said:

They were emptied, and once they had been crowded together, they departed in the morning, leaving behind their stone-boundaries and their thimam (a shrub).

This was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿So scheme against me all together, then give me no respite﴾ [Hud: 55] in Surah Hud. Thus the word "jami'an" encompasses the various kinds of polytheists, despite the differences in their sects and their beliefs in their polytheism. The polytheist Arabs had various sects, some borrowing from others, and they did not hold a doctrine with coherent beliefs and statements unmixed with what contradicts one another.

The purpose of this verse is to refute their claim concerning the angels, that they are the daughters of God, and their saying, ﴿Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 20], as in Surah al-Zukhruf. They used to confuse the angels with the jinn and establish kinship between them. They would say: the angels are the daughters of God, from the nobles of the jinn.

[Page 222]

A tribe from Khuza'a was known as Banu Mulayh (pronounced with a damma on the mim, a fatha on the lam, and a sukun on the taḥtiyya), who worshipped the jinn and the angels. The restriction to the angels, and calling them as witnesses against the polytheists, is because refuting the divinity of the angels entails refuting the divinity of what is lower than them among those worshipped besides God, by way of dalalat al-fahwa (inference by implication), that is, a fortiori. For that confirmation is the reason for which the gathering was instituted.

Addressing the angels with this interrogative is used as an indirect allusion to the polytheists, in the manner of the proverb: "It is you I mean, but listen, O neighbour."

The demonstrative "hā'ulā'" (these) refers to a group who had worshipped the angels and the jinn, and those among the remaining polytheists who supported them in their statements.

Placing the object before "ya'buduna" (they worship) is for emphasis and for the sake of the rhyme (fasila).

The speech of the angels is related without a conjunction, because it occurs within a dialogue, as has been mentioned more than once. For this reason the past tense is used in it, since that is the predominant form in narration.

The answer of the angels implies an affirmation together with a disavowal of the wording that they were worshipped. This is like one who relates the disbelief of someone and says, "He said: he is a polytheist with God," whereas the one who actually spoke said, "I am a polytheist with God."

The locus of the disavowal in the angels' words "Glory be to You" is that someone other than God should deserve to be worshipped, together with the necessary implication, which is that they know this and therefore are not harmed by being worshipped.

"Al-waliyy" means the helper, the ally, and the friend. It is derived from al-walyi, the verbal noun of waliya (on the pattern of 'alima). Each of the doer of al-walyi and its object is a waliyy, because walaya is a relation that requires two parties. For this reason waliyy, being fa'il, is suitable both in the sense of the active and in the sense of the passive. Thus the term waliyy applies to the one who befriends (with a kasra on the lam) and to the one who is befriended (with a fatha on the lam), and both meanings occur frequently in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech.

So the meaning of "You are our waliyy" is: we do not befriend other than You, that is, we do not accept anyone else as a waliyy. Worship is a bond of walaya between the worshipper and the worshipped, and the worshipped's approval of his worshipper's worship of him is a bond of walaya between the worshipped and his worshipper. Thus the angels' words "Glory be to You" are a disavowal of approving that the polytheists worship them, because the angels, having made themselves allies of God, have denied the polytheists who claimed divinity for them, since the worshipper cannot be the worshipped.

The discussion of the word waliyy has already been given at His saying ﴿Say, "Shall I take as a waliyy other than God?"﴾ [al-An'am: 14] in Surah al-An'am, and at the end of Surah al-Ra'd.

"Min" is extra, for emphasis, and "dun" is a noun with the meaning of "ghayr" (other than). That is: You are our waliyy, and they are not our awliya' (allies), and we do not accept them because of their disbelief. So "min dunihim" is an emphasis on what the sentence "You are our waliyy" conveys of restriction, by defining both parts.

"Bal" is for a transitional turning away (idrab intiqali), moving from disavowing them to testifying against them and against those who beautified for them the worship of other than God the Exalted. It is not an idrab of cancellation (ibtal), because the polytheists being spoken of did worship the angels. The meaning is: rather, most of these used to worship the jinn, and the jinn were pleased with their worship of them. The summary of the meaning is: we deny their worshipping us, and we did not command them to it, but the jinn beautified for them the worship of other than God, so they worshipped the jinn and they worshipped the angels.

The clause "akthoruhum" (most of them) refers to the polytheists, and the pronoun in "bihim" (in them) refers to the jinn. The context returns each pronoun to its referent, even when the pronouns are identical, as in the words of 'Abbas ibn Mirdas on the day of Hunayn:

We turned back, and had it not been for us, their host would have encircled the Muslims and seized what they had gathered.

That is: the host of the polytheists seized what the Muslims had gathered of spoils.

The majority of readers read "nahshuruhum" and "naqulu" with the nun of majesty. Hafs from 'Asim read them with the third-person yā' in both, and the pronoun refers to "my Lord" from His saying ﴿Say, "Indeed my Lord extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him"﴾ [Saba': 39].
