Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 42:

﴿So today none of you will have power to benefit or harm one another.﴾

The more evident view is that this is part of God Most High's address to the polytheists and the jinn. The *fa'* here is *fasiha* (an "eloquent" or explanatory *fa'*, which introduces a result or consequence of what has preceded), arising from the preceding dialogue. It is a statement addressed by God Most High to the angels, and its intended purpose is an allusion to the misguidance of those who worshipped the angels and the jinn, since the angels already know the content of this report, so it is not intended to inform them of it. The meaning is: since you have known that you blamed the jinn, then today none of you will have power to benefit or harm another.

Page 224

It is also possible that it is an address from the angels to both groups after the testimony has been given against them, as a rebuke to them and a manifestation of anger towards them, in order to confirm disavowal of them. The *fa'* here is again *fasiha*, and it is clear.

The adverbial phrase ("today") has been placed before its governing verb, because on that day both benefit and harm have become exclusively God Most High's, both small and great, in contrast to what was the case in this world, where the jinn benefited their worshippers with some worldly benefits, and the polytheists benefited the jinn by serving their whisperings and carrying out their aims of temptation and misguidance. Likewise, harm in this world as well.

The word *mulk* (power) here means *qudrah* (capability), i.e., none of you is able to provide any help or benefit to another.

This was previously discussed at His saying ﴿Say: "Who could prevent God from anything if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary"﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 17), in Surat al-'Uqud [the Surah of Al-Ma'idah].

He placed *naf'* (benefit) within the scope of negation as a way of despairing them, because they hope that they will intercede for them on that day and say ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾ (Yunus: 18).

He conjoined the negation of harm to the negation of benefit to indicate the removal of their capability over anything at all, for some beings are able to harm but not able to benefit, such as the scorpion.

* * *

﴿And We will say to those who did wrong: "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ This is conjoined to His saying "Then We will say to the angels," and the report of this statement came after the report of the dialogue that takes place between the angels and the polytheists on that day, to show that they deserve this severe judgment. However, it functions as if it were an object governed by His saying "none of you will have power to benefit or harm another."

The word *dhawq* (tasting) is a metaphor for sensation in general, and its choice over the literal sense is due to the commonness of its usage.

Describing the Fire with "which you used to deny" within the relative clause indicates their error and their regret.

Here the denial has been linked to the Fire itself, so the relative pronoun appropriate to it was used, and it was not linked to the punishment, as in the verse of Surat al-Sajdah, where it was said to them: ﴿Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny﴾ (al-Sajdah: 20). This is because the statement reported here is God Most High's statement and His judgment, and He had already brought them to Hell and they witnessed it, as He said earlier ﴿And they will conceal their regret when they see the punishment﴾ (Saba': 33). For what is seen is that by which the punishment comes. As for the statement reported in Surat al-Sajdah, it is the statement of the angels of punishment, as is evident from His saying ﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it, and it will be said to them: Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny﴾ (al-Sajdah: 20).

The fronting of the prepositional phrase ("of the Fire") is for emphasis and attention, placed before the closing word of the verse (*fasila*, the rhyme-end).

Page 226

This is a shift from narrating their disbelief, arrogance, self-admiration, and denial of the foundations of the religion, to narrating their denial of the Messenger ﷺ. He followed this with their denial of the Book and of the religion he brought, so it serves as a summary (*fadhlaka*, a concluding recapitulation) of what came before concerning their disbelief.

The clause "*idha tutla*" ("when it is recited") is coordinated with the clause ﴿wa-yawma nahshuruhum jami'an﴾ [al-An'am: 22], as a coordination of one narrative with another narrative (*'atf al-qissa 'ala al-qissa*). The pronoun in "*'alayhim*" ("upon them") refers to "those who disbelieved," who are the polytheists of Makkah.

Mentioning their denial of the Messenger ﷺ, restricted to the time when the clear signs of God are being recited to them, is a expression of astonishment at their audacity, since they denied him at the very time when they should most have believed him, because that is the moment when the proof of his truthfulness becomes manifest to every discerning intellect.

Because of the emphasis on this circumstantial phrase and on the astonishment regarding what it governs, the adverbial phrase is placed before its verb, and this creates anticipation for the statement that follows, namely that it proceeds from slander and open disbelief.

The "clear signs" (*al-ayat al-bayyinat*) refers to the verses of the Qur'an. Describing them as "clear" is to make manifest that they come from God, because of their inimitability, which challenged them and which they could not match, and because of the clear proofs of the truthfulness of what they call to that their meanings contain. Thus they are preserved by clarity, in both their wording and their meanings.

The agent of the recitation is omitted because it is evident that it is the Messenger ﷺ, since he is the reciter of God's signs. Therefore the reference in their words ﴿ma hadha illa rajulun yuridu an yasuddakum﴾ ("This is none but a man who wishes to turn you away") is to the Messenger ﷺ. They referred to him by a demonstrative rather than by name, to indicate that he was present in the assembly of recitation, and this is part of the completeness of their audacity. The Prophet ﷺ used to recite the Qur'an to them in their gatherings, as is reported in the hadith of his reciting Surah Fussilat to 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, and his reciting the Qur'an to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul in Madinah in the incident in which the Muslims and the polytheists quarrelled.

They began by attacking the reciter, because he is the target at which they aimed. They attributed to him the intention of turning them away from the religion of their fathers, with the aim of stirring some of them to zealous anger against others. This is because they regarded their fathers as the people of sound judgment in what they thought and as the rightly guided in what they did, so they saw nothing but truth and did nothing but what was correct and wise. Therefore it follows inevitably that whoever wishes to turn them away from it is attempting falsehood and is lying in his statement, since truth conforms to reality, and so declaring what they hold to be true to be false is a statement not conforming to reality, which is lying.

The verb "*kana*" ("was") in their words ﴿'amma kana ya'budu aba'ukum﴾ ("from what your fathers used to worship") indicates that they meant that this worship is ancient and established. In this there is an incitement of their people's hearts and a kindling of their breasts, so that they would unite against the Messenger ﷺ and cling more firmly to their religion. They also restricted the Messenger ﷺ, peace be upon him, to the attribute of intending to turn them away, a restriction by relation (*qasr idafi*), meaning: "he is only a man who is truthful, but he is not a messenger."

They followed the description of the reciter with a description of what is recited as a lie fabricated (*muftara*). The repetition of the verb of saying is a established repetition, to emphasise each of the two strange statements, in order to make them repulsive in the minds of the listeners. Thus the clause ﴿wa-qalu ma hadha illa ifk﴾ ("And they said: This is none but a lie") is coordinated with the clause ﴿qalu ma hadha illa rajulun yuridu an yasuddakum﴾, and the two verbs share the same temporal setting.

The second reference, to the Qur'an, is contained in "*tutla*" (is recited), since it is the only thing that can be meant by it.

"*Ifk*" means lie. Its description as "fabricated" (*muftara*) may be directed either to attributing it to God, the Exalted, or it may mean that the thing itself is a lie, and they added to this by making it something invented by the Prophet ﷺ, not preceded by any precedent.

So its being a lie refers to all that is in the Qur'an, and its being fabricated they attribute to its contents of

Page 227

the stories of the earlier peoples. This statement is part of their slander, because they often say: "tales of the ancients" (*asatir al-awwalin*). Therefore "*muftara*" is not an emphasis of "*ifk*."

Then their denial that embraces everything the Messenger ﷺ brought, whether revelation that is recited, or a call to monotheism and other things, or argument for it, or a miracle, is narrated by their words ﴿in hadha illa sihrun mubin﴾ ("This is none but evident magic"). This third statement encompasses what preceded it and other things, so the narration of this statement of theirs serves in place of a concluding summary (*tadhyil*). The speakers are named explicitly, rather than by implicit reference to what came before, by saying ﴿wa-qala alladhina kafaru li-l-haqqi lamma ja'ahum﴾ ("And those who disbelieved said of the truth when it came to them"), and it does not say "and they said of the truth when it came to them," to indicate that disbelief is what prompted this statement of theirs.

The referent was made explicit before the demonstrative in their words ﴿li-l-haqqi lamma ja'ahum in hadha illa sihrun mubin﴾, because there is no indication of it in the preceding speech. That is, when there was shown to them what is true, such as proof of monotheism, or information about the unseen, or the resurrection, they said: "This is none but evident magic." So what is meant by "the truth" is something more general than the verses of the Qur'an, because magic has two methods. One is the enchantment of words whose meanings are not understood, which magicians invent to make people imagine that there is conversation with the jinn in them, so that they can enable them to do what they want and thereby terrify them. The second is actions that have hidden causes concealed by tricks and sleight of hand, through which they make people imagine that these are the result of the jinn granting them power over hidden things. When they hear the Qur'an, they attach it to the first method, and when they see miracles, they attach them to the second, as the woman who witnessed the miracle of the multiplication of water during some of the expeditions of the Prophet ﷺ said to her people: "I have come from the greatest of the people in magic, or he is a prophet, as they claim." The meaning of "*mubin*" (evident) is that it appears from it that it is magic, so its clarity is from itself, meaning that whoever hears it knows that it is magic.

The clause ﴿wa-qala alladhina kafaru﴾ ("And those who disbelieved said") is coordinated with the clause "*wa-idha tutla*" ("and when it is recited").

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 44:

﴿And We did not give them any books which they study, nor did We send to them before you any warner.﴾ The waw is for the circumstantial clause (wa li-l-hal), and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to the pronoun in His saying ﴿They said: This is nothing but a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship﴾ [Saba': 43], and so on,

to ridicule their ignorance and to express wonder at their state in two respects.

The first: they did not realize the advantage that comes to them by the coming of the truth to them, since Allah had prepared them through it to be among the nations possessing a Book, and at the beginning of a state that brings them to the level of knowledge, for no book from Allah nor messenger from Him had previously come to them. So the meaning of the verse would be: how then did they reject following the Messenger and receiving the Qur'an, when they should rather have been glad of that? This meaning is suited to His saying "which they study," that is, they were not people of study, so it was fitting that what came to them of the truth should delight them.

The second: they were not upon guidance nor a religion attributed to Allah the Exalted, such that their adherence to it and their fear of falling into error should, if they neglected it, lead them to hesitate about the truth that came to them and the truthfulness of the Messenger who came to them with it. Thus there would be for them, in turning away from both, some measure of excuse. The meaning, then, is: wonder at their rejecting the truth when nothing prevents them. The phrase ﴿And We did not give them any books﴾ etc. is therefore not to be understood as coordinated (ʿatf) nor as a report (ikhbar), because its content is known and the purpose does not depend on informing about it. Rather, as a circumstantial clause (hal), it conveys wonder and ridicule. Upon this meaning the commentators have proceeded.

Al-Dirasah (dirasah): reading with deliberation and comprehension. It has already been discussed at His saying the Exalted ﴿and what you used to study﴾ [Al 'Imran: 79] in Al 'Imran.

The giving of the Books was not restricted by a qualifier as the sending was restricted by His saying "before you," because the giving (ita') is enabling someone to possess a thing, and they were not enabled with the Qur'an. By contrast, the sending of a warner is accomplished whether they accepted him or turned away from him.

As for one who inclines to the view that the verse's meaning compares their state with the state of the People of the Book, that is a weak course, because it leads to giving excuses to the People of the Book in their clinging with the molars to their religion. Moreover, during the period of the revelation's descent in Makkah there was no connection of the Islamic call with the People of the Book; the Prophet (ﷺ) called them in Madinah. Also, the restriction by "before you" would have no particular benefit, as you have learned. There are other interpretations, far more remote and much further from the intended meaning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 45:

Page 229
﴿And those before them denied, and they had not attained a tenth of what We had given them, yet they denied My messengers. So how was My rejection?﴾ This is a consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) and a threat to those who denied him. The place of the consolation in it is His saying: "And those before them denied," and the place of the threat is the rest of the verse. The consolation lies in the fact that he has a model in the earlier messengers, and the threat lies in reminding them of the earlier nations who denied their messengers, and how Allah punished them for that, although they were stronger than the Quraysh and more formidable in might than them. This is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then We destroyed those who were mightier than them in strength﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 8].

The object of "denied" (kadhdhaba) is omitted, indicated by what follows it, i.e., they denied the messengers, which is indicated by His saying (﴿so they denied My messengers﴾).

The pronoun in "balaghu" (they attained) refers to those before them, and the object pronoun in "ataynahum" (We had given them) refers to those who disbelieved in His saying ﴿And those who disbelieved said of the truth when it came to them, "This is nothing but obvious magic"﴾ [Saba: 43]. The context requires that every pronoun return to its referent, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Most of them believed not in them﴾ [Saba: 41].

Al-mi'shar (a tenth) means one tenth, the tenth part, like al-mirba' (a quarter), which was set aside for the commander of a battalion from the spoils of the army in the pre-Islamic period.

Two other possibilities were mentioned for the return of the two pronouns in His saying ﴿and they had not attained a tenth of what We had given them﴾, but the context of the verse does not agree with them.

The clause "﴿and they had not attained a tenth of what We had given them﴾" is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD), and the insertion with it serves as a preparation for the threat and a bringing it closer, by the fact that the punishment of these people is easier than the punishment of those before them, according to common human understanding, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And He it is who originates creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27].

The fa' (so) in His saying "fakadhdhabu rusuli" (so they denied My messengers) is for sequence (tafri') upon His saying "wa kadhdhaba alladhina min qablihim" (and those before them denied), on the basis that what is made consequent is ﴿fa-kayfa kana nakir﴾ (so how was My rejection). Accordingly, the clause "fakadhdhabu rusuli" serves as an emphasis of the clause ﴿wa kadhdhaba alladhina min qablihim﴾. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, so they denied Our servant﴾ [al-Qamar: 9] in Surat al-Qamar.

Page 230
As for the second fa' in His saying ﴿fa-kayfa kana nakir﴾, it is a verbal emphasis of the fa' in His saying "fakadhdhabu rusuli."

And His saying ﴿fa-kayfa kana nakir﴾ is consequent upon His saying ﴿wa kadhdhaba alladhina min qablihim﴾.

"Kayfa" is an interrogative about the state, and it is used here in affirmation and consequence, like al-Hajjaj's saying to al-'Udayl ibn al-Farkh, "So how did you see that God made Him more able over you?", meaning, made me able over you, in the story of his flight.

So the two clauses ﴿fakadhdhabu rusuli fa-kayfa kana nakir﴾ are, in effect, a single clause consequent upon the clause ﴿wa kadhdhaba alladhina min qablihim﴾. The implied meaning is: "And those before them denied, so how was My rejection upon their denial of the messengers?" But since the clause ﴿wa kadhdhaba alladhina min qablihim﴾ was intended primarily as a consolation to the Messenger, it was restricted to that purpose, out of concern for that aim and as Allah's support for His messenger (ﷺ). Then the lesson of denial as the cause of punishment was specified by a clause devoted to it, to magnify the denial. This is one of the situations of elaboration (iTnab). It so happened that the content of the two clauses was unified, as the unity of cause for two effects or of reason for two results, like the reason for theft being amputation and liability. The structure was built on this elegant method to avoid the burden of repeating the clause plainly. So the second was made consequent upon the first, the object of "kadhdhaba" was made explicit in it, and upon it was built the reproachful interrogative of affirmation. Alternatively, the specific denial is made consequent upon their general habitual denial, according to the second interpretation of the meaning of "﴿wa kadhdhaba alladhina min qablihim﴾" as mentioned earlier. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, so they denied Our servant and said, "He is possessed," and he was driven off﴾ [al-Qamar: 9].

Al-tankir (rejection) is a term for denunciation, which is regarding a thing as disapproved, i.e., hateful. It is used here metaphorically (kinayah) for anger and the imposition of punishment upon those who came with that disapproved thing, so it is a symbolic metonymy (kinayah ramziyyah).

The meaning: "So how was My punishment upon them for what they brought, which I disapproved of?", i.e., it was a severe punishment in accordance with Our rejection of their denial.

"Nakir" is with a kasra on the ra' and is in construct with the first-person ya' (my). The ya' is elided for lightness, with its presence indicated by the kasra remaining at the end of the word, and to match the fasila (verse-ending) and its sister. It is written in the Mushaf without a ya', and it is pronounced in pause with a sukun.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 46:

[Page 231]
﴿Say: "I admonish you with one thing: that you stand up for God, in pairs and singly, and then reflect: there is no madness in your companion. He is only a warner to you before a severe punishment."﴾
He opened with the command to speak here and in the four sentences after it, for the sake of emphasis on what they contain. This is a resumption (isti'naf) for the transition from narrating the state of the disbelief of the polytheists, and what intervened in that of refutation, argument, consolation, threat, and describing their aversion and obstinacy, to calling them to fairness. So by contemplating the realities, their error in what they committed of harshness in receiving the call of Islam and in what they attached to it and to the one who called to it would become clear to them. They were guided to the manner of considering their situation and being alone with themselves to hold themselves accountable for their conduct, as a thorough proof for them and an excuse for them in the dispute: ﴿So that whoever perishes might perish upon clear proof, and whoever lives might live upon clear proof﴾ [al-Anfal: 42].

For this reason the construction of restriction with (innama) was brought in, meaning: I admonish you only with one thing, folding up the carpet of debate and sending down the essence of the past disputes, and bringing closer the gap of disagreement between us and you.

It is a restriction relative to what is other than it, meaning: not with other detailed admonitions. That is, if you have multiplied the proofs and grown weary of the refutations and attacks, then I shorten the argument into one word. They used to complain about the Qur'an to Abu Talib: "Will your nephew not stop insulting our gods and our fathers?" This is like how the debater or disputant says, after laying out the evidence: "The summary or conclusion is such-and-such."

In this call he has taken the approach of bringing the paths of reflection close to them by abbreviating it, so it was described as one matter, lest they frown upon engaging in the reflection which they had resolved to reject. So they were informed that this does not burden them with effort nor waste time for them, so let them reflect on it briefly and then settle their matter. The speech is in the tongue of the Prophet ﷺ, whom God commanded to address them with it.

Admonition (wa'z): speech containing warning against what is disliked and encouragement toward its opposite. It was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything an admonition and a detailed explanation of everything﴾ [al-A'raf: 145] in Surat al-A'raf, and His saying "God admonishes you" in Surat al-Nur.

[Page 232]
"One" (wahida) is an adjective of an omitted noun which the context indicates and which the listener supplies, such as: "with one quality," or "with one matter," or "with one word."
The purpose of this description is to minimize it, bringing it close to understanding, abbreviating the reasoning, condensing the composition of speech, and luring down the bird of their aversion and turning away. This "one" is constructed by His saying ﴿that you stand up for God, in pairs and singly﴾ to the end. So the verbal noun formed from "an" and the verb is in the position of an apposition (badal) to "one," or say it is an explanatory apposition (atf al-bayan), for the explanatory apposition is the matching badal. The expressions for it differed among the earlier scholars, so do not delve into trying to distinguish between them as they delved.

The standing in His saying "that you stand up" is intended in its figurative meaning, which is readiness for action and striving in it, as in His saying ﴿and that you stand up for orphans with justice﴾ [al-Nisa': 127].

The lam is for causation, meaning: for the sake of God and for His own essence, that is, making your action for God, not for pleasing a companion or a clan. This is the opposite of His saying ﴿And he said: "You have only taken, apart from God, idols out of affection between you"﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25]. Or for the sake of knowing God and contemplating His attributes.

The word mathna is formed by changing the phrase "ithnayn ithnayn" (two by two) by repeating the word "ithnayn," a repetition which conveys the meaning of arranging multiple things by making each group counted by two arranged in the manner of its number.

The word furada is formed by changing the phrase "fardan fardan" (one by one), a repetition which likewise conveys the meaning of arrangement. Likewise all the number words up to nine or ten; and among them is His saying ﴿Then marry what is good for you of women, two, three, or four﴾ [al-Nisa': 3], which was mentioned in Surat al-Nisa'.

Mathna and furada are in the accusative as circumstantial accusatives (hal) from the pronoun in "taqumu," meaning: that you be in standing in these two states. So it is possible that the meaning is: that you stand for the right of God and its manifestation in whatever state, whether in gathering or in solitude, so "mathna" is a metaphor for multiplicity, using the sense of duality for repetition, because duality is the first of repetition; so repetition was made a necessary consequence of duality by claim, as in His saying ﴿Then return the gaze twice; your sight will return to you dazed while it is weary﴾ [al-Mulk: 4], for the sight does not return dazed from repeating a single glance, but rather what is meant is repeating the looking. From this is their saying: "labbayka wa sa'daydak" and "dawalayk."

It is also possible that the meaning is: that you stand for the right of God, with one of you seeking help from a companion, or alone by himself, for among the people of reflection there are those whom study with others energizes more than solitude does, and among them are those whose state is the opposite. Therefore it is restricted to "mathna" and "furada," because what exceeds that is not a necessity. He placed "mathna" first because seeking help is more aiding to understanding. So the intended meaning is removing the obstacles to reaching the truth through sound reflection, which is not confused by a possessor of desire or doubt, and in which the reflector does not fear ridicule or reputation. For when crowds gather, their gathering is never free of one with desire, one with doubt, one with deceit, and one with interest, and these, with the corruption their intentions necessarily imply, are accompanied by audacity that leaves in them no restraint from falsehood, no barrier against fabricating and distorting statements, intentionally or by error, and no shame to refine their sharpness in dispute and harm, then they spread rumors and the deeds of the base.

So for safety from these obstacles and escape from those calamities that block the path of truth, "mathna" and "furada" were mentioned here, for when a person is alone with himself in contemplation, he does not accept for himself anything but sincere advice; and when he is the second of two, he chooses as his second the closest of his companions to him and the nearest in opinion, so each of the two is safe from the deceit of the other.

The particle (thumma) indicates a difference in rank, because reflecting on the state of the Prophet ﷺ is more important for reforming the state of those addressed who turn away from his call, unlike standing for God, for they do not refuse it.

Reflection (tafakkur): exerting thought, which is knowledge; it was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿Will you not reflect?﴾ [al-An'am: 50] in Surat al-An'am.

His saying ﴿there is no madness in your companion﴾ is a negation that suspends the verb "tatafakkaru" from acting because of the negating particle.

The meaning: then you should know the negation of madness from your companion, that is, you should know the content of this.

So the clause ﴿there is no madness in your companion﴾ is the object of "tatafakkaru," and whoever stops at "tatafakkaru" has not mastered reflection.

By "companion" is meant the one who associates with you generally, whether in agreement or opposition, and it is a metaphor for insight into his nature, like al-Hajjaj's saying in his sermon to the Kharijites: "Were you not my companions in al-Ahwaz when you intended treachery and concealed disbelief?" meaning: your intentions are not hidden from me. It was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿Did they not reflect on what there is in their companion of madness?﴾ [al-A'raf: 184] in Surat al-A'raf.
The expression "your companion" is an explicit noun in place of the pronoun, since the expected form would be "there is no madness in me," because the speech is proceeding on the tongue of the Messenger ﷺ as was mentioned just before.

Its benefit is to draw attention to the fact that his state is known to them and not obscure to them, due to the intensity of his association with them, an association that leaves no room for ignorance. They knew him and he grew up among them until he came to them with the truth. So this is like His saying: ﴿I have already lived among you a lifetime before it. Will you not reason?﴾ [Yunus: 16].

The restriction of the reflection sought to the absence of madness from the Prophet ﷺ is because the root of disbelief is attacking his prophethood, and when they attacked him they said: "a madman," and said: "a sorcerer," and said: "a liar." So he began in bringing them back to the truth by negating madness from him, until when they acknowledged that he was among the sane, attention turned to the fact that what he brought could only be brought by a sane person; and they had begun their fabrication by saying he was mad, as is mentioned in the Qur'an. God said: ﴿You are not, by the blessing of your Lord, a madman﴾ [al-Qalam: 2], in the second surah in order of revelation. And He said: ﴿And your companion is not a madman﴾ [al-Takwir: 22], in the seventh surah. This was what they persisted in, as He said: ﴿Then they turned away from him and said: "A taught, mad one"﴾ [al-Dukhan: 14], for the claim of madness was more widespread among the people of Makkah, because madness comes upon a person suddenly, so they found no pretext closer to acceptance than the claim that he had been seized by madness, as 'Ad said to Hud: ﴿We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾ [Hud: 54], and Thamud said to Salih: ﴿You were among us a hope before this﴾ [Hud: 62].

So their claim remained that he was a sorcerer, a soothsayer, a poet, and a liar, God forbid. As for sorcery and soothsaying, their negation was easy by negating their distinctive features. As for the negation of sorcery, it is clear, for it requires the effort of learning and long practice, and the Prophet ﷺ was among them, his affair not hidden from them. As for poetry, its trace is negated from the Qur'an, as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said. So there remained in the quiver of their attacks only their claim that he was a liar against God, and this is refuted by their saying "your companion," for they knew him for soundness of intellect, truthfulness, and trustworthiness in his youth and maturity. How, then, would he become a liar after that? As al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said:
"When you saw grey in his temples, you said: 'A poet.'"

[Page 235]
"And you said: 'A soothsayer,' and you said: 'A madman.' By God, he is none of those." And if he does not lie to people, how would he lie against God? As Heraclius said to Abu Sufyan when he asked him: "Did you ever find him lying before he said what he said?" Abu Sufyan said: "No." He said: "Then you know that he would not leave lying to people and lie against God."

Because of this gradual progression folded beneath the clause ﴿there is no madness in your companion﴾, he followed it by restricting his affair to warning of a imminent severe punishment, that is, to warning and true messengership.

Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: That is, such a claim is undertaken only by one of two men: either a madman who does not care about being exposed when asked for proof, or a sane man of sound intellect who does not claim such a thing unless he is confirmed by evidence. For a sane person does not benefit from claiming a thing for which there is no proof. You know that Muhammad ﷺ is not mad; rather you know him to be the most intelligent of Quraysh, the most steady of forbearance, the sharpest of mind, the most sound of judgment, the most truthful of speech, and the most gathered of what men are praised for. So he was the reason you should think well of him and give preference to truthfulness over falsehood regarding him. End.

So the restriction derived from ﴿He is only a warner to you﴾ is a restriction of a described subject to an attribute, a relative restriction, meaning: he is restricted to the attribute of warning; the attributes with which you have slandered him do not revolve around him.

The meaning of ﴿before a severe punishment﴾ is proximity, that is, the nearness of occurrence, which implies priority, i.e., before a punishment. It was mentioned earlier in this surah, and the intended punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 47:

﴿Say: Whatever reward I have asked of you, it is yours. My reward is only from Allah, and He is, over all things, Witness.﴾ This is a thorough addressing of the remnants of the doubts of denial, to refute them, whether among them are the claims they attached to, such as their saying: "He is a soothsayer (kahin), a poet, and a madman," or what they did not claim but which may occur to one of them, that they might allege he intends by this call some benefit for himself that would be a reward for him for teaching and guidance.

When they claimed that he was a sorcerer, or a poet, or a soothsayer, it followed from their claim that he would be seeking the prize of the poet and the gift (hulwan) of the soothsayer. So when those qualities were negated from him, no arrow of accusation remained in their quiver, except that they might allege that he seeks a reward for guidance. So it was said to them: ﴿Whatever reward I have asked of you, it is yours﴾, meaning: if you suppose that I benefit from you by what I call you to, then whatever reward there is for me from it, take it. This is a wonderful method of ironic metonymy (al-kinayah al-tahakkumiyyah) for his not benefiting from what he calls them to: by supposing it as though it were actual, then ordering upon it his abstention from it and the return of what has passed from him, so that thereby he arrives at his disassociation from it and from seeking it. It is therefore a symbolic metonymy, and they know that he did not ask them for a reward. ﴿Say: I do not ask you any reward for it, and I am not of those who pretend﴾ [Sad: 86] ﴿It is only a reminder to the worlds﴾ [Sad: 87]. Or: if I had asked you for a reward, then do not give it to me, and if you have given anything, then take it back. Thus by this condition, whose negation is certain, is alluded to the negation of his being one who seeks a reward from them, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. This is what he stated right after it in His saying ﴿My reward is only from Allah﴾. So the condition was couched in the past tense to indicate the negation of that in the past, so that its negation in the future is more fitting. Moreover, its occurrence within the context of a condition entails its negation in the future too. This runs in the manner of a challenge, for if they or any of them had knowledge that he sought a reward from them, they would have hastened at this challenge to confront him and demanded that he return it to them.

From this he moves on to specifying that what he calls them to does not benefit others besides them with salvation from punishment. The disavowal of his wanting from them any reward or seeking any benefit has been repeated in the Qur'an, because the absence of that, despite the hardship he meets in the call, is evidence that he is commanded to it by Allah and does not seek any recompense from them.

"Ma" may be conditional, with "min ajr" as an explanation of the ambiguity of "ma", and the clause "fahuwa lakum" as the response of the condition. It may also be that "ma" is negative, and "min" serves to emphasize the generality of the indefinite noun in negation, and the "fa" in His saying (﴿fahuwa lakum﴾) is a consequence of the negation of the reward, and the pronoun "huwa" refers to the Qur'an, understood from the context and from the preceding His saying ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾ [Saba: 43]. That is: this Qur'an is for your benefit, not for my benefit, because His saying ﴿Whatever reward I have asked of you﴾ indicates that there is no benefit for him in this call. The meaning of the verse is then similar to the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: I do not ask you any reward for it, and I am not of those who pretend﴾ [Sad: 86] ﴿It is only a reminder to the worlds﴾ [Sad: 87].

The word "ajr" has been mentioned earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿That he may reward you for having watered [the flock] for us﴾ [al-Qasas: 25] in Surat al-Qasas. The clause (﴿My reward is only from Allah﴾) is a resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), answering an implied question that the hearer might ask: how is it that he has no reward for what he undertook? So it is answered that his reward is guaranteed, which Allah has promised him, because he undertakes his act only seeking Allah's pleasure and obeying His command, so his reward is upon Him.

The particle "ʿala" (upon) indicates that it is a right of Allah, with regard to His true promise. Then He concluded this with Allah's testimony over his inner intention and his purpose, which is among the existents over which Allah is Witness and whose hidden matters He knows. So it is of the type of ﴿Say: Allah suffices as a witness between me and you﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43], that is, He is a witness to all of that.

"Ajr" (reward): a beneficial return upon an action, whether it is wealth or other than it.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read the yaʼ of "ajri" with a fatha (ajriya). Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with sukun, and both are two of the ways of the first-person yaʼ in the idafah.

Therefore, when argument and debate have reached their conclusion, it is fitting to move on to proclamation among them, with the truth made manifest, so that their disputation is dispensed with.

The verb "qul" (say) is repeated to express concern with what is being said, as we have indicated just above.

The emphasis (ta'kid) serves to affirm the reality of this report.

The expression of the Name of God by the word "Rabb" (Lord), and its attribution to the first person pronoun, indicates that the truth lies on His side, and that this is a confirmation from his Lord, for the Lord supports and strengthens His servant. Thus the lordship intended here is the lordship of patronage and special care, not absolute lordship, which encompasses all people.

The placing of the subject before the predicate verb indicates exclusivity rather than emphasis, because the emphasis of the sentence has already been achieved by the particle of emphasis. This exclusivity is in view of the meaning of "helper" contained in "yaqdhifu bi'l-haqq" (He casts the truth), meaning: He is the one who supports me, not you; so what will your reliance on your wealth, your children, and your strength benefit you?

The word "qadhf" means throwing something from the hand, and it has been applied, metaphorically, to the manifestation of the truth; the proclamation of the truth is likened to the throwing of a stone or the like. The meaning is: My Lord casts the truth against you.

Or it is a reference to His saying, ﴿Nay, We cast the truth against falsehood﴾ [al-Anbiya': 18]. In either case, it is an allusive threat and warning of God's victory of the believers over the polytheists.

The specification of the attribute ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾ among the divine attributes indicates that He knows the intentions, and that the one who speaks knows this; so whoever knows this does not dare to invent a falsehood against God by claiming that He sent him to you. The announcement of this attribute here resembles the use of a report for the implication of its benefit, which is knowledge of the reported ruling.

It is also possible that the meaning of (﴿yaqdhifu bi'l-haqq﴾) is "He sends down the revelation," i.e., upon whomever He wills of His servants, as in His saying, ﴿He sends down the Spirit by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾ [Ghafir: 15]. And His saying (﴿'Allam al-ghuyub﴾) would then indicate that He is most knowing of where He places His messages, because the polytheists used to say: "Why was not the angel sent down to us instead of Muhammad?"

"'Allam" is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., He is the Knower of the unseen; or as an adjective of the subject of "inna," either as a detached epithet, or in consideration of the position of the subject of "inna," since it has completed its predicate; for the rule of the attribute is, according to most grammarians, the rule of the conjunctive coordination, and this is the correct view. Al-Farra' said: raising this noun is the most common usage of the Arabs. Similar to this is the appositive in His saying, ﴿Indeed, that is the truth: the dispute of the people of the Fire﴾ [Sad: 64].

The majority read (al-ghuyub) with a damma on the ghayn. Abu Bakr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the ghayn, just as both forms occur for the bay in "buyut."

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 34, verse 49:

﴿Say, "The truth has come, and falsehood can neither originate nor restore."﴾ The verb "say" is repeated for emphasis on what is being said, as was mentioned just above.

The clause "The truth has come" (قُلْ جاءَ الحَقُّ) is a confirmation of the clause ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord casts the truth"﴾ [Saba': 48]. The truth has indeed come with the revelation of the Qur'an and the call of Islam. The phrase "﴿and falsehood can neither originate nor restore﴾" is conjoined to "﴿the truth has come﴾" because when the truth arrives, falsehood is dispersed from the place in which the truth has settled.

"Yubdi'u" (يُبْدِئُ) is the present tense of abda'a, which has a hamza at its beginning and a hamza at its end. The hamza at its beginning is for augmentation, like the hamza in ajā'a and asrā. Attributing origination and restoration to falsehood is either a rational metaphor (majāz 'aqlī) or a metaphor (isti'āra).

The meaning of "﴿falsehood can neither originate nor restore﴾" is a metonymy (kināya) for its annihilation and disappearance, which is what is expressed by "zuhūq" (vanishing) in the Almighty's words ﴿Indeed, falsehood was ever bound to vanish﴾ [al-Isrā': 81] in Surah al-Isrā'. This is because an existing thing that has effects either has its effects renewed or repeated. If it has neither origination nor restoration, then it is non-existent. Its root is taken from the activity of a living being, so "what originates and what restores" is a metonymy for destruction, as 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras said:

"He has become poorer than his people, 'Ubayd; today he neither begins nor returns."

He means himself.

They also say: "So-and-so neither begins nor returns," meaning he does not speak with a beginning or a return, that is, he does not improvise speech and does not answer another's speech. The verb "bada'a" (with a hamza at its beginning) and the verb "a'āda" are most often used together, in affirmation or negation. The Almighty's words ﴿Have they not seen how Allah originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ [al-'Ankabūt: 19] have already been discussed in Surah al-'Ankabūt.

[Page 239]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 34, verse 50:

﴿Say: If I go astray, I go astray only to my own detriment; and if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me. Indeed, He is All-Hearing, Near.﴾ When the discussion of truth and falsehood had come up, and they used to assume, from the totality of their statements, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was not truthful in his claim of prophethood from Allah, their statements required their claim that he was upon misguidance. The response to them was decisive in declaring that he was upon guidance, through His saying ﴿Say: The truth has come, and falsehood can neither originate nor restore﴾ [Saba': 49]. He then moved here to leaving off their disputation and leaving them to themselves, because returning to them yielded little benefit.

This is a particular session, folded up as the conclusion of a single gathering, so it does not necessitate that he would continue in leaving off their disputation, because the reality contradicts that. The Qur'an was revealed after that for a long time, comprising their call, their warning and their admonition.

The construction of restriction (qasr) in His saying ﴿then I only go astray to my own detriment﴾ is to restrict the supposed misguidance: that is, to my own self, not upon you, because they were attempting to make him desist from what he called them to, and they did not limit themselves to their aversion.

The transitive use of (adalla) with the particle (ʿalā, "upon") includes a metaphor by implicit comparison (istiʿāra makniyya), as he likened misguidance to a burden upon him, so he transitivized it with the particle commonly used for things one is compelled to and that are unpleasant, unlike (lām, "for"). Mentioning the particle of elevation (istiʿlāʾ) is an imaginative element (takhyīl) for the implicit metaphor. And it is not said that (uḍill, "I go astray") is here construed with the meaning of (ajnī, "to bear the consequence of"), because "ḍalaltu" (I went astray), which is the supposed conditional verb, is not construed with the meaning of another verb.

As for His saying ﴿And if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me﴾, it serves as a safeguard against his situation being limited to the supposition of his being a locus of misguidance, together with what it contains of acknowledging to Allah His blessing: that whatever good he attains is by the guidance of Allah, not from himself, because he would not have reached that while he was surrounded by an ignorant community, had Allah's guidance not come to him, as He, exalted is He, said ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit from Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor faith﴾ [al-Shura: 52].

The verb ﴿ihtadaytu﴾ ("I am guided"), which is the reflexive form (muṭāwiʿ) of "hudan" (guidance), was chosen on the side of guidance because of what it contains of an allusion to the fact that he has a guide, and He explained it by His saying ﴿by what my Lord reveals to me﴾, so that his thanks to Allah would be attained in summary and then in detail. And in His saying ﴿by what my Lord reveals to me﴾ there is an allusion that he is upon guidance, because he affirmed that a revelation from Allah comes to him.

It has been deduced that if the supposed misguidance were to occur, its cause would be from his own self, from the attribution of the verb "adalla" to the speaker's pronoun, and then from what follows it of restricting misguidance to occurrence from the speaker; and this is more intensely attached to him. The purpose of that statement is not to explain causation, but rather that the supposed misguidance should not extend to them, since they would follow him in what he was involved in. Such a thing was not employed on the side of supposing his guidance, because his guidance was what had actually occurred, and it encompassed him and others who followed him, since his guidance was bound up with his call of people to follow him. Also, because the purpose of the two conditionals differs, although it is known from the contrast that the cause of misguidance and of guidance differs in meaning, especially when he gave preference to the side of his guidance by His saying ﴿by what my Lord reveals to me﴾.

Moreover, the contrast between the two conditionals brings to the hearer's mind that misguidance comes from the enticement of the self, and that if it occurred it would be a crime of the self against him; and that guidance comes from Allah, and that it is a benefit He brought to him through His revelation.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, He is All-Hearing, Near﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyīl) for what the two preceding statements conveyed of the alternation in the attribution of guidance and misguidance: that is, Allah knows whether I am upon guidance or its opposite, and from this arises knowledge of contrast regarding the states of his opponents, because He is All-Hearing of what both parties say, and Near to what they conceal, so nothing is hidden from Him.

Here "near" (qarīb) is a kinaya (allusion) for knowledge and encompassment in it, so it is a metaphorical nearness. And this is an indirect allusion (taʿrīḍ) to threat.

**[Page 241]**

When the allusion to the threat came to them, from the necessary implication of the abandonment indicated by His words ﴿Say: If I go astray, I go astray only to my own loss; but if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me﴾ [Saba': 50], and since it is known that the one who goes astray deserves punishment, He followed their condition, when terror befalls them upon witnessing what they were threatened with.

The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) as a consolation to him, or to every addressee. The answer to ﴿Lo⁠ (law)﴾ is omitted for dread-inspiring effect. The implied meaning is: "You would see a dreadful matter."

The object of ﴿you see (tará)﴾ may be omitted, meaning "if you could see them," or "if you could see their punishment," and then ﴿when they are terrified﴾ is an adverbial clause of time modifying "you see." It may also be that ﴿when (idh)﴾ itself is the object, stripped of the adverbial sense, meaning "if you could see that time," that is, you would see what it contains.

*Fazaʿ* is sudden fear. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Ansar: "Indeed you are many at the time of fear and few at the time of greed." This terror at the Resurrection indicates that they had not prepared, for this time, the means of deliverance from its terror.

*Akhdh* (seizing) literally means taking hold, but here it is a metaphor for overpowering and gaining control over them, like His words ﴿So He seized them with a overwhelming seizure﴾ [al-Haqqah: 10]. The meaning is: they were held and seized in order to meet the punishment prepared for them.

The clause ﴿there is no escape (fawt)﴾ is a parenthetical clause placed between the conjoined clauses. *Fawt* is slipping away and escaping punishment. Ruwaysh al-Ta'i said:

If you commit sins, then a group of your own comes to me,
their excuse will not be an escape from the sin they committed.

That is: if you sin and then a group of you come with excuses, that will not avert your recompense for your sin.

In *al-Kashshaf*: "﴿law⁠ (if)﴾, ﴿idh (when)﴾, and the verbs ﴿they were terrified﴾, ﴿they were seized﴾, and ﴿there was placed between them﴾ are all in the past tense, but what is meant is the future, because what God will do in the future is as if it had already happened and existed, for its certainty." End of quotation. The verb ﴿and they said﴾ is added to these.

The "near place" is the place of gathering, meaning they were seized from it toward the Fire. By mentioning *min* (from) of origin, He dispensed with mentioning the end point, because every starting point has an end. The nearness of the place means that it is close to Hell, such that they will find no respite to delay the punishment.

Between the two words "near" (qarīb) here and the one in His words ﴿Indeed He is Hearing, Near﴾ [Saba': 50], there is nothing resembling a monotony of rhyme, since the two words differ in actual and metaphorical sense. Thus, in combining them, there arises the embellishment of complete paronomasia (*jinās tāmm*).

﴿And they said⁠﴾ is conjoined to ﴿they were seized⁠﴾, meaning: they will say at that time, "We believe in Him."

The pronoun in ﴿in Him⁠ (bihi)﴾ refers either to the threat, or to the Day of Resurrection, or to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to the Qur'an, if the pronoun is quoted from their own speech, since everything that can be a referent of the pronoun is witnessed by them and by the angels. They were vague about what belief is directed toward, because the time had become too narrow for them, so they hastened to it with what they supposed would save them from punishment. If the pronoun is part of the narration (from God), then it refers to the Truth in His words ﴿Say: My Lord hurls the truth﴾ [Saba': 48], because the Truth includes all of that.

**[Page 242]**

Then the speech digressed, due to their saying ﴿We believe in Him⁠﴾, to their squandering of the time of faith, through the clause ﴿And how can they reach (al-tanāwush) from a distant place?⁠﴾ through to its end.

*Annā* here is an interrogative about place, used in the sense of denial.

*Al-tanāwush* was read by the majority with a *waw* vowelled with *ḍamma* after the *alif*. It means easy or light reaching, and its most common use is for camels drinking lightly from a pool or the like. Ghaylān ibn Ḥurayth said:

They spent the night reaching for the pool with light sips from above,
sips by which the ends of the wilderness are cut.

He describes his journey: they take the water from its top and their muzzles do not plunge into it.

The clause ﴿And how can they reach (al-tanāwush) from a distant place?⁠﴾ is a figurative composition (*tamthīl murakkab*), indicating the likening of their condition, when they neglected the means of deliverance while able to take them, at the time the Prophet (ﷺ) was calling them, urging them, and warning them, and God had given them a lifespan in which whoever would take heed could take heed. Then they came seeking deliverance after its time had passed, in a condition like one who wants to reach it while being in a place far from what he must grasp.

This figure can also be taken in parts, by likening the striving to what is attained quickly, the "reaching," and likening the failure to attain the goal to the distant place, like the pool.

Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Abū Bakr (from ʿĀṣim), and Khalaf read it with a hamza in place of the *waw*. Al-Zajjāj said: this is from replacing a *waw* with a *ḍamma* by a hamza, for the purpose of lightening the pronunciation of the *ḍamma*, like His words ﴿their time was appointed (uqqitat)⁠﴾ [al-Mursalāt: 11], and the saying "ujūh," the plural of "wajh" (face). Abū Ḥayyān examined this. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj also said: it is from *nā'asha* with a hamza, meaning to be slow and late in an action. From it is the saying of Nahshal ibn Ḥarīy al-Nahshalī:

He wished, too late, that he had obeyed me,
but after the matters came to pass, matters had happened.

That is: he wished belatedly.

Al-Maʿarrī in *Risālat al-Ghufrān* explained *nasīshan* as meaning "after what has passed." On both interpretations, the meaning of *tanāwush* is a description of their saying "We believe in Him" as a faith whose time was delayed or whose time had passed.

**[Page 243]**

Between "a near place" and "a distant place" there is the embellishment of antithesis (*ṭibāq*).

The clause ﴿And they had disbelieved in Him before⁠﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: how can they say "We believe in Him" at the time of missing out, when in fact they disbelieved in Him before, at the time of ability? It is like His words ﴿And they were being called to prostration while they were sound⁠﴾ [al-Qalam: 43].

﴿And they hurl⁠﴾ is conjoined to "they disbelieved," so it is a second circumstantial clause. The implied meaning is: "and they used to hurl at the unseen." The choice of the present tense is to narrate the state, like His words ﴿and he builds the ark⁠﴾ [Hud: 38].

*Qadhf* is throwing with the hand from a distance. Here it is used metaphorically for speaking without deliberation or evidence, meaning they speak about matters of the Hereafter that lie beyond reasoning, with no knowledge of them, since they denied the Resurrection and recompense, and said to their associates: "They are our intercessors with God."

You may also take ﴿they hurl at the unseen from a distant place⁠﴾ as a figurative image, like the one in His words ﴿And how can they reach (al-tanāwush) from a distant place?⁠﴾, where they are likened to someone who throws something while being absent from it, not seeing it, so he never hits it at all.

The object of ﴿they hurl⁠﴾ is omitted because the verb ﴿And they had disbelieved in Him before⁠﴾ indicates it, meaning: they hurl things of disbelief, casting them at random.

*Al-ghayb* is what is hidden. The *bāʾ* is for accompaniment, and the phrase it introduces is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "they hurl," meaning: they hurl while being absent from what is hurled, from a distant place.

﴿A distant place⁠﴾ here is used in its literal sense, meaning the world, which is a distant place from the Hereafter. There is no need to use it metaphorically for what is not seen from it, because of the word "unseen (bil-ghayb)" as you have understood, so it is fixed in its literal sense, since that is the original meaning. For this reason, there is no resemblance to monotony between the word "distant" mentioned here and the one in His words ﴿And how can they reach (al-tanāwush) from a distant place?⁠﴾, since the two words differ between figurative and literal sense.

Between "a near place" and "a distant place" there is the embellishment of antithesis (*ṭibāq*).

The clause ﴿And they had disbelieved in Him before⁠﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: how can they say "We believe in Him" at the time of missing out, when in fact they disbelieved in Him before, at the time of ability? It is like His words ﴿And they were being called to prostration while they were sound⁠﴾ [al-Qalam: 43].

﴿And they hurl⁠﴾ is conjoined to "they disbelieved," so it is a second circumstantial clause. The implied meaning is: "and they used to hurl at the unseen." The choice of the present tense is to narrate the state, like His words ﴿and he builds the ark⁠﴾ [Hud: 38].

*Qadhf* is throwing with the hand from a distance. Here it is used metaphorically for speaking without deliberation or evidence, meaning they speak about matters of the Hereafter that lie beyond reasoning, with no knowledge of them, since they denied the Resurrection and recompense, and said to their associates: "They are our intercessors with God."

You may also take ﴿they hurl at the unseen from a distant place⁠﴾ as a figurative image, like the one in His words ﴿And how can they reach (al-tanāwush) from a distant place?⁠﴾, where they are likened to someone who throws something while being absent from it, not seeing it, so he never hits it at all.

The object of ﴿they hurl⁠﴾ is omitted because the verb ﴿And they had disbelieved in Him before⁠﴾ indicates it, meaning: they hurl things of disbelief, casting them at random.

*Al-ghayb* is what is hidden. The *bāʾ* is for accompaniment, and the phrase it introduces is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "they hurl," meaning: they hurl while being absent from what is hurled, from a distant place.

﴿A distant place⁠﴾ here is used in its literal sense, meaning the world, which is a distant place from the Hereafter. There is no need to use it metaphorically for what is not seen from it, because of the word "unseen (bil-ghayb)" as you have understood, so it is fixed in its literal sense, since that is the original meaning. For this reason, there is no resemblance to monotony between the word "distant" mentioned here and the one in His words ﴿And how can they reach (al-tanāwush) from a distant place?⁠﴾, since the two words differ between figurative and literal sense.

[Page 245]

﴿And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire, as was done with their like before. Indeed, they were in disquieting doubt.﴾

This is coordinated (ʿuṭifa) upon the verbal clauses similar to it, which are the clauses "﴿They will be terrified﴾ [Saba': 51]", "﴿And they will be seized﴾ [Saba': 51]", and "﴿And they will say﴾ [Saba': 52]". The meaning is: and the situation of their being thrust into the Fire, with a barrier between them and what they hoped for of salvation, by their saying "﴿We have believed in Him﴾ [Saba': 52]". What they desired is salvation from the punishment, or their return to the world. Other verses report that they wished for this, as in "﴿So they will say, 'Oh, if only we could be returned, and not deny the signs of our Lord, and be among the believers.'﴾ [al-An'am: 27]" and "﴿Our Lord, bring us out, and we will do righteous deeds other than what we used to do.﴾ [Fatir: 37]".

The comparison in His words "﴿as was done with their like before﴾" is a comparison of one barrier to another barrier, namely the barrier that came between some nations and respite when the punishment of this world descended upon them, such as Pharaoh and his people when he said "﴿I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believed, and I am of the Muslims.﴾ [Yunus: 90]". Likewise the people of Noah when they saw the Flood. No nation was struck by punishment without wishing for faith at that time, but it did not benefit them, except the people of Jonah.

The ashyaʿ (those alike) are those who resemble one another in their creed, even if they were earlier in time. The root meaning of mushayaʿa is following in action, alliance, and the like. Then it was applied here to mere similarity, by way of majāz mursal (metonymy in which a more general or related sense is used for a particular one), with the indication of His words "min qablu" (before), meaning: as was done with their like in the world before. As for the Day of Gathering, a barrier is placed between them and what they desire, and likewise their like at one and the same time.

The benefit of this comparison is to remind the living among them, who are the polytheists of Makkah, of what befell the nations before them, so that they may be certain that the way of God is one, and that their idols, which they supposed to be intercessors with God, will not benefit them.

The clause "﴿Indeed, they were in disquieting doubt﴾" is brought as a causal explanation (taʿlīl) of the clauses before it.

All of what you have heard was done to them because in their lives they were in doubt about that Day and about what had been described to them of its terrors.

Their state was described as doubt because they were doubting in some matters and certain in others. Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He, "﴿You said, 'We do not know what the Hour is; we only suppose a supposition, and we are not certain.'﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 32]". If doubt led to that punishment, then certainty is more deserving of it. The outcome of doubt and certainty in terms of absence (of faith) is one, since both result in the absence of belief in it and the absence of reflection on its proof.

[Page 246]

It is also permissible that the clause "﴿Indeed, they were in disquieting doubt﴾" is a resumptive clause of explanation (istiʾnāf bayānī), arising from a question raised by His words "﴿And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire﴾", as if a questioner asked: Were they hoping to obtain what they wished for? It is answered that they used to wish for that but doubted that it would be granted. So when a barrier was placed between them and it, despair overtook them, and despair after doubt is more effective in causing grief than despair that is rooted from the start.

Al-murīb is that which causes ribab (suspicion). Rayb means doubt, so describing doubt with it is describing it with something derived from its own root, to convey intensification, like the expressions "shiʿr shāʿir" (poetry of a poet) and "layl alyal" (a very dark night), or "layl dājin" (a dark night). Seeking any other explanation is strained.

[Page 247]

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Surat Fatir. It is called "Surat Fatir" in many copies of the Qur'an in the East and the West, and in many exegetical works. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari and in the Sunan of al-Tirmidhi, and in many copies of the Qur'an and exegetical works, it is called "Surat al-Malaʾika" (the Surah of the Angels) only. Al-Suyuti, the author of al-Itqan, mentioned both names.

The reason for calling it "Surat Fatir" is that this description occurs at the opening of the surah and does not occur at the beginning of any other surah. The reason for calling it "Surat al-Malaʾika" is that the attributes of the angels are mentioned at its beginning and not in any other surah.

It is a Meccan surah by consensus. Al-Alusi related from al-Tabarsi that al-Hasan excepted two verses: the verse "﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of God﴾ [Fatir: 29]" and the verse "﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants﴾ [Fatir: 32]". I have not seen this reported from anyone other than him.

This surah is the forty-third in the order of revelation of the surahs of the Qur'an. It was revealed after Surat al-Furqan and before Surat Maryam.

Its verses are counted as forty-six according to the count of the people of Madinah and Syria, and as forty-five according to the count of the people of Makkah and Kufa.

* * *

The purposes of this surah: This surah includes the affirmation of God's exclusive divinity (infirād bi-l-ilāhiyya). It therefore opens with what indicates that He deserves praise for what He originated of the creatures, and the origination of these indicates His exclusive divinity, Exalted is He.

[Page 248]

It also includes the affirmation of the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ in what he brought, and that the messengers before him brought the same. And the affirmation of the Resurrection and the Last Abode.

And reminding people of God's favor upon them through the blessing of origination and the blessing of sustenance; and that what the polytheists worship besides Him does not avail them anything, and those before them who worshipped them did not benefit them either.

And the strengthening of the Prophet ﷺ regarding what he encounters from his people; and the exposure of their intentions in turning away from following Islam, because they guarded their honor.

And warning them that there may befall them what befell the nations before them who denied.

And praise for those who received Islam with assent, and the opposite of the state of the deniers.

And reminding them that they used to wish that a messenger would be sent to them, but when a messenger came to them, they grew arrogant and disdainful.

And that they have no escape from the descent of punishment upon them, for they have witnessed the traces of the denying nations before them; and that they should not be deceived by God's giving them respite, for God does not break His promise.

And warning against the delusion of Satan, and reminding them of his enmity toward mankind.
